Season 3, Episode 50: “All In”

Dr. Evil had nearly finished speaking when Brian began exercising in his sleep.

At first, the doctor assumed it was dissent.

Brian sat on a folded cloth near the end of the submarine's bench. His little feet hung clear of the floor. Without the cloth, the table edge would have cut across his eyes; with it, he had a commanding view of everybody's wrists. His notebook rested against his stomach, and his bare head had tipped backward just enough to expose the expression of a man who believed unconsciousness was somebody else's administrative problem.

His knees opened.

Closed.

Opened again.

Dr. Evil stopped beside the table.

Brian's hips lifted off the cloth.

He made a strained, determined grunt.

Dutch lowered the stores list.

“Brian?”

Another thrust. Another breath forced through clenched teeth.

His knees kept working, out and in, with the defeated determination of a squid trying to escape an extremely small pair of trousers.

Clifford looked up.

“What's he lifting?”

“My opinion of leaving him ashore,” Dr. Evil said.

Brian's hands tightened around the notebook. His little heels rose another inch.

He sounded as though he had reached the final repetition of something a doctor would advise against on a form with no pictures.

Dutch leaned closer.

“He's asleep.”

Dr. Evil watched the knees close.

“Then his contribution has improved considerably.”

Brian grunted harder.

The doctor waited.

“Briefly.”

Clifford moved his cup farther from the bench.

“Does he do that?”

Dutch considered the question with the weary seriousness it deserved.

“He appears to.”

Brian's notebook slid sideways. Dr. Evil caught it before it fell, holding it between two fingers.

Brian's hands continued gripping the place where it had been.

“Remarkable,” the doctor said. “We have removed the work and retained the effort.”

Brian's knees opened again.

Clifford looked at Dutch.

Dutch looked back.

They both looked at Dr. Evil, who had just caught himself watching the entire movement like it might eventually produce a report.

“Wake him.”

Dutch touched Brian's shoulder.

The little man stopped. Opened his eyes. Looked at the three faces above him.

“What?”

Dr. Evil held out the notebook.

“Your training session.”

Brian took it.

“I was listening.”

“With your pelvis?”

Brian looked down at himself.

His legs were still apart.

He brought them together.

“I adjusted my position.”

Clifford nodded.

“Several times.”

Brian tucked the notebook under his arm.

“Busta Rhymes would understand active recovery.”

Dr. Evil looked beneath the bench.

“Was he spotting you?”

Brian slid off the bench. His feet found the rung beneath it; he lowered himself onto that, then down to the floor, where the table immediately erased everybody except their shoes.

“If the meeting is over, I'll retire.”

Dr. Evil looked down toward the voice.

“Take the gymnasium with you.”

Brian walked out beneath the table's projecting corner without needing to duck. It spoiled the dignity of an otherwise perfectly serviceable exit.

That was the night after the harbor interview. While TPP discovered that Brian could lose an argument without being conscious, the Sins camped inland on the road back toward the works.

They spent the following day walking the surviving route. Arthur's map saved them one useless climb and sent them around a washout that hadn't improved since the outward journey. They slept again before reaching the settlement below the furnace terraces on the third day.

The driver was there.

The foreman found him sitting outside a wheelwright's shed, his injured leg stretched onto a low crate. He'd lost a cart, kept the mule and acquired a limp he had no intention of discussing with the man who'd broken the upper road.

Kaze stopped in front of him.

“The one with the horns.”

The driver looked toward the foreman.

“Maul,” Arthur said. “Asked for your map.”

“Took it.”

Arthur held up the torn survey.

The man's expression changed.

“That's mine.”

Arthur let him examine it. Kept the wrapped weapon in his satchel, away from the conversation.

“Where'd he come from?” Kaze asked.

“Across the gap.”

“Before that.”

“I didn't see.”

Kaze waited.

The driver shifted his bad leg.

“My cart was going over. I was still in it. He was on the other side when it stopped falling.”

“He say why he wanted me?”

“Didn't know your name till I gave it.”

The wind moved through the broken wheel hanging beside the shed.

Kaze looked at him more carefully.

“You gave it.”

“He asked who caused the broken ground. I told him what people said.”

“Then?”

“Your tree friend spoke to him.”

The foreman looked down.

Nobody supplied a joke.

Kaze had followed a weapon toward the coast, then a driver's knowledge back inland. At the end of the route sat a man who had been frightened of a falling cart. He hadn't seen a doorway to another world. He hadn't received instructions from whoever Kaze had imagined might be waiting behind Maul.

He'd passed on a name.

Kaze's own name.

“That's it?”

The driver nodded.

“That's it.”

Kaze looked toward the terraces where K.K. had gone to see something interesting.

Arthur folded the torn survey carefully.

“Mind if I keep this till we're clear of the broken roads?”

The driver considered the paper, then Kaze.

“Keep it.”

Arthur nodded his thanks.

Kaze stayed beside the shed long enough for the driver to become nervous about the silence.

Then he stepped away.

“Didn't come looking for me,” he said to Arthur.

“Not till he heard of you.”

Kaze looked back down the road they'd spent two days following.

“Motherfucker.”

It wasn't directed at the driver.

They found a place to stop below the works, where a former cart barn had become a drinking house. The broad doors and high rafters accommodated workers, freight hands, Daynuh and a pit bull whose shoulders stood higher than some of the customers' heads.

The keeper asked them to keep the dog away from the cooking door.

Daynuh looked at Mahnuh.

“Hear that?”

The dog's nose remained pointed at the cooking door.

“Course you did.”

They settled in the yard beside the barn. Arthur went to speak with the foreman about the open road beyond the works. Daynuh lay back against their packs with Mahnuh beside him, tired from the walk and already wondering which of his friends was going to describe the next bad idea as a short trip.

Kaze looked through the open barn doors.

People were playing cards at a long table.

He watched a pile of silver move from one side to the other.

Then looked at Billy's great, impassive face.

“Tell Chris I got something better than looking for dead men's directions.”

Billy smiled.

“I am almost afraid to interrupt him.”

Inside, Chris had opened a battered box of mixed ironmongery in his stored salvage. Four good brass hinges lay beneath bent brackets and a handful of rusted fittings.

He lifted one. Worked it. Checked the pin.

“What?” he asked through the outward channel.

“Kaze has found recreation.”

Chris looked at the hinges.

Then at the exterior monitor, where the tavern's pantry door sagged visibly from its upper fastening.

“Bring these out first.”

Billy returned the small wrapped bundle to Arthur's waiting hands when Arthur came back. Then he yielded. Chris was outside now, Billy full-sized inside; Arthur gave the same four hinges to Chris.

Chris unwrapped the hinges with the solemnity of an outlaw about to liquidate part of his fucking personality.

The keeper examined the hinges.

“Four silver.”

“Six. And a beer for the big one when he comes in.”

“They're used.”

“So's your door. Yours is trying to become a window.”

The man worked the hinge twice.

“Six. One beer.”

Chris accepted the coins. Left the hinges. The keeper put the promised beer aside for Daynuh and began examining his newly acquired fittings.

Kaze watched the silver go into Chris's hand.

“There.”

Chris looked at him.

“I sold something.”

“You can get over it.”

“Give me a fucking minute.”

The night before, back aboard the submarine, Brian had left his sleeping place and entered the crew galley with his eyes barely open.

Dutch saw him from the passage.

“Brian?”

Brian didn't answer.

He picked up a folded cloth. Put it on a stool. Climbed onto the stool using the lower brace, hauled one knee over the edge and stood on the cloth so he could reach the preparation surface.

Dutch followed.

Brian took two pieces of bread from the covered board. His small body obscured the butter dish while he fussed over it, then he laid the bread precisely beside one another.

Then picked up a spoon.

Held it upright.

Put it down on the bread.

Dutch watched him consider the arrangement with closed eyes.

Dr. Evil appeared in the passage.

“What is he doing?”

“I believe he's asleep.”

“That narrows very little.”

Brian moved the spoon to the other piece of bread.

Clifford arrived behind the doctor, stopping where he could see without crowding Dutch against the stool.

“Making something?”

“A case,” Dr. Evil said.

Brian reached toward a cup beside the old coffee pot. It was a normal crewman's cup, meaning that against Brian it had the proportions of a modest village well.

He put both hands around it.

Lifted.

Dutch moved closer in case he fell.

Brian got the rim up to his face and leaned backward to compensate for the weight. A small amount of coffee came over the edge onto his shirt.

“Hot,” Brian said.

Dr. Evil looked at the pot.

Then at Dutch.

The coffee had been left since earlier that evening. No steam. The pot sat cold beside the unused heat.

Dutch touched the side of the cup as Brian lowered it.

“It isn't.”

Brian made an offended little sound, as though temperature were a management decision nobody had consulted him about.

He put the cup down.

Stood motionless.

Dr. Evil leaned slightly toward him.

“You have burned yourself with room temperature.”

Brian placed the second piece of bread over the spoon.

Pressed once.

Clifford considered the sandwich.

“Crunchy.”

Dutch took the spoon out before Brian could pick the food up.

Brian's hands continued with the task. He lifted the two pieces of bread together, held them against his chest and began turning toward the stool's edge.

Dutch put a hand beside his shoulder.

“Brian. Stay there.”

Brian opened his eyes fully.

Looked at the bread.

At the wet patch on his shirt.

At the three men watching him.

“What?”

Dr. Evil folded his hands behind his back.

“We were waiting for the menu.”

Brian set the bread down.

“I got up for something.”

“You appear to have found most of it.”

He looked at the coffee.

“Spilled.”

“Yes.”

“It was hot.”

Dutch held the cold cup where Brian could touch it.

Brian did.

A pause.

“Must've cooled.”

Dr. Evil turned toward Clifford.

“I want that kind of confidence in our pricing.”

Brian began climbing down. One foot found the brace. The other searched beneath the stool, briefly extending into the empty air like a tiny surveyor disputing a cliff.

Dutch kept his hand nearby until both feet reached the floor.

Brian straightened his damp shirt.

“I don't require supervision.”

Dr. Evil looked at the two pieces of bread.

“The cutlery disagrees.”

Brian left with as much dignity as a man could recover while walking beneath an audience's elbows.

Nobody applauded.

Clifford picked up the spoon.

“He buttered the handle.”

By the time Daynuh woke in the barn yard the following afternoon, Kaze had introduced Chris to the card table.

“You don't have to like your cards,” Kaze said. “You gotta decide how much they hate finding out.”

Chris sat opposite him. Three local players had made room: a cordmaker, a broad woman with a mason's scarred hands, and a freight clerk who'd been dealing.

The clerk finished explaining their five-card draw game. No opening ante on this table. A player could fold without paying; money went in when somebody actually bet.

Chris looked at the two coins Kaze had taken from his six.

“That's mine.”

“Bankroll.”

“That's a new word for mine.”

“You want the lesson or you wanna argue about hinges?” Kaze asked.

“You're teaching me.”

“Then listen.”

Kaze turned his cards facedown and pushed both coins forward.

“All in.”

The mason looked at him.

“You've barely looked.”

“You saw enough?”

“For that, yes.”

Chris examined his own cards.

Two fours. Nothing helping them.

He looked at Kaze's money.

Then pushed his own two coins in.

“Fuck it.”

Billy spoke through the banjo.

“A stirring school motto.”

The clerk folded. The cordmaker and the mason matched the bet.

“Draw?” the clerk asked.

Kaze tapped three cards. Chris gave back three. They received replacements.

The cordmaker looked over his hand at Chris.

“First money game?”

“First lesson.”

“He explain folding?”

Chris looked toward Kaze.

Kaze smiled.

“He can leave whenever he wants.”

Chris won that practice-sized pot with three fours and looked more offended by his success than he had by the sale of the hinges.

“Wait.”

The clerk pushed the eight coins toward him.

Chris counted them.

Then looked at his cards again.

“Oh, I see what the fucking problem is.”

Mahnuh appeared in the broad doorway.

He'd left the sleeping Daynuh, crossed the yard and followed the smell of cooked meat into the barn. Chris saw him before he reached the pantry door.

“Here. Come here.”

The dog turned toward the familiar voice.

Kaze looked down at him.

Then at Chris's winnings.

Chris's smile grew.

“We got room for one more?”

The clerk looked at the dog.

At Chris's eight coins.

“If somebody handles his cards.”

Mahnuh lowered himself beside the table. His great jowls settled near its edge. Chris placed a small piece of his own ordinary food beside the dog's paw, then put two of the coins in front of him.

“Watch.”

He pushed the coins toward the middle.

“All in.”

Mahnuh sniffed the spot where Chris's fingers had been.

“Not eating those.”

Kaze laughed.

Chris drew the coins back and waited until the dog looked toward his hand again.

Pushed them forward.

Gave him another little piece of food.

Billy leaned toward the actual interior feed.

“Christopher.”

“What?”

“Do you propose to teach the animal restraint?”

Chris looked at Kaze.

Kaze was already putting two borrowed coins in front of himself.

“No.”

“Splendid. I should hate to mistake the institution.”

Daynuh sat up outside.

His dog wasn't beside him.

He checked the yard, saw the broad pawprints leading out, and stood with the slow irritation of a man whose peaceful afternoon had acquired a familiar missing weight.

He looked through the loading arch next door. Checked the path around the barn. A worker pointed back toward the drinking house before Daynuh had finished asking.

“In there.”

Daynuh closed his eyes.

Again.

At least this place sold beer.

He went through the broad doors.

The keeper reached for the mug he'd set aside.

“Your friend paid for one.”

Daynuh accepted it.

Took one drink.

Then turned toward the sound of Chris's voice.

“All in.”

Kaze pushed his silver after it.

“All in.”

Mahnuh put his nose against the little pile in front of him and shoved.

Coins scattered into the betting space. One struck Kaze's wrist.

The dog looked at Chris.

Chris put a tiny piece of food beside his paw.

Daynuh stood with the beer halfway down from his mouth.

At the table sat Kaze, Chris, three locals and his fourteen-hundred-pound missing dog, who had apparently spent his disappearance entering finance.

“What the fuck is this?”

Chris looked up.

“Cards.”

Daynuh looked at Mahnuh's coins.

“I can see cards. Why's my dog got investments?”

Kaze leaned back, grinning.

“He's learning.”

“From who?”

Chris put a hand on the back of his own chair.

Daynuh followed the gesture.

Looked at Kaze.

Then back at Chris.

“You couldn't just pass him a fucking illness?”

The mason laughed into her cards.

Mahnuh's tail moved along the floor.

Daynuh pointed at him.

“Don't wag at me. I know you don't know what a full house is. You think that's a poultry shop before you get inside it.”

Chris covered his mouth.

Billy spoke from the banjo.

“His approach is admirably consistent.”

Daynuh looked down toward the instrument.

“You're watching this.”

“Intently.”

“And you're letting them.”

“I don't have a seat.”

“You got an opinion.”

“Several. None favors caution.”

Daynuh took another drink.

The clerk collected the betting coins into a clear little pile.

“We finishing the hand?”

“Yes,” Chris said.

“What he got?” Daynuh asked.

Chris looked at Mahnuh's cards, which he held separately from his own.

“Not telling you.”

“He ain't gonna tell me either. That's why I'm asking the man who gave him money.”

The clerk waited for the last player to decide. The cordmaker folded. The mason matched the three two-coin bets, then asked for one new card.

Chris made the dog's draw for him. A familiar hand moved food, coins moved after it, and a roomful of people had agreed that this constituted a player.

That is also how I understand most investment conferences, but the dog has better breath than the last keynote speaker I met.

They showed their cards.

Kaze had an ace, an eight and a small collection of missed opportunities.

Chris had two nines.

The mason had a pair of kings.

Mahnuh had three queens.

The clerk counted the eight-coin pot and pushed it toward the dog.

Mahnuh sniffed it.

Looked at Chris.

Chris gave him the promised bite.

Daynuh stared at the cards.

“You're fucking kidding.”

The mason put hers down.

“Wish I were.”

Kaze started laughing.

Not a little evil chuckle. He bent forward with one hand against the table, delighted by the woman's expression, the dog's complete disinterest in his own good fortune and Daynuh standing there holding a prepaid beer like it had become a fucking subpoena.

Chris laughed with him.

Mahnuh's tail swept a wider arc.

“You realize,” Daynuh said, “he thinks you're paying him to move his fucking nose.”

“He's up,” Chris said.

“He's a dog.”

“Both things can be true.”

The clerk reached for the cards.

Daynuh set his beer on a sound part of the table and leaned down toward Chris.

“I told you when you find him wandering, bring him to me.”

Chris looked toward Mahnuh.

“He's right here.”

“You brought him to a table.”

“You found him quicker.”

Daynuh straightened slowly.

“You hear yourself before it comes out, or you finding out with the rest of us?”

Billy's laughter came through the banjo.

Chris glanced at Kaze.

Kaze wasn't going to help him.

He was busy placing two of Mahnuh's winnings in front of himself.

“Another.”

Daynuh watched Chris take two of Mahnuh's eight winnings for Kaze, leaving six beside the dog. Chris still had four of his own coins behind his cards.

The clerk began dealing.

Daynuh moved his beer out of range of the dog's tail.

“You teach him to bluff, I'm telling him your duck's back in stock.”

Chris's smile faltered.

Mahnuh's ears turned at the familiar voices.

Kaze looked at his next hand.

Didn't bother changing his expression.

“All in.”

Chris looked at his own hand.

Two twos.

He pushed the four coins after Kaze's two.

“All in.”

Mahnuh saw the hands move.

His nose followed.

Six coins went into the middle, accompanied by a short, expectant breath and a string of drool the clerk carefully avoided with his sleeve.

Daynuh watched the three piles settle.

“You didn't even show him his fucking cards.”

Chris looked.

A king, a nine, a five, a three and a two.

“Wouldn't change much.”

“Then why are you—”

Daynuh stopped.

Looked at Kaze.

Kaze was biting the inside of his cheek to keep from laughing again.

“This is what you wanted.”

“Look at him.”

Mahnuh waited for the food.

Daynuh looked at his dog.

Then at the pot.

Then at the three people who'd independently decided to keep playing against this arrangement.

“Well. At least you're not making anybody be here.”

“I can stop,” the cordmaker said.

He put his cards down.

“Watch.”

The mason counted six coins from her own money and slid them forward.

“I won't.”

The clerk separated the unequal bets. Eight coins everybody still in the hand could win. A second pile of six for the players who'd put in four or more. The last four belonged to the contest between the mason and the dog.

Daynuh stared at the little piles.

“My dog has layers of debt.”

“No debt,” the clerk said. “Only what's on the table.”

“Thank fuck somebody came with a limit.”

They drew. The clerk kept each hand distinct, passed Mahnuh's replacements to Chris, and waited for the show.

Kaze still had nothing.

Chris still had his twos.

Mahnuh had acquired a jack and no further reason to care.

The mason laid down a straight ending at the eight.

Then drew all three little piles toward herself.

Eighteen silver coins.

The table went quiet.

Mahnuh looked at Chris.

Chris looked at the last little piece of food beside his hand.

Gave it to him anyway.

“You did your part.”

Daynuh put his mug down.

“How much you start with?”

“Six,” Chris said.

“How much you got?”

Chris looked at his empty place.

Kaze spread his hands.

The dog finished chewing.

“Collectively,” Billy said, “an education.”

Daynuh's mouth tightened.

Then a laugh escaped through his nose.

He tried to stop it. Looked at the three of them again. Failed.

“You sold my good hinges for this?”

Chris pointed at him.

“They were not your hinges.”

“Could've been. I had aspirations.”

Kaze was laughing again before Chris found an answer.

The mason stacked the coins.

“Another?”

“With what?” Daynuh asked. “His fucking collar?”

Chris shook his head. Kaze left the cards where they were and watched the woman gather her winnings. She tapped the neat little stack against the table, aligning its edges. He grinned at the care she took with it.

Mahnuh put his chin against Daynuh's thigh. Daynuh rubbed behind his ear, still watching Chris.

“Next time, teach him something that brings him home.”

“He did come to us.”

“Keep talking. Beer ain't that strong yet.”

Arthur came over from the doorway. He looked at the bare space in front of Kaze, then at the satisfied woman gathering her silver.

“Finished?”

“Apparently.”

“Foreman knows which road's open beyond the works.”

Kaze looked at the torn survey in Arthur's hand.

“Which one goes toward Swain?”

Arthur studied his face.

“You aiming to ask another question?”

Kaze glanced toward the mason.

“Where's he keep himself?”

She finished closing her purse before answering.

“Grand General? Capital. That's where you ask for him.”

She hadn't promised he'd be waiting beside a door. Kaze hadn't asked for an appointment.

He stood.

“Let's find out which way that is.”

Daynuh finished his beer.

Mahnuh rose beside him, ears turning toward Chris as the man picked up his empty food cloth.

Chris held it open.

“We're both out.”

The dog sniffed it anyway.

Season 3, Episode 41: “His Own Two Feet”

Chris put the cap back on Daniel's bottle.

He missed the thread twice.

Arthur watched from beside the blanket, then looked toward the higher ground beyond the stream.

“Up there. Above the flood line.”

Daynuh nodded. Kaze was already walking toward the slope.

They made the grave with their hands. Daynuh broke the hard ground; Kaze pulled out stones and tore through roots. Arthur cleared the loosened earth. Chris stayed by Daniel until they were ready to carry him.

No one told him to help.

K.K stood back among the trees. Mahnuh lay beside the blanket with his head on his forelegs. When Daynuh came to lift Daniel, the dog got up and followed.

Arthur removed the purse from Daniel's belt before they lowered him. He left it tied shut.

“I'll hold this.”

Chris looked at it, then nodded.

The spear lay across Kaze's knees while the others settled the blanket. He rubbed a thumb over a mark on its shaft.

“Keep that,” Daynuh said.

Kaze looked at him.

“For now.”

Kaze stood with it.

They covered Daniel before the light had gone.

Arthur placed a stone at the head. Chris watched the last loose earth slide down the side of it. Then he stepped forward and pushed the stone a little farther into the ground.

“He'd have something fucking stupid to say.”

Daynuh looked at the grave.

“Yeah.”

Chris waited, as though knowing that might provide the words.

It didn't.

Behind him the banjo stayed quiet. Billy had heard every scrape through Chris's headlamp feed. Inside, Meatwad sat against the old catfish's side. The camera remained on the table, facing away.

Kaze went down to the stream and washed the dirt off his hands.

Arthur came beside him.

“You see something back there?”

“Somebody else's blood. Fur.”

“Enough to follow?”

Kaze looked at the current.

“Not from here.”

Arthur waited.

“I can go back to the yard,” Kaze said. “Look again.”

“Morning.”

“You deciding that?”

“I'm saying it's getting dark and Chris ain't moved from that fucking rock.”

Kaze looked over.

Chris had sat down with the bottle between his feet. His rifle rested across his legs. K.K was near him, neither speaking nor attempting to fill the space with an explanation.

Kaze dried his hands on his pants and went back.

He sat beside Chris.

For a while, neither said anything.

Then Chris looked at the spear.

“Don't lose that.”

Kaze laid it between them.

“I won't.”

Earlier that day, at the port, Brian discovered that the pain at his waist eased when Tracy's shoulder began to throb.

This was the fourth day since the ground had broken. The three nights Dutch had bought were over. He paid two more silver to keep the back room until the following morning, leaving seventy, then went to examine the harbor with the stolen cargo ledger.

Tracy stayed behind with Clifford.

“My arm's asleep,” he said.

Clifford looked up from the wheel he was cleaning.

“You been lying on it?”

“I been lying next to it. This motherfucker lives on it.”

Brian glanced down at the place where his miniature torso joined Tracy's shoulder. Under the skin, something moved against the direction of Tracy's pulse.

He had felt movement there before. He had also spent a great deal of time claiming it meant progress without knowing what the fuck was progressing.

Now he could see a narrow ridge running toward his own waist.

He pressed it with his little palm.

Tracy flinched.

“Don't do that.”

Brian let go.

The ridge relaxed. A cramp passed through his own stomach. Beneath him, in tissue that had never contained a separate lower body, something pulled tight.

He pressed again.

Tracy slapped his hand away.

“I said don't.”

Brian looked offended enough to hide how interested he was.

“I'm trying to understand our situation.”

“Understand it with your hands in your lap.”

“I don't have a lap.”

“Then that's a problem for the pants department. Leave my fucking shoulder alone.”

Clifford turned his wheel another quarter rotation and picked grit from the axle.

“If it hurts, stop doing it.”

Brian waited until neither man was looking.

Then he touched the ridge again, more gently.

The organism beneath their joined skin contracted around his fingers. It wasn't answering a command. It had found pressure, warmth and an open route into living tissue.

Brian held the route open.

By afternoon, he had a knee.

It lay folded beneath the skin at his waist, pale and small, pushing against Tracy's shoulder as though someone had packed a doll into a sausage casing.

Tracy stood in front of the room's little mirror and pulled his collar down.

“What is that?”

Brian twisted to look with him.

“Development.”

“It got a joint.”

“Yes.”

“Why does my shoulder got somebody else's joint?”

“Technically, it's mine.”

Tracy looked at Brian's face in the glass.

“Then why am I paying for it?”

He pushed away from the mirror. His right hand shook. Brian could feel that tremor through the tissue between them; his own tiny hands had become steadier.

That was the point when he understood the exchange.

Not all of it. Not the organism's history, what it wanted or what it might do after this. Enough.

What was growing on Brian's side was coming out of Tracy's.

He covered the swelling with a fold of Tracy's shirt.

“We should rest.”

Tracy pulled the cloth back down.

“We should find somebody to get this shit out of me.”

Brian's little fingers tightened.

“We don't know what cutting it would do.”

“I know what leaving it is doing. I got a goddamn ankle in my armpit.”

He went toward the door.

His knee buckled.

Clifford locked his chair and caught Tracy's forearm before he hit the floor. The brace beneath Clifford's suit took his weight as he stood long enough to get Tracy against the bed.

“Sit.”

“I'm sitting. The floor applied early.”

Brian slid his hand under the collar.

“Don't touch it,” Clifford said.

Brian brought the hand back out.

Tracy was looking at him now.

“What did you do?”

“I didn't put it there.”

“I didn't ask who put it there.”

For a moment, the room was very quiet.

Dutch came back carrying the ledger beneath his arm. He stopped at the sight of Tracy against the bed.

“What happened?”

“He keeps fucking with it,” Tracy said.

Brian pointed at his own waist.

“I'm growing. That's not an accusation. That's an observation.”

Dutch came closer. He saw the swelling, the little foot-shaped bulge and the red branching marks spreading down Tracy's chest.

“Can you make it stop?”

Brian looked down.

“I've been trying.”

He had been trying several things. Stopping wasn't one of them.

Dutch put the ledger aside and went back out to look for help. Clifford stayed by the bed, where he could see Brian's hands.

Tracy kept himself awake by talking.

“When I get you off me, I'm putting you in a bowl.”

Brian watched the door.

“You don't have to be like that.”

“With a little lid. Air holes. A fucking raisin. You can tell the raisin about distribution.”

Clifford moved his chair closer.

“You thirsty?”

Tracy nodded. Clifford held the cup while he drank.

Brian looked away from the water running down Tracy's chin.

He could feel two feet now.

Not guesses. Toes that moved when he tried to move them. A minute ago his whole life had still depended on somebody else's decision to stand up.

He flexed them again.

Tracy felt it.

His hand closed around Brian's little wrist.

“You enjoying that?”

Brian looked at him.

“I want to get down.”

“Then get down without taking me with you.”

Brian didn't answer.

Clifford saw Tracy's grip tighten. He put the cup aside.

“Brian. Whatever you're doing.”

“I stopped.”

The ridge beneath Brian's other palm was still taut.

Tracy followed Clifford's eyes.

Then he grabbed Brian around the middle.

“Get your fucking hand off it.”

The little man screamed as Tracy pulled. The skin at their joining opened just enough to expose something dark and wet stretched between them.

It recoiled from the air.

Tracy let go, gasping. Clifford caught his wrist before he could tear at it again.

“Hold still. Dutch is coming.”

Brian's new legs kicked inside the thin membrane at his waist.

The organism began pulling them back toward the shared mass.

He felt the freedom receding before he'd used it.

“No.”

He pressed both hands against the moving ridge and pushed his body away from Tracy's shoulder.

Tracy arched against the bed.

“Stop.”

Brian pushed harder.

The thing between them tightened into a living cord. Under Tracy's chest, something dragged toward it. His next breath came out in a wet, unfinished cough.

Clifford seized Brian's wrists.

“Let go.”

For one instant Brian did.

Tracy drew air.

Brian's feet curled back beneath him.

He put his mouth against the cord and bit.

The organism convulsed.

The split spread down Tracy's shoulder. A dark sheath peeled away with Brian's forming hips, hauling red tissue out through the opening. Clifford grabbed the shirt and pressed it against the wound while Brian pulled clear onto the bed.

His legs came with him.

Tracy tried to say his name.

He never got past the first sound.

Clifford kept the pressure on. He shouted for Dutch, then shouted again. Brian lay beside them, kicking free of the collapsing membrane, while the large body that had carried him went still.

When Dutch came through the door, there was no one behind him yet.

He took one look at the bed and went to Clifford's side.

Clifford didn't take his hand away.

Brian sat up.

Below his waist were two bare little legs. A twitch ran through the dark seam at his hip, independent of anything he had asked it to do.

He put one foot on the blanket.

Then the other.

“Don't step over him,” Clifford said.

Brian froze.

His foot hovered above Tracy's arm. He brought it back down on the blanket.

Dutch pulled a clean section of the blanket over Tracy's face. Clifford stayed beside the bed until Dutch touched his arm.

Then he sat back in his chair.

Brian climbed down by the bedframe. His new foot found the floor. His other foot followed. He stood there, completely separate, no taller in spirit and considerably more naked than he had prepared for.

He took a step.

His knee folded.

He struck the floor chin first.

No one helped him up.

Now, I know. Some of you were waiting for the triumphant little walk. Brass section. Soft light. A man finally free to pursue his dreams and inconvenience a different shoulder. Unfortunately, he built the fucking legs out of someone who asked him to stop. We are not getting the inspirational sneaker commercial. We are getting a naked piece of shit discovering distance.

Brian pushed himself upright against the bedpost.

“I didn't mean—”

Clifford looked at him.

Brian abandoned the sentence.

Dutch picked up the ledger.

“You knew.”

Brian looked toward the covered face.

“I didn't know how far it would go.”

“You knew enough to lie.”

Dutch went outside.

He called the proprietor. There was no longer anybody in the room to save. Clifford stayed beside the bed while Dutch explained what they would have to leave behind. Brian remained by the bedpost until the latch closed.

Then he began the walk to the door.

It took him a very long time.

By morning, the port had acquired something worse than a rumor.

At first it was a line of white water beyond the damaged outer quay. Then the water swelled, lifted a fishing float and rolled it backward against its rope.

A black curve rose beneath it.

The harbor bells began again.

Dutch stood at the quay with Clifford, who had put his helmet back on. They had left Tracy's body in the net-mender's room under the proprietor's care. Brian sat on the closed cargo ledger in Clifford's lap, wrapped below the waist in a strip cut from the room's blanket.

He had tried walking the whole way. Clifford had watched him take seventeen furious steps before saying they would all be dead of old age.

He had not called it forgiveness.

The submarine surfaced beyond the broken berth.

Water streamed from a long metal hull. A raised command tower climbed clear of the sea; behind it, more black steel kept arriving where there had been open water. Ropes snapped taut on the nearest moored boats. Men on the quay ran to free them before the wash crushed them against the pilings.

Dutch backed Clifford's chair away from the edge.

The vessel slowed. Water churned beneath its stern, holding it off the damaged stone. A hatch opened. Crew in gray came onto the deck and began preparing lines.

No cannon fired. Nothing needed to. A functioning piece of another world's industrial arrogance had just made the entire harbor rearrange its afternoon.

Morning. Sorry. The penis submarine threw me. I can be professional about a lot of things, but a Bond villain arriving in a horizontal architectural erection while our smallest executive is wearing a blood-adjacent napkin—give me a second.

The crew secured the vessel beside the surviving section of quay. A gangway came down under mechanical control, wide enough for Clifford's chair. At its upper end stood a bald man in a gray, high-collared suit.

He had a scar beside one eye and the expression of somebody who had paid a great deal of money to enter a room last.

Dr. Evil surveyed the harbor.

“Well.”

Behind him, a crewman waited with a chart.

Dr. Evil looked at it, then at the broken waterfront.

“I preferred the diagram.”

The crewman said something too quietly for the quay to hear.

“Yes, I can see that. There are several clues.”

He came down the gangway.

Dutch moved forward before anyone else could decide what sort of welcome the city intended.

“Quite an entrance.”

Dr. Evil looked him over.

“Was it? I couldn't hear the exterior speakers.”

He turned back toward the deck.

“We discussed a musical arrival.”

The crewman pointed toward the waterline.

Dr. Evil followed the finger.

“Then why would you put them there?”

The man began to explain.

“No. This is a disappointment. It doesn't require a tour.”

He adjusted his collar, looked back at Dutch and made a small, deliberate effort to recover the entrance he'd imagined.

Dutch waited. He knew the value of allowing a man to finish being disappointed in his own people.

“You appear to be a man who understands an operation,” he said.

Dr. Evil faced him again.

“I run several.”

“Dutch van der Linde.”

“Doctor Evil.”

Dutch gave the name the respectful pause it clearly expected.

“Doctor.”

“Thank you.”

Behind Dutch, Brian got to his feet on the ledger.

“We represent Tampon Pandemic Productions.”

Dr. Evil looked down.

Then farther down.

“Do you?”

“I'm the founder.”

“Of which part?”

Brian drew himself up inside the strip of blanket.

“The organization.”

“Ah. I thought perhaps you'd founded the gentleman's lap.”

Clifford lifted Brian off the ledger and set him on the armrest.

Dr. Evil's attention shifted to the black helmet.

It stayed there.

His posture became noticeably more careful.

“And this is your associate?”

Dutch glanced back.

“He is.”

“Excellent.”

The word came out with a small, private satisfaction.

Dutch took the ledger from Clifford and opened it to the harbor entries.

“You need to know where you've arrived. What can still be supplied. Which roads carry goods inland.”

“You have a chart?”

“I have the records of people who've been moving cargo through here.”

“Legitimately acquired?”

Dutch smiled.

Dr. Evil smiled back.

“Good. I was worried we were about to become tedious.”

He looked across the water toward his own vessel.

Its charts had not matched this coast. Its crew had brought it into the first harbor they could inspect, using what they could actually see. The engines worked. The provisions were real. Their familiar world, apparently, was no longer available by turning around.

What he lacked stood in front of him carrying a stolen book.

Dutch turned a page.

“We know people with influence. We also know several people who ought to be removed from it.”

“How many people work for you?”

Brian lifted his hand.

Dutch did not look at him.

“You're looking at our present company.”

Dr. Evil studied them again.

One persuasive cowboy. One very interesting armored associate. One extremely small man who had apparently been supplied without trousers.

“And what does your company require?”

Dutch closed the ledger.

“A base. Equipment. Enough room to stop confusing survival with progress.”

Brian nodded vigorously.

“Exactly. That's what I've been—”

“I'm speaking with Dutch.”

Brian stopped.

Dr. Evil waited until the interruption had finished being absent.

“I can provide those things. In exchange, you will help me understand this place. Its authorities. Its vulnerabilities. The people who can be bought and the people who insist on making that difficult.”

Dutch watched him.

“A partnership.”

“An organization. I find partnerships become crowded when everybody wants the same chair.”

“We've had difficulties with people mistaking independence for disobedience,” Dutch said.

“How unfortunate.”

“We believe a man's loyalty should be earned.”

Dr. Evil folded his hands.

“I agree. What are you offering to earn mine?”

Dutch's expression barely changed.

Brian's did.

For three glorious seconds he looked as though somebody had opened a window in Dutch's fucking cathedral.

“We have enemies,” Dutch said. “Unusually dangerous ones. Men who think strength places them beyond consequence.”

“Doesn't it help?”

“Until they're met by greater strength.”

Dr. Evil considered that.

“Yes. Much better. Lead with the problem next time. I was beginning to think you wanted to read me a saddle.”

Dutch looked at the gray-suited man, then at the machinery behind him.

“You want useful information. The ledger gives you warehouses, suppliers and consignments. I can show your people which entries concern the coast and which roads have ceased to be roads. But you don't get every grievance we've ever had by offering us breakfast.”

“Of course not.”

Dr. Evil paused.

“Have you had breakfast?”

Nobody answered quickly enough.

“Then let us begin with the inexpensive part.”

He signaled toward the deck. A member of the crew took the ledger only after Dutch opened it to the relevant pages and kept a hand on the cover. Dutch indicated the harbor entries. The man copied the headings onto his chart and returned the book.

Dr. Evil watched the exchange.

“There. Useful. Nobody needed to mention destiny.”

“I hadn't mentioned destiny.”

“You were circling it.”

Dutch smiled despite himself.

“Perhaps.”

Brian stepped forward on the armrest.

“I handled our original branding and conceptual direction.”

“Yes, you mentioned the tampon.”

“The full name has a rhythm.”

“So does a man falling down stairs. It doesn't mean I want it on the side of my vessel.”

“We also have a production component.”

“What do you produce?”

Brian looked at Dutch.

Dutch let him.

“We're restructuring.”

Dr. Evil's eyes dropped briefly to the blanket around Brian's waist.

“I can see that.”

Clifford turned his helmet toward the ship's interior.

“Is there somewhere to wash?”

The question ended Brian's presentation. Blood had dried in Clifford's glove from holding Tracy's wound closed. He had cleaned the wheel grips before coming out; the dark seam between two fingers remained.

Dr. Evil noticed it.

“There is. And a place to sit. Properly.”

“I'll use my chair.”

“Very well.”

He accepted the answer with none of the irritation he'd given Brian. His glance returned to the helmet, briefly admiring, then moved away before Clifford could ask about it.

Brian watched the difference in treatment.

He had spent the morning learning to stand. Apparently, the qualification he needed was a fucking hat with a front door.

Behind him, aboard the vessel, men were moving equipment without asking any of the three visitors to pay for the rope.

Dutch considered the gangway, the dry interior beyond it and the rows of lights that remained lit without a man carrying a flame along them.

He had spent the night beside another dead member of an organization that could barely afford its room.

“And my position?”

“You deal with the people here. Directly with me. If something becomes ridiculous, I would prefer to hear it from you before it reaches the room.”

Dutch glanced at Brian.

“That may be difficult.”

“I appreciate your candor.”

Clifford put a hand on his wheel.

“I keep my weapons.”

“Naturally.” Dr. Evil looked at his helmet again. “I was rather hoping you'd say that.”

“And my chair stays accessible.”

Dr. Evil looked at the gangway.

“Yes. I believe we've already exceeded your current building.”

Clifford considered him, then nodded once.

Dutch held the ledger beside the armrest. Brian climbed onto the closed cover, and Dutch brought the book back against his side.

“I have concerns about the structure.”

“You should,” Dr. Evil said. “It's very high from where you are.”

“Management structure.”

“Oh.”

“I created this group. I named it. We can't simply have somebody arrive and—”

Dr. Evil looked toward the submarine.

Brian followed his eyes.

The ship hummed. Warm air came through the open hatch. Somewhere inside, a member of the crew was eating from an actual plate.

“There will be a place for you,” Dr. Evil said.

“What place?”

“We'll find something appropriate.”

“I can make strategic contributions.”

“Wonderful.”

“Not just be present.”

“Then we already have a goal.”

Brian's fingers curled around the ledger's binding. Behind him, the quay's surviving traffic had begun moving again. The submarine would remain there whether he approved of its owner or not. Dutch had found somebody who could support an operation instead of another speech about one.

The little man looked at Clifford, seeking an ally.

Clifford looked back through the black mask.

Brian remembered the hand pressing Tracy's shirt against the wound.

He tried Dutch instead.

Dutch adjusted his grip on the ledger, making Brian grab the binding.

“We have terms,” Dutch said. “We can discuss the work inside.”

“Excellent.”

Dr. Evil turned to his crew.

“Food for our guests. And a room beside mine for Dutch. We have a great deal to discuss.”

Dutch inclined his head. The arrangement had acquired a door, a meal and a place beside the man giving orders.

Dr. Evil stepped aside and let him take the first part of the gangway. Clifford followed under his own power, wheels moving steadily up the incline. Brian remained on the book in Dutch's hand.

Halfway up, he looked back at the quay.

He had legs. He had left Tracy behind. There was nobody attached to him who could decide where his body went.

“Put me down,” he told Dutch.

Dutch did.

Brian stood on the metal gangway, clutching his improvised garment. Ahead of him, the other men continued toward the hatch.

He started after them.

Then ran.

“Hold the fucking door.”

Season 3, Episode 41: “Cluck Around and Find Out”

Chris screwed the cap onto Daniel's bottle, missed the thread, and tried again.

They buried Daniel above the stream that evening. Daynuh broke the ground. Kaze pulled out the stones. Arthur took the unopened purse off Daniel's belt before they lowered the blanket, and kept it separate.

Chris set the marker.

When he returned to the water, Kaze was sitting with Daniel's spear across his knees.

“Don't lose that,” Chris said.

“I won't.”

By morning, the grave was behind them. It wasn't farther away.

Daynuh fell asleep beside Mahnuh while Chris worked over the cooking fire. They were keeping the stream camp for another few days: shelter, water, the planted pear tree, and a place to return to while Kaze checked the crusher yard again. Nobody had identified Daniel's killer. Nobody had volunteered to march in a random direction and pretend that counted.

Chris had just lifted the pan when Daynuh woke.

His hand moved over empty ground.

“Mahnuh?”

He sat up.

Looked behind himself.

Then beneath the blanket, which was ambitious. His dog stood five feet seven inches at the shoulder. Unless the blanket had developed a fucking basement, the search was over.

Chris pointed his spoon toward the trees.

“He was here.”

“When?”

“When he was here.”

Daynuh stood.

“Useful. If I find him yesterday, I'll tell you.”

He checked the bank, then the road beyond the trees. Chris put the pan aside and followed. At his belt, the banjo carried a low, interested chuckle.

Inside BELLY, full-sized Catfish Billy was watching the second monitor. Chris's amber headlamp supplied the actual view. The first monitor wasn't showing their search. Nobody was playing the game.

“Christopher. Lift your head. If the animal is hiding beneath your boots, we've already lost him.”

“Looking for tracks.”

“Then I withdraw my concern. We shall recover whichever shoe you wore here.”

They reached the road as a local watchman came up from the market settlement downstream. He saw Daynuh, slowed, and stopped outside arm's reach.

“You missing a dog?”

Daynuh's face changed.

“Where?”

“Poultry shop.”

“Outside?”

The man shook his head.

“Inside.”

Daynuh looked at Chris.

Chris looked toward town.

Billy made one pleased note through the banjo.

“Oh, I should like to see the premises.”

Cluck Around and Find Out occupied a stone shop beside a broad loading yard. Its painted chicken had one raised foot and the unpleasant confidence of a bird unaware of the rotisserie beneath it.

Mahnuh couldn't read the sign.

He had followed hot chicken through the open loading doors.

Which is how most religions would recruit me, if they stopped getting distracted by my moral condition.

Four customers stood outside. One still held his money out in front of him, as though the transaction might resume at a safer address.

The poultry seller stood behind the counter.

Mahnuh stood in front of it.

His great blue-gray head hovered above an empty tray. His tail moved slowly enough to suggest that, from his perspective, everybody was having a lovely morning.

Daynuh stepped through the door.

“Mahnuh.”

The dog's ears turned.

“Come.”

Mahnuh looked at the seller.

The seller looked at Daynuh.

“He already had it.”

“How much?”

“One roast.”

Chris inspected the tray.

“Clean work.”

“He ate my chicken.”

“I'm talking about the tray. You could see your fucking childhood in that.”

Billy's voice rolled out of the banjo.

“Sir, have you considered serving something less persuasive?”

The seller stared at Chris's belt.

Chris shook his head.

“That's a whole other problem. Finish the dog first.”

Daynuh put a hand against Mahnuh's neck.

“Out.”

The dog followed him. At the threshold he stopped, turned, and took one scrap from beside the counter.

The seller made a strangled sound.

Daynuh looked down.

“Mahnuh.”

The dog swallowed.

Chris put a hand over his mouth.

Daynuh turned toward him.

“You laughing?”

“No.”

Billy said, “He is obstructing the evidence with his fingers.”

Daynuh led Mahnuh outside. He didn't pretend a scolding would restore a chicken. He told the seller he'd return to settle the loss, then walked his dog home.

No spell had compelled the theft. No secret history of chicken crime explained it.

An open door had smelled good.

The people had moved.

The chicken had become available.

Mahnuh learned something.

Unfortunately, so did Chris.

The following morning the dog returned along the stream with a duck hanging from his mouth.

Chris saw the wrapping first.

Then the duck.

Then Mahnuh stopped directly in front of him.

Chris glanced toward camp. Daynuh was farther up the bank, working a split handle loose from their pan. Arthur sat nearby cleaning one revolver.

Chris crouched.

“Where'd you get that?”

Mahnuh lowered the duck beside his boots.

Billy leaned toward the monitor.

“My goodness.”

“Quiet.”

“I haven't accused anyone of anything.”

Chris opened the paper.

He smelled juniper, browned skin, warm fat.

For a moment, professional respect overcame every remaining obligation.

“That bastard put the aromatics beneath the skin.”

Mahnuh sat.

“Don't look at me like that.”

The dog continued looking.

Chris pulled off a small boneless piece.

Billy laughed softly.

“Careful, Christopher. You're approaching a decision.”

“He brought it over here.”

“Yes. In his mouth. A method of acquisition you've apparently accepted as a receipt.”

Chris gave Mahnuh the piece, then ate one himself.

“Look at you,” he murmured. “Face like somebody stuffed a sofa into a condom, and you got better taste than half the people I cooked for.”

Mahnuh leaned forward.

“Don't get emotional. There's bones.”

The duck was excellent.

That made the next several decisions considerably easier.

He removed the string and paper, wiped the dog's chin with a wet cloth, and pushed the remaining duck behind his knee as Daynuh called down the bank.

“He with you?”

“Right here.”

“Where'd he go?”

“Had a little walk.”

Mahnuh went back to Daynuh and lay down with his head on his paws.

Chris looked at the banjo.

Billy waited.

Chris waited.

Then Billy said, “A thigh.”

“What?”

“When I come outside. One proper thigh. Skin intact.”

“You're charging me for silence?”

“I'm joining the meal.”

“You didn't steal it.”

“Neither did you, a moment ago. And yet you've found a place at the table.”

Chris looked down at the duck.

He tore off another piece.

Now, I have watched villains negotiate over planets. I have watched men threaten entire civilizations because somebody disrespected their stupid little helmet.

These two had just formed a criminal partnership over poultry, while the only member taking actual risks had gone to sleep beside his owner.

By the next afternoon, Mahnuh knew the route.

The seller had learned too. Cooked birds no longer sat at the front counter. A hinged barrier blocked the loading entrance. Behind it, a worker carried food through an inner door.

Mahnuh came up to the barrier.

Stopped.

Sniffed.

The seller watched from inside.

“No.”

Mahnuh waited.

“No.”

A customer approached carrying a basket. He saw the dog and placed his basket on the ground so he could retreat with both hands available.

Mahnuh turned.

The customer retreated farther.

Chris arrived in time to see the dog picking up the abandoned basket.

“Nope. Put that down.”

Mahnuh brought it to him.

The basket held bread, eggs, smoked meat and a small pot of fat.

Chris took the handle.

Mahnuh sat.

The seller came outside.

“You again.”

Chris held out the basket.

“Found this.”

“It was beside him.”

“Hell of a coincidence. Saved us a search.”

The customer peered around the corner.

“That's mine.”

Chris gave it back.

The man accepted it without approaching Mahnuh.

The dog watched the basket leave.

Billy spoke from Chris's belt.

“A disappointing end to a promising assortment.”

Chris lowered his voice.

“You said a thigh. You don't get to expand the arrangement.”

The seller looked at him.

“What arrangement?”

“Talking to the banjo.”

“Why?”

“Because it won't shut the fuck up.”

Chris took Mahnuh home without a reward.

He made it halfway before the dog stopped at a puddle, lowered his head, and presented his greasy chin.

Chris stood over him.

“Oh, you motherfucker.”

Mahnuh waited.

Billy's delight was audible.

“He remembered the service.”

Chris wiped the dog's face.

From the road above them, unseen behind the bank, Daynuh watched the last part.

He didn't call out.

He watched Chris fold the cloth and put it away.

That evening Mahnuh refused the last of his ordinary food.

Daynuh looked at the bowl.

Looked at the dog.

Then looked at Chris, who had developed an extraordinary interest in keeping a clean cloth beside his knee.

“He sick?”

Chris looked up.

“Doesn't look sick.”

“Didn't ask how he looks.”

“Could be tired.”

“From what?”

Billy made a small sound through the banjo.

Chris covered it with a cough.

Daynuh waited.

Chris reached for a spoon.

Daynuh took the spoon before he could start cleaning it.

“Leave that alone. It's cleaner than your fucking answer.”

Arthur lowered his revolver.

Kaze, returning from the yard with no new name to follow, stopped beside the fire.

“What'd he do?”

“Don't know yet,” Daynuh said.

Chris spread his hands.

“That's a hell of a way to introduce an investigation.”

“Then help me finish it.”

Mahnuh rolled onto his side.

His belly made a low, satisfied noise.

Everybody looked at him.

Billy said, very softly, “An unreliable witness.”

Daynuh turned toward the instrument.

“You're enjoying this.”

“I have a limited view and an excellent seat.”

“Keep it.”

Daynuh got up and went toward town.

Chris watched him leave.

Billy said, “We may need to reconsider the thigh.”

The next morning, Chris found Mahnuh beside the road.

The dog wasn't carrying food.

He was staring at a two-wheeled delivery cart.

A worker had stopped outside the poultry shop. Behind the cart's raised slats sat closed tins of cooked meat, cooling on racks. The seller stood in the doorway, checking each one as it came down.

The goods were covered. The loading gate was shut. Customers kept their baskets in their hands.

For several minutes, everything worked.

Chris stood beside Mahnuh.

“See? That's it. Business is over.”

The dog sniffed toward the cart.

“Don't.”

Mahnuh looked at him.

Chris pointed back toward camp.

“Come on.”

Then a lid lifted.

Steam crossed the yard.

Mahnuh's head followed it.

Inside BELLY, Billy sat up so sharply that the monitor became a window worth occupying.

“Turn a little to the left.”

“No.”

“Christopher.”

“What?”

“I am trying to see what they have done with the skin.”

Chris looked.

Billy sighed.

“There. Look at that. A bird should shine a little. Not wet. Not varnished like a dead uncle in a cheap coffin. Just enough to make a man reconsider his commitments.”

“You don't know a fucking thing about roasting.”

“I know what encourages travel.”

The worker carried the tin through the inner door.

Mahnuh moved to follow.

Chris caught his attention.

“No. Here.”

The dog stopped beside him.

The seller noticed.

For the first time all morning, he smiled.

“That's better.”

Chris nodded.

“Yeah.”

“Keep doing that.”

Chris looked at him.

“Doing what?”

“Keeping him away from the food.”

The seller went inside.

Chris watched the door.

Then looked down at Mahnuh.

Billy said, “You've been mistaken for the solution.”

“I heard.”

“There are opportunities in a misunderstanding.”

Chris took a slow breath.

The worker returned for another tin.

Chris pointed toward the cart's rear wheel.

“Your pin's walking out.”

The worker looked.

It was.

Chris crouched, braced the wheel and pushed the loose retaining pin back into place. He checked the split end, bent it farther, then stood.

“Road'll shake it loose again if you leave it straight.”

The worker thanked him.

An ordinary useful thing had happened.

Then Chris asked, “Anything getting thrown out?”

The worker looked toward the shop.

“A few ends.”

“Dog's behaving.”

Mahnuh sat.

“Could take those off your hands.”

The worker brought him a small bundle of scraps.

Chris accepted it.

Billy watched through the headlamp.

“Well. Honest success. How unsettling.”

Chris gave Mahnuh one piece.

Kept another.

The dog followed him home.

He had not stolen anything that morning.

Chris told Daynuh that part with the confidence of a man who had discovered the most convenient six minutes of the truth.

Daynuh listened.

Then he asked, “Where's the duck?”

Chris stopped chewing.

Behind him, Arthur leaned back against a tree.

Kaze looked at the banjo.

The instrument remained silent.

Chris swallowed.

“What duck?”

“The one the shop lost the other morning.”

Chris looked toward Mahnuh.

Mahnuh had lain down.

Daynuh nodded.

“You can stop checking whether he's gonna tell me.”

“I was checking if he—”

“He's a dog, Chris.”

“I'm aware.”

“Then quit looking at him like he's the weak part of your story.”

The banjo gave one involuntary, delighted chuckle.

Chris looked at it.

Daynuh did too.

“And you.”

Billy cleared his throat.

“I believe my involvement has been overstated.”

“I haven't stated it yet.”

“Then we've caught this at a fortunate moment.”

Daynuh held out a greasy scrap of wrapping.

“The seller recognized this. Found it where you were crouching.”

Chris looked at the paper.

There was no ingenious explanation available.

He tried a bad one anyway.

“Could've blown.”

“Under your fucking knee?”

The banjo laughed.

Chris pointed at it.

“He wanted a thigh.”

Daynuh slowly turned his head.

Billy waited.

“A modest interest,” the fish said.

Daynuh folded the wrapping.

“You knew I was looking for him.”

“First time, no,” Chris said.

“After.”

Chris's mouth tightened.

“After, yeah.”

Daynuh let that answer stand.

He wasn't stupid. He also wasn't going to build a jail around a dog because two grown men had discovered poultry with the lights turned low.

“You want to feed him something, tell me. You find him wandering, bring him back. Don't stand there helping him disappear, then watch me go look.”

Chris looked down.

“Yeah.”

Billy said, “Entirely reasonable.”

Daynuh pointed toward the banjo.

“You don't get to climb onto the good side of this conversation.”

The fish fell silent.

Mahnuh lifted his head at Daynuh's voice.

Daynuh scratched behind his ear.

“And you been having a wonderful fucking time.”

The dog's tail struck the ground once.

Kaze put another stick on the fire.

“So who got the duck?”

Chris stared at him.

Kaze waited.

Arthur covered his mouth.

Daynuh closed his eyes.

For half a second, the camp sounded almost normal.

The seller wasn't finished adapting.

He stopped bringing cooked birds through the yard during the busiest hour. The tins traveled in a closed box secured across the cart. Two men unloaded it. One stayed with the mule. The other carried the tins directly through the loading gate.

Mahnuh stayed beside Daynuh that morning.

Until Daynuh went down to the stream to wash his hands.

The dog rose.

Stopped beside Chris.

Sniffed his empty fingers.

Chris looked at him.

“No.”

Mahnuh moved closer.

“No. I have been spoken to.”

From the banjo came Billy's low, rolling voice.

“In the old wetlands, a heron once tried to keep me out of a nesting ground. Now, I admired the ambition. Bird was built like a pair of scissors somebody taught to hate. He'd stand there with one leg raised, announcing that all the frogs on his side of the water belonged to him.”

Chris shut his eyes.

“Don't.”

“I offered a division.”

“I'm not doing a fucking history lesson.”

“He declined. Very proud animal. Terrible landlord. By dusk he'd built a second fence, and by dawn I'd discovered he had enclosed the water but left his eggs outside it.”

Chris looked at Mahnuh.

Mahnuh looked toward the road.

Billy continued.

“The point, Christopher, is that possession can become a very narrow way of looking at supper.”

“Did this happen?”

“In the emotional particulars.”

“You ate some eggs.”

“They had overinvested in security.”

Mahnuh walked away.

Chris called him.

The dog stopped.

Then a mule brayed from the road.

Mahnuh's nose rose.

Chris stood.

“Oh, for fuck's sake.”

He followed.

This time he told Arthur where he was going.

That small improvement would later be raised in his defense and found insufficient.

At the shop, the cart stood parallel to the loading entrance. The mule waited at its front. The closed box occupied most of the bed.

Mahnuh went past the seller's gate.

Past the front counter.

Around the cart.

Chris reached him at the back.

The dog was sniffing a separate wicker hamper lashed behind the box.

Live chickens shifted inside it.

Breeding birds, being delivered to a yard beyond the shop.

All that careful defense around the cooked food.

The fucking ingredients had arrived in a picnic basket.

Chris seized the hamper's handle before Mahnuh could take it.

“Leave.”

Mahnuh backed up.

The wicker creaked.

Chris looked down.

One of the lashings had already frayed against the wheel.

He caught the basket as it slipped.

A chicken thrust its head between two strips of wicker and pecked his thumb.

“Little bastard.”

Billy chuckled.

Chris set the hamper on the ground to retie it.

Mahnuh put his nose against the lid.

“Don't help.”

A wing struck the wicker.

The dog jerked back.

The handle came up in Chris's hand.

The lid, which had been secured to that handle, came with it.

For one second, Chris stood holding the empty top of the problem.

Then the chickens left.

Not all in one direction.

That would have implied leadership.

One shot beneath the cart. Two went toward the shop. Another flapped directly into Chris's chest and used his shirt as a ladder.

Mahnuh lunged after the first moving bird.

Chris caught him across the shoulders.

“Stay!”

The dog stopped.

The mule did not appreciate the chicken under its feet.

It lurched forward.

The cart rolled.

One wheel mounted the stone lip beside the loading gate.

The closed food box tilted toward the worker carrying a tin below it.

Daynuh caught the cart before it came down.

He'd followed Arthur's direction and arrived in time to see Chris wearing a live chicken.

His hands braced the raised side. He set his feet, took the weight, and lowered the wheel back onto the road.

The worker got clear.

Daynuh looked over the cart.

“Where's the dog?”

Chris turned.

Mahnuh had stopped chasing chickens.

He was standing beside the shop's inner door.

The poultry seller had left it open when the cart tipped.

The dog looked at Daynuh.

Then at the doorway.

Then, with magnificent fucking timing, he stepped inside.

Chris still held the hamper lid.

Daynuh stared at him.

Billy said, “The heron made a comparable error.”

The chicken on Chris's chest pecked his chin.

Chris pulled it off.

“Shut up about the fucking heron.”

The seller came out of the loading door carrying a broad paddle.

“Mahnuh!” Daynuh called.

The dog emerged with a whole roast held gently between his teeth.

He crossed the yard.

Passed Chris.

Passed the overturned hamper.

And laid the chicken at Daynuh's feet.

Everybody watched.

Mahnuh sat.

Daynuh looked at the roast.

Then at his dog.

Then at Chris.

The banjo began to shake with Billy's laughter.

“Don't,” Daynuh said.

Billy tried.

He really did.

Then he said, “He's brought his recommendation directly to management.”

Chris dropped the lid.

Daynuh pointed at him.

“You are not enjoying this.”

“I ain't said a fucking word.”

“Your whole face said it.”

The seller approached.

Daynuh held up one hand.

“I'm taking him out of here.”

“And the birds?”

Chris looked around.

There were chickens on the cart, chickens beneath the cart, and one standing in the shop window as though it had acquired the business.

The worker checked the food box's latch.

That much, at least, had held.

Daynuh looked at Chris.

“Get the loose ones.”

Chris opened his mouth.

“Because you opened the basket,” Daynuh said. “Not because you're getting a fucking career.”

Billy's laughter stopped just long enough to become a cough.

Chris glared at the banjo.

Daynuh picked up the stolen roast, handed it back to the seller, and led Mahnuh clear of the gate.

The dog followed without a struggle.

Chris caught the chickens.

He did it quickly and competently, which denied him the relief of blaming the task.

Eight went back into the hamper.

The ninth was on the seller's shoulder.

Neither man was enjoying it.

Chris lifted it off.

The seller looked him in the eye.

“I know you ate the duck.”

Chris held the chicken.

“Good duck.”

“I know.”

A pause.

“Juniper under the skin,” Chris said.

“My father's way.”

Chris nodded.

“Keep doing it.”

The seller took the chicken from him.

“You keep your hands off it.”

Behind them, Daynuh crouched beside Mahnuh.

The dog pressed his head beneath his arm.

Daynuh rubbed his neck.

“You ain't starving.”

Mahnuh leaned harder.

“And you can't keep bringing me evidence.”

Chris made a small noise behind the cart.

Daynuh didn't turn.

“I can still hear your fucking face.”

By afternoon, the birds were accounted for, the cart pin had been checked, and the seller had moved the live deliveries to a separate yard. He sent a worker down the surviving road toward the port to ask what secure storage and guarded deliveries would cost.

The man left before sundown. The seller went back to work.

Chris returned to camp carrying no poultry.

Mahnuh lay beside Daynuh.

Arthur looked up.

“Find him?”

Chris stopped.

Kaze was turning the pan over the fire.

Arthur's expression remained almost polite.

Chris pointed at him.

“You knew where I was.”

“Just asking.”

Kaze looked toward the banjo.

“Fish get his thigh?”

“No,” Chris said.

Billy's voice was wounded.

“An entire morning spent advising a young enterprise, and not so much as a wing.”

“You told a story about eating a bird's children.”

“Precisely. Relevant experience.”

Daynuh sat beside the fire.

“Mahnuh's coming with me when I go into town.”

Chris nodded.

“And if he shows up with food?”

“I bring him to you.”

“And if you want some?”

Chris looked at him.

Daynuh waited.

“I ask.”

Billy said, “An elegant arrangement.”

Daynuh looked at the banjo.

“You too.”

A long silence.

Then Billy said, “May I have some duck?”

Arthur bent forward.

Kaze had to take the pan off the fire.

Chris sat down so abruptly that his knee struck a stone.

Daynuh looked from one man to the next.

Then he started laughing.

Not because the food was paid for. It wasn't. Not because the dog was reformed. He wasn't.

Because the old fish had finally asked, in the voice of a riverboat executioner requesting permission to attend a fucking birthday party.

Mahnuh rose at the sound.

Came to the fire.

Chris held out both hands.

“Nothing.”

The dog sniffed them.

Walked past him.

And put his enormous head in Daynuh's lap.

Daynuh scratched behind one ear.

“Yeah. Stay there.”

For a while, he did.

Chris reached for the pan.

Daynuh caught his wrist.

“Wash your hands.”

“I did.”

“You caught nine chickens.”

Chris looked at the banjo.

Billy said nothing.

Chris looked at Arthur.

Arthur spread his clean hands.

Kaze turned away before Chris could try him.

Chris stood and went down to the stream.

Behind him, Mahnuh watched until he was out of sight.

Then the dog's nose rose toward the pan.

Daynuh put one hand over it.

“No.”

Mahnuh looked at him.

Daynuh looked back.

The dog settled his chin on the man's knee.

From the banjo, Billy murmured, “Ask.”

Daynuh threw a piece of firewood at Chris's empty seat.

“Don't fucking coach him.”
