Season 3, Episode 42: “A Very Important Call”

The piece of firewood struck Chris's empty seat.

At the stream, Chris looked up from washing his hands.

“What?”

“Nothing,” Daynuh called.

The banjo at Chris's belt remained suspiciously quiet.

Chris narrowed his eyes at it.

“Whatever you said, remember you live with me.”

Inside BELLY, Billy leaned back from the headlamp monitor.

“An arrangement I have considered at length.”

Five mornings earlier, at the port, Dutch van der Linde had paid six silver to keep the net-mender's back room for another three nights.

Seventy-two became sixty-six.

He counted it twice.

Then he put the purse away before Brian could describe the expenditure as an investment.

The room held one bed, Clifford's chair, a basin, and four men with very different ideas about who was taking up too much space.

Tracy sat on the bed.

Miniature Brian was still conjoined to his shoulder.

“Quit moving,” Tracy said.

“I'm not moving.”

“Something moving.”

Brian looked down.

A narrow ridge beneath their joined skin contracted against his little palm.

He had felt it before. That morning it was warm.

He pressed.

Tracy flinched.

“That's you.”

“I'm examining—”

“Examine your fucking attitude. Take your hands off me.”

Brian lifted them.

The ridge slackened.

A cramp passed through the tissue beneath his waist.

He pressed again, gently.

Something on Tracy's side tightened.

Something on Brian's side unfolded.

Not a miracle.

Not a benevolent little surgeon awarding independence for good behavior.

The separate organism in their shared flesh had found two bodies and a very selfish man willing to keep the useful side open.

By midday, a small pale foot pressed against the skin beneath Brian's torso.

Tracy saw it in the mirror.

For several seconds he said nothing.

Clifford looked over from his chair.

“What?”

Tracy pulled his collar down.

“There is a fucking heel in my shoulder.”

Brian looked too.

His toes moved.

Tracy's hand trembled.

Brian's didn't.

He noticed that.

Then he pulled the collar up.

“Could be temporary.”

Tracy pulled it down again.

“That's a foot. Where it's going temporarily?”

Dutch put the cargo ledger aside.

He came closer, looked at the swelling, then at Brian.

“Does it hurt?”

“Not particularly.”

“I was asking him.”

Brian's face tightened.

Tracy sat back on the bed.

“My arm feels like somebody been drinking it.”

Dutch looked at the red marks spreading below the join.

He went for help.

Clifford stayed.

He could stand with his supports. He could also remember what it cost when somebody with a convenient explanation got careless with another man's body.

“Hands where I can see them,” he told Brian.

Brian folded his arms.

“I am not a fucking child.”

“Then this ought to be easy.”

Tracy tried to laugh.

It came out wrong.

Brian felt the laugh pass through the joining tissue. He also felt his new knee bend.

He moved it again.

Tracy caught his wrist.

“Stop.”

“I didn't make this happen.”

“Didn't ask who started it.”

Clifford rolled closer.

Brian looked between them.

“I can feel my feet.”

Tracy stared at him.

“Good. Feel them away from my lungs.”

The ridge tightened.

Brian's second leg pushed through a thin sheath beneath his waist.

He made a sound he hadn't intended anybody else to hear.

Delight.

Tracy heard it.

His hand closed around Brian's middle.

“Get your hands off that thing.”

He pulled Brian away from the shoulder.

The joining skin opened.

A dark wet cord stretched between them, then contracted, dragging the little man back.

Both screamed.

Clifford caught Tracy's wrist.

“Don't tear it.”

Brian's feet began curling back into the sheath.

He could feel them going.

That was the moment.

Not the mysterious twitch. Not the first swelling. Not whatever ancient fucking biology had attached a miniature executive to a comedian like a skin tag with a business proposal.

This.

Tracy was trying to breathe.

Clifford was telling him to let go.

Brian could stop pressing.

For one breath, he did.

Tracy's chest rose.

Brian's legs began folding backward.

“No.”

He put both palms against the cord and pushed.

Tracy grabbed his arm.

Clifford grabbed the other.

Brian twisted his head and bit into the dark tissue between them.

The organism convulsed.

A red fold dragged out of Tracy's shoulder, stretched white, then tore.

Clifford shoved a rolled section of shirt against the opening.

Brian fell onto the bed.

His legs came with him.

Tracy's hand found the edge of the blanket.

He tried to sit forward.

Couldn't.

“Brian.”

It was the first time all day he had said the name without an insult attached.

Brian looked at him.

Clifford shouted for Dutch.

Then he shouted again.

Tracy's fingers loosened.

Brian's new feet kept moving.

When Dutch returned, the old net-mender was behind him.

They were too late.

Clifford remained beside the bed with both hands pressing the shirt.

Dutch touched his shoulder.

Only then did he sit back.

The net-mender looked at the wound, at Brian, and at the little legs kicking free of the wet sheath.

“What is he?”

Brian drew himself upright.

“I am a person.”

The old man looked at Tracy.

“Wasn't asking about the shape.”

Brian climbed down the bedframe.

His first foot found the floor.

The second followed.

He stood.

For the first time, nobody else's body was holding him up.

He took a step.

His knees folded.

He landed face first.

Beneath the wet edge of his new waist, the dark seam twitched without his asking. He pressed a palm against it until it settled.

Nothing about the organism had promised him it was finished.

Clifford didn't move.

Dutch covered Tracy's face.

Brian pushed himself onto his hands.

“I didn't know it would—”

“You knew it hurt,” Clifford said.

Brian looked up.

“You don't understand what it's like.”

Clifford looked down at his own chair.

Brian stopped.

Now, there's an inspirational poster for you.

A little man finally standing on his own two feet, having manufactured both of them out of somebody who repeatedly asked him to stop.

Put it above the gym's water fountain. See if anybody still wants to improve themselves.

Dutch spoke quietly with the net-mender. Tracy's body would remain covered in the room while the old man arranged for it to be taken out. The net-mender would bring him the bill. Dutch nodded.

Brian reached the door long after they finished talking.

He hadn't asked anybody to carry him.

Nobody had offered.

The next morning, the harbor bells began ringing.

Clifford put on his helmet before they went outside.

The black suit and supports had given him a way to walk. They had not made walking free. He used the chair down the uneven road, his gloved hands working the wheels.

Brian walked beside him.

For seventeen steps.

Then Clifford stopped.

“Get on.”

“I can walk.”

“I can die waiting. Get on.”

He lifted Brian onto the closed ledger across his lap.

The little man had wrapped a strip of cloth around his lower body. One corner trailed behind him, making his arrival resemble a furious napkin being served to a man in mourning.

Dutch went ahead.

Beyond the broken outer berth, the water rose.

Not a wave passing through.

Something beneath it was continuing upward.

A long black hull broke the surface. Water ran down steel flanks. A raised command tower emerged, followed by a broad stretch of deck.

Ropes snapped taut on the nearer boats.

Dockworkers ran to ease them.

The vessel's stern churned, holding it off the damaged stone while men in gray came through a hatch.

Dutch took the handles of Clifford's chair and pulled him back from the quay.

Brian grabbed the ledger.

For once, he didn't introduce himself.

The submarine slowed beside the surviving berth.

A mechanical gangway lowered.

At its upper end stood a bald man in a high-collared gray suit.

Scar beside one eye.

Hands folded.

The expression of somebody whose entrance had been designed before any consideration was given to the people expected to witness it.

A crewman came beside him with a small case.

The bald man nodded.

The case opened.

Nothing happened.

He waited.

The crewman touched something inside.

A thin squeal came from a deck speaker.

Three gulls left the quay.

The man in gray closed his eyes.

Then opened them.

“Stop.”

The squeal stopped.

He descended without music.

On the quay, a dockworker was already approaching with questions.

The gray-suited man held up one finger.

“Please. I've just arrived. Allow me to be mysterious for a moment.”

Dutch watched the worker hesitate.

Then he stepped forward.

“Perhaps I can help.”

The bald man looked him over.

“Can you?”

“I know the harbor. I have its cargo records. And you appear to have brought several things this harbor presently lacks.”

“Such as?”

“A building that still works.”

The man looked back at his submarine.

Then at the broken waterfront.

“Yes. Very good.”

He offered a hand.

“Doctor Evil.”

Dutch shook it.

“Dutch van der Linde.”

Dr. Evil waited.

Dutch added, “Doctor.”

“Thank you.”

Clifford wheeled closer.

Dr. Evil saw the helmet.

His expression changed.

Not dramatically.

Just enough.

The controlled little smile acquired an entirely different problem.

Brian stood on the ledger.

“We represent Tampon Pandemic Productions.”

Dr. Evil continued looking at Clifford.

“I see.”

“I'm the founder.”

“Are you?”

“Yes.”

“How unfortunate for everyone who has had to say it.”

Dutch lifted the ledger from Clifford's lap and opened it.

“The name is one part of the operation.”

“One hopes.”

He examined the pages.

The figures and destinations meant little to him yet. They meant something to the crewman who had brought the chart.

Dr. Evil gestured.

The crewman came down.

Dutch kept a hand on the ledger while the man compared its harbor headings with their own chart.

The coast didn't match.

The machinery worked.

The familiar world wasn't waiting on the other side of a badly drawn line.

Dr. Evil looked at Dutch again.

“You understand the authorities here?”

“Some.”

“And the people who supply them?”

“Enough to begin.”

“Excellent. We shall begin.”

Brian raised his voice.

“Before we begin, there is a question of structure.”

Dr. Evil looked down at him.

“Is there?”

“I run conceptual development.”

“Then develop the concept of waiting.”

Dutch closed the ledger.

“We require quarters. Equipment. A place to operate without paying for every night as though we're purchasing the darkness individually.”

“I have quarters.”

“And what would you require?”

“Information. Local contacts. People capable of carrying out an instruction without turning it into a childhood memory.”

Clifford's helmet turned slightly.

Dutch saw it.

Dr. Evil didn't.

“Useful work,” Dutch said. “In exchange for useful resources.”

“Yes.”

“Then I deal directly with you.”

“Obviously. I'm not discussing regional strategy with the gentleman dressed as a discarded bandage.”

Brian looked down at his cloth.

Clifford made a small sound inside the mask.

It might have been a laugh.

Dr. Evil looked at him with immediate, misplaced warmth.

“Please. Come aboard.”

Brian pointed at himself.

“I named this organization.”

“Yes,” Dr. Evil said. “And now we must all be brave.”

Dutch didn't shake on the arrangement yet.

“Before we go up there. My people don't become your property because you have beds.”

Dr. Evil considered him.

“Do your people presently enjoy a great many beds?”

“No.”

“Then let us avoid making this sound like a sacrifice.”

Clifford put one gloved hand against his wheel.

“I keep my weapons.”

“Naturally.”

“And the chair.”

Dr. Evil glanced at the gangway.

“We have lifts.”

Clifford looked toward the deck. A crewman was guiding a wheeled equipment case over the broad metal ramp.

“Doors wide enough?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He rolled forward under his own power.

Dutch watched him.

That wasn't devotion. It was a man choosing an entrance he could actually use.

Dr. Evil had noticed the practical question too.

He simply believed it meant something considerably more famous.

Brian raised both hands.

“And my position?”

Dr. Evil looked down.

“You're on a book.”

“Within the organization.”

“We shall find something suitable.”

“I designed its entire presentation.”

Dr. Evil examined the strip of cloth.

“Perhaps we should begin by finding something suitable for that.”

A dockworker approached with a coil of rope over his shoulder. He looked at the gangway, then at Dr. Evil.

“Who pays for this berth?”

Dr. Evil turned.

“Who owns it?”

“Harbormaster.”

“Then why am I negotiating with the rope?”

The worker's face hardened.

Dutch stepped between them before either could improve the encounter.

“He's asking who to send.”

“Then he should send them.”

The worker looked at Dutch.

Dutch nodded once.

The man went.

Dr. Evil watched him leave.

“This place appears very comfortable asking strangers for money.”

“It was comfortable before the ground broke,” Dutch said. “Now it has reasons.”

He opened the ledger again.

“Your machine can bring people here. It doesn't tell you which warehouse has a floor, which road ends in a hole, or who kept collecting after their goods stopped arriving.”

The crewman with the chart leaned closer.

Dutch turned the book toward him, keeping hold of it.

Two harbor headings matched names on the surviving pier markers. The crewman copied them.

The third referred to a road that now ended at the fissure.

Dutch struck a finger against that line.

“Don't send your men there with a load.”

The crewman marked it.

Dr. Evil watched the change appear on the chart.

At last, something useful had happened in front of him without needing applause.

“Very good.”

He looked at Dutch.

“You will deal with the people onshore.”

“Through you.”

“Through me.”

“And when I advise you against something?”

“I shall consider it.”

“Before it's underway.”

Dr. Evil paused.

“Yes. That would be the traditional sequence.”

Dutch closed the book.

Brian folded his arms.

“I have been asking for a planning meeting for weeks.”

“And look,” Dr. Evil said. “We've had one standing beside you.”

Brian looked at Dutch for support.

Dutch was examining the gangway.

A functioning headquarters. Actual staff. Dry quarters. A man with resources who needed somebody to make those resources useful.

He could work with that.

He could also see exactly how much the little man hated being unnecessary.

“We'll hear your proposals inside,” Dutch told him.

“My proposals?”

“Your useful ones.”

Dr. Evil gave Dutch a small, approving nod.

There it was.

His right-hand man had performed his first unpleasant task before either of them had named the position.

Brian climbed down onto the ledger.

“I'm not agreeing to a subordinate creative role.”

Dutch lifted the book.

Brian grabbed its binding.

The distinction continued up the gangway without improving his height.

The gangway took Clifford's chair without difficulty.

That alone did more for Dutch's opinion of their host than another ten minutes of promises could have achieved.

Inside, lights remained lit without lamps being carried between them. Crew worked at fixed stations. Somebody was washing an actual plate.

Dr. Evil gave Dutch a room near his own and ordered food brought for the visitors.

Clifford asked for water to wash his gloves.

It arrived.

Brian asked who would be responsible for creative direction.

Dr. Evil asked whether anyone had found him trousers.

The difference was not lost on him.

A crewman led them into a compact briefing room.

Gray walls. Metal table. Chairs that matched.

One end of the table had a raised seat.

Dr. Evil inspected it.

Then looked at the crewman.

“Why?”

“For visibility, sir.”

“I'm visible.”

“Yes, sir.”

“I have been visible throughout this conversation.”

The man lowered the chair.

Brian watched this with the dangerous interest of somebody discovering a much better version of his own worst habit.

Dutch sat where Dr. Evil indicated.

Clifford stayed in his chair.

Dr. Evil accepted that immediately.

Brian pulled himself onto the table by the edge.

No one had supplied a smaller chair.

He stood beside an empty glass, breathing harder than he wanted anyone to notice.

Dr. Evil folded his hands.

“Now. Our objectives.”

Dutch opened the ledger.

Dr. Evil glanced at Clifford's helmet.

Then glanced again.

He had been waiting for the appropriate moment.

Unfortunately, his appropriate moment was currently obstructing the useful meeting.

He rang a small bell.

The crewman returned.

“The long case.”

Dutch looked up.

Brian looked toward the door.

Clifford remained still.

The case arrived carried in both hands. Dr. Evil took it personally, set it on the table and opened the clasps.

Inside lay a metal hilt.

He turned the case toward Clifford.

“I have admired your work for a very long time.”

Clifford's helmet tilted.

Dr. Evil smiled.

“A very long time.”

Dutch looked at the weapon.

Brian stepped closer.

“Is that—”

“Not for you.”

Brian stopped.

“I hadn't asked for it.”

“Then we've saved time.”

Dr. Evil lifted the hilt.

“A genuine weapon. Real laser beams.”

He let that sit.

Then, unable to resist:

“Real frickin' laser beams.”

He activated it.

A bright blade sprang from the hilt.

The room's gray surfaces caught its light.

Brian stepped backward so quickly that he struck the empty glass.

It rolled.

Clifford caught it before it fell off the table.

Dr. Evil looked delighted.

Dutch looked at the blade's distance from the ceiling.

“I'd give him room.”

“Of course.”

Dr. Evil switched it off and presented it hilt first.

Clifford accepted it.

The metal settled in his glove.

No mystical recognition passed between man and weapon.

No power filled his limbs.

He had acquired a dangerous object from somebody who had apparently decided that he ought to have one.

“That's quite a gift,” he said.

Dr. Evil's smile widened.

“I thought you would appreciate it.”

Clifford rested the hilt across his lap.

“What's it need?”

The crewman explained the activation control and showed the secured power assembly. He did not promise an endless charge. He pointed out the safe grip and the clearance the blade required.

Clifford listened.

Then asked him to repeat the control sequence.

Brian stood beside the glass.

“His weapon has a briefing.”

Dr. Evil ignored him.

The crewman stepped clear. Clifford pointed the hilt toward the empty end of the room and activated it once.

Light filled the space.

He held it steady.

Switched it off.

“Again,” he told the crewman.

The man repeated the sequence.

Clifford checked the recessed control with his thumb.

Dutch watched the door while another crewman found a strap that could secure the hilt to Clifford's chair without fouling the wheel.

Brian sat on the edge of the case.

“Just so I understand the criteria.”

“No,” Dr. Evil said.

“I haven't stated the criteria.”

“And already they're exhausting.”

It took another half minute to find a place where the strap wouldn't catch Clifford's coat.

He tested the wheel.

Moved his hand past the hilt.

Tested it again.

By the time he looked up, nearly two minutes had passed since Dr. Evil had handed him the weapon.

Clifford put both hands beside his helmet.

“I ought to thank you properly.”

Dr. Evil inclined his head.

Clifford removed the mask.

The room remained exactly the same.

Which was unfortunate.

Some part of Dr. Evil had clearly expected the universe to intervene.

Instead, he was looking at an adult cowboy with a slightly crooked neck, rough unfinished tattoos, and a very sincere expression of gratitude.

“Thank you,” Clifford said.

Dr. Evil stared.

Then looked at the mask.

Then at the hilt already secured to the chair.

Dr. Evil had thought he was giving Darth Vader a lightsaber.

He had instead armed an injured cowboy with a lifetime of unsolicited follow-up questions.

The gift had acquired a strap.

He had personally supervised the strap.

For the first time that morning, the man who owned a submarine appeared to have misplaced the means of leaving a room.

“Yes,” he said.

A pause.

“You're very welcome.”

Clifford waited.

Dr. Evil smiled harder.

Clifford waited patiently. That made it worse. A less considerate man might have interrupted with something useful, such as his fucking name.

“Very welcome, Mister…”

He left enough space for a name.

More than enough.

Brian looked from one face to the other.

Dutch sat back.

Clifford said, “Jack.”

Dr. Evil nodded with immediate, fraudulent recognition.

“Jack.”

“Jack Marston. Though nowadays I go by Clifford.”

“Of course.”

“Not a name I chose.”

Dr. Evil's smile held.

Clifford looked down at the mask.

“Arthur and Chris started that. Before the cliff business. There was a dog involved, originally. Then the tattoos.”

Brian lifted one hand.

Dr. Evil pointed at it without looking.

“No.”

“I wasn't—”

“No.”

Clifford continued.

“My father wanted me to be something else. A man with books, a life that didn't end with a gun in his hand. Then the government killed him. My mother died after. I found the man responsible.”

Dutch's attention sharpened at the mention of John.

Dr. Evil glanced toward the door.

It was still there.

No incoming emergency had come through it.

Clifford rested one hand on the hilt.

“After that I thought I'd finished something. Instead, I came here. Chris pushed me off another cliff, and Arthur—”

Dr. Evil picked up the receiver beside his chair.

It hadn't rung.

“Yes.”

Clifford stopped.

Dr. Evil listened intently to absolutely fucking nothing.

“Yes. This is he.”

Brian's mouth opened.

Dr. Evil looked straight at him.

The little man closed it.

“I understand,” Dr. Evil said.

He covered the receiver.

“My apologies, Jack. A very important call.”

Clifford held the mask against his chest.

“Didn't mean to take up your time.”

“Not at all. Fascinating work.”

Dutch's eyes moved to Dr. Evil.

Dr. Evil kept smiling.

“One of the men will show you where to secure the case. We shall continue shortly.”

Clifford looked at the weapon, then at him.

“Still. Thank you.”

“You are most welcome.”

He waited until Clifford had wheeled out.

Then he pointed toward Brian.

“One of the men has something you can wear. Ask him.”

Brian looked down at his cloth.

Dr. Evil waited until Brian had climbed down the chair beside the table.

Waited while the little man crossed the room on his new legs, visibly furious that an exit could take this long.

Brian stopped at the door.

“I'm still the founder.”

“Excellent. Found the corridor.”

Brian left.

The latch clicked.

Dr. Evil lowered the receiver.

Dutch remained seated.

A long silence.

Then Dr. Evil said, “Who the fuck was that cowboy?”

At the stream, four days later, Chris dried his hands on his pants and came back to the fire.

Daynuh had one hand resting over Mahnuh's muzzle.

Arthur was looking very carefully into his own cup.

Kaze was smiling.

Chris stopped beside his empty seat.

Saw the piece of firewood lying across it.

He looked at the banjo.

Billy said, “I believe we should discuss the menu.”

Season 3, Episodes 43–44: “Audience Participation”

“The menu,” Chris repeated.

From the banjo, Billy said, “Yes.”

Chris lifted the firewood off his seat.

“It's pork.”

“Then we have established the animal. I was hoping to participate in what happens to it.”

Daynuh looked up. “You can participate in eating what the fuck he makes.”

“A popular arrangement among people who have already obtained a seat.”

Billy was full-sized inside BELLY, watching the campsite through Chris's headlamp. Outside, the pan held the last usable pieces of the pork they had brought from the tollhouse, sliced thin with onions. Nothing about the smell suggested a grievance. That hadn't stopped him developing one.

Chris stirred.

“You want it crisp?”

“Along the edge.”

“That's where crisp happens.”

“Then we are approaching agreement.”

Arthur took his cup away from his mouth. “Hell, Chris. Let him order. First customer you've had all week who ain't paying with a dog.”

Mahnuh lifted his head.

“Nobody said chicken,” Daynuh told him.

Kaze slid the pan nearer the heat. Chris immediately moved it back.

“Don't do that.”

“Thought you wanted crisp.”

“I want browned. You put it over there, it's gonna come out looking like a belt somebody pulled out of a crematorium.”

Kaze looked at the pan, then at him.

“Make mine like that.”

Chris considered him.

“I believe you. That's what bothers me.”

He separated a little portion, gave it the hotter edge, then went back to cooking the rest properly. Kaze watched the deliberate accommodation with a small, pleased smile.

A man wanted his dinner ruined in a particular direction, and another man possessed the skill to disappoint him accurately.

I'm Wade, by the way. Still here. Marvel Jesus, voluntarily officiating a pork argument beside a creek because apparently resurrection doesn't come with career counseling.

Billy asked, “Will there be enough?”

Chris stopped stirring.

That was a real question. A very large appetite was watching a very small pan.

“For a taste.”

“I can enjoy a taste.”

“Without telling me you once ate a migrating species?”

“I shall attempt to experience this onion without consulting the fossil record.”

Chris finished cooking. He left the pan on the flat stone beside the fire, put his utensils down and agreed to exchange places.

The change took his whole exterior with it. Flesh folded through the impossible passage, Chris went inward, and Billy's enormous body unfolded outside. Chris was now inside, full-sized, looking out through the existing feed while Billy lowered himself beside the stone.

Arthur had already moved his cup.

Billy inspected the little helping Daynuh set before him.

One careful bite. A moment of stillness.

Then the old fish said, “Oh, that's lovely.”

Inside, Chris stopped reaching for the monitor's volume.

“Yeah?”

“You left the onion sweet.”

“Didn't crowd it.”

“No. You didn't.”

For a few seconds they managed the appalling indignity of liking the same thing without turning it into a fight.

Then Mahnuh approached Billy's empty plate.

Billy lowered one eye toward him.

“I admire an optimist.”

Daynuh called the dog back before optimism became a jurisdictional dispute.

Later, after Billy had enjoyed the fire and chosen to return inside, Chris came back out to a clean pan and a saved portion. Arthur handed it over without comment.

Kaze's deliberately blackened scraps were gone.

Chris looked at the clean patch where they'd been.

“How was it?”

“Crunchy.”

“You ate the onion too?”

“Eventually.”

Chris sat down very slowly.

Before they settled for the night, Daynuh brought up the money he owed the poultry seller.

“Comes out of what we have,” Arthur said.

Chris looked up. “I can—”

“Tell us the price when you have it,” Arthur continued. “Ain't buying you another duck. Settling the ones already missing.”

Kaze nodded toward the banjo.

“Charge him interest.”

Billy said, “On a thigh I never received?”

“Loss of potential income.”

“That would be my loss.”

Kaze smiled. “Sounds expensive.”

Daynuh rubbed his forehead. “You all agreeing to pay, or should I let the fucking birds come back and decide?”

Chris agreed. So did Arthur and Kaze. In the morning Arthur counted nine silver from the common money into Daynuh's hand, with the rest to be settled if the actual price differed.

Daynuh took Mahnuh into town with him.

The poultry seller saw the dog, shut his lower gate and continued serving the customer already in front of him. He wasn't going to conduct his entire remaining life around a pit bull with excellent attendance.

Daynuh stayed outside.

“Need to talk about what he ate.”

“I know what he ate.”

“Then we can skip the fucking description.”

The seller finished wrapping the customer's order before answering.

They settled on nine silver for the first roast and the duck. Daynuh paid with the nine Arthur had given him. Their common money was now two thousand one hundred eleven silver. The seller counted it, put it away, and kept the gate shut.

“There. We understand each other.”

Daynuh looked at Mahnuh.

“Some of us.”

Before he left, the seller called him back.

“Man came asking for your friend. Arthur.”

Daynuh turned.

“What man?”

“Dressed better than the road deserved. Said his name was Dutch. He's waiting at the old lime shelter beyond the fork. Said Arthur could choose whether to come.”

“When?”

“This morning. He's been asking along the road. One of the carters finally sent him here.”

Daynuh looked down the surviving road toward the coast.

The seller added, “Didn't ask for the dog.”

“Smart man.”

When Daynuh brought the message to camp, Arthur's hand paused above his tobacco.

Chris saw it.

“Want company?”

“No.”

Chris waited, letting the answer finish being an answer.

Arthur put the tobacco away.

“If he wanted you, he'd have sent a worse message.”

Kaze looked up from the fire.

“If he asks you to join something, ask what happened to the last thing.”

Arthur gave him a crooked smile.

“I know Dutch.”

“That's why I said ask.”

Arthur went alone, on foot, taking the road through town. Daniel's separate, unopened purse stayed secured on him.

Dutch waited beneath the broken roof of the lime shelter. No followers. No banner. Just the familiar waistcoat, the carefully held posture and a face that looked older when it wasn't addressing anybody.

He rose when Arthur approached.

“Arthur.”

“You look expensive.”

“You look difficult to kill.”

“Been disappointing people.”

They stood a little apart.

Dutch looked at the red mechanical eye under Arthur's hat, then at the part of his right hand visible below the poncho. He had seen what Arthur had become. Seeing it again didn't make it ordinary.

“You came.”

“You asked.”

“It used to take less consideration.”

Arthur sat on the shelter's low stone wall.

“You used to ask for smaller things.”

Dutch accepted the space beside him.

For a while, neither said anything. Beyond the fork a mule dragged an empty cart over a repaired stretch of road. Its owner cursed the wheel, the stones and the mule in an order that suggested no settled theory.

Dutch watched it pass.

“We have a new arrangement.”

“There it is.”

“I'm not asking you to join.”

“Then you can say it slower. I might enjoy it.”

Dutch smiled despite himself.

He described the submarine. Actual rooms, working machinery, men who knew how to run it. A man called Dr. Evil who had resources and needed local knowledge. Dutch had made himself the person through whom that knowledge passed.

Arthur listened without pretending the arrangement sounded worthless.

“Useful.”

“It is.”

“Name's a little hopeful.”

“Which one?”

Arthur looked at him.

Dutch's smile went away.

“Yes. Well.”

He folded his hands.

“There's something I need to ask you. Jack said things about Chris. About you. The way you knew him when he was a boy. The things Chris says about us.”

Arthur's gaze stayed on the road.

“Jack says plenty.”

“Some of it happened.”

“Didn't say it didn't.”

Dutch let that admission remain where Arthur had put it.

“Five days ago our new associate asked me a question I cannot answer honestly by giving him another speech. I told him I would ask you. Finding you took rather longer than asking the question.”

Arthur turned toward him.

“That bad?”

“Who are we to these people?”

The cart's wheel struck a stone. The owner resumed his argument with all three suspects.

Arthur took out a thick cigar and rolled it between his fingers.

“Chris has a machine,” he said. “You sit in front of a picture. Move a little thing with buttons. Picture moves back.”

Dutch waited for the trick.

“And?”

“There's a story in it. Our country. Our gang. Me. You. John.”

Dutch didn't move.

Arthur looked at him properly.

“Called Red Dead Redemption Two.”

“A story about us.”

“A game. Man sitting there makes some of the choices. Some things happen whatever he does.”

Dutch's eyes narrowed.

“Makes your choices.”

“Makes that version's choices. Ain't got his thumb up my ass now.”

The distinction did not amuse Dutch as much as Arthur had hoped.

“You've seen it?”

“Finished it. Another one too. Red Dead Redemption. First one they made. Happens later.”

“The first happens later.”

“Yes.”

“And the second happens first.”

“You're doing fine.”

Dutch stood up.

He took three steps toward the road, stopped, and returned without having found a better world out there.

“And Jack?”

“Grown Jack comes out of that later story. John does most of it. Jack's at the end.”

Dutch looked past Arthur toward the town.

He had heard a young man speak about John's death. He had seen impossible bodies and machinery. Now those experiences had acquired a category that did absolutely nothing to improve them.

“Does it show what happens to all of us?”

“Some.”

“Arthur.”

“I'm not reading you your fucking obituary beside a lime pit.”

Dutch's jaw tightened.

“I didn't ask for that.”

“You were getting there.”

Arthur struck a light and got the cigar going.

“Listen. There's things Chris did sitting at that machine that weren't my life before this mess. There's things I remember that were. And there's things that happened here that no picture ever showed. These hands, for a start.”

He raised his right hand. Metal, living connective tissue and his own practiced gesture, all occupying the same ordinary little movement.

“You hear about something in that story, it don't make it something you've done here.”

Dutch studied him.

“Is that reassurance?”

“It's a warning against getting lazy.”

That landed better. Not kinder. Better.

Dutch sat again.

“He makes jokes about Tahiti.”

“Yes.”

“About plans.”

“You do give him material.”

“And he knows things.”

“Yes.”

“Which he uses as though knowing a man's story grants him ownership of the man.”

Arthur watched smoke leave the end of the cigar.

“You'd hate that.”

Dutch heard the rest without Arthur supplying it.

For a moment, he looked genuinely wounded.

Then he said, “I came to ask a question, Arthur. Not to reclaim you.”

“Then we both got something out of this.”

Dutch took the answer without trying to improve it.

Arthur asked after the others.

That was how he learned Tracy was dead.

Dutch didn't call it an unfortunate complication. He told him what Brian had done, what Clifford had tried, and what the net-mender had found when they returned.

Arthur lowered the cigar.

“And you're keeping him.”

“He's aboard.”

“Wasn't what I asked.”

“No.”

Dutch's gaze hardened.

“I haven't mistaken him for innocent.”

Arthur looked at the road again.

“Daniel's gone.”

Dutch turned.

Arthur gave him the pieces he actually knew. The yard. The recovered body. The damage that told them there had been a fight. No name for the other fighter. They had buried him above the stream.

Dutch removed his hat.

No speech arrived.

Good. We don't have to put every dead man on a little revolving stand and wait for a lesson to come out. Sometimes the useful thing a mouth can do is close.

When Dutch put his hat back on, he asked, “Is there anything you need?”

“A name.”

“I'll listen.”

Arthur nodded once. It was an actual offer and an actual acceptance, small enough that neither had to pretend it repaired everything else.

Before leaving, Dutch asked whether men from the ship could speak with Chris and Arthur about the games. Not Dutch's men from a vanished gang. Dr. Evil's crew, sent to understand the people their employer had just hired.

Arthur considered it.

“They can ask. Tell them to come to this shelter tomorrow. Don't bring a fucking wagon of them.”

“Two.”

“And tell them not to call Jack a costume.”

Dutch looked at him.

“I believe that particular problem has already introduced itself.”

He took the coast road back. The journey occupied the rest of the day and part of the night; the broken road didn't become shorter because the conversation had been important.

At the port he stopped at the net-mender's house. Twelve silver paid the agreed charge for Tracy's handling and burial. The old man pointed him toward the small burial ground where the body had been taken. Dutch went there before returning to the ship.

He came aboard with fifty-four silver left in the purse, road dust on his clothes and no inclination to give Brian a report.

Dr. Evil received him in the briefing room.

“Well?”

Dutch sat.

“According to Arthur, we come from a game called Red Dead Redemption Two. Jack comes from Red Dead Redemption One.”

Dr. Evil kept his hands folded.

“A game.”

“Played on a machine.”

“Yes. I had reached that possibility before cards.”

Dutch explained the order.

Dr. Evil listened to the second being first and the first being later with the expression of a man discovering that even the cowboys had brought a franchise.

“So Jack is your sequel.”

“Not precisely.”

“And you are his prequel.”

“If you prefer.”

“I don't. I find it needlessly hostile.”

He stood.

“Arthur has agreed to speak with two of your men,” Dutch said. “Chris may explain the machine.”

Dr. Evil turned back.

“Excellent. Have them prepare a study.”

“Of what?”

“The games. Both games. Relevant personal details. Interests. References. Things a longtime admirer would naturally know.”

Dutch allowed a careful pause.

Dr. Evil added, “To supplement what I already know.”

“Of course.”

“I would have done it myself. However, I am occupied.”

“With the organization.”

“Exactly.”

Dutch let him have that.

Now. There are men who will admit they made a mistake. There are men who will double down. Then there's this magnificent chrome-plated testicle, who had commissioned a research expedition because saying “Sorry, I thought you were Darth Vader” would apparently bring down the foundations of civilization.

The following morning, two crewmen reached the lime shelter. Arthur met them and brought them to the stream. Chris looked up from sorting his gear.

“What're they here for?”

“Your game.”

Chris put down the part in his hand.

“What about it?”

“They want to understand it.”

The change in his expression was disgusting.

It was like watching somebody tell a raccoon that the bin had a basement.

The older crewman carried a notebook. The younger had a small portable recorder from the ship. With no connection home, they would have to bring back what they could learn here.

They had two men who knew the games, access to an actual copy if its owner agreed, and a very strange afternoon ahead of them.

“Who's asking?” Chris said.

“Our employer.”

“Dutch's new guy?”

“Yes.”

“And he wants to know about Red Dead?”

The crewman nodded.

Chris looked at Arthur.

Arthur's expression said that he was not doing this for him.

“Billy?” Chris asked.

From the banjo came a leisurely, “Two guests. Briefly. No wandering.”

One crewman looked at the instrument.

“Was that—”

“Your host,” Chris said. “Be polite. He's got enough teeth to comb a fucking waterfall.”

Chris put down his exterior gear before he and Billy exchanged. Billy emerged as Chris went inside; the crewmen stepped backward, then stopped when Arthur didn't.

Billy lowered himself until his enormous face was level with theirs.

“Gentlemen.”

The younger man's recorder clicked against his own belt.

“You are welcome to visit. You are not welcome to explore. Is that understood?”

Both said yes.

Billy opened his jaw. One guest at a time, the impossible intake took them through the protected route into the persistent living interior, away from the digestive space. Arthur stayed outside. Billy remained the sole exterior body.

Inside, Chris met them on the inhabited platform and led them directly to his gaming area. Beyond their permitted path, the place continued in shapes and sounds they hadn't been invited to investigate.

The older man stared at the functioning screen.

Chris pointed to the seat.

“That's the game. This is the controller. Don't touch the buttons unless I give it to you.”

The younger man raised the recorder.

“May I?”

“Film the screen. Leave my room out of it.”

He waited until the lens was pointed where he'd said.

Then he sat down and loaded the existing game.

The picture opened on the same saved game Chris had been playing. He kept the controller in his own hands, steering the view while the younger man adjusted the recorder to keep the screen legible.

The older crewman began with a sensible question.

“Which one is Mr. van der Linde?”

Chris showed him.

Then he stopped talking for a second.

Because there he was. Game Dutch, in a world where the familiar voices still happened in their familiar places. Outside, somewhere on a submarine, the living Dutch was making a different set of choices with a dead twin brother behind him.

Chris rubbed his jaw.

“Don't get the two confused.”

The crewman looked at him.

“That's a record. That's not a leash.”

He returned to the controller before the moment could grow comfortable.

The younger crewman asked whether Chris could hold the picture still while he adjusted the recorder.

Chris paused the game.

Everything on the screen stopped.

Outside, a distant bird called. Something heavy shifted above them as Billy made himself comfortable.

The crewman looked toward the sound.

“Does that work on—”

“No.”

“I only meant—”

“No. That man outside with the red eye keeps walking. You pause this Dutch, the actual Dutch still gets up and finds a way to need money.”

The older crewman put his pen down.

“It's a recording with choices.”

“Now you're getting it.”

Chris unpaused. Movement resumed inside the picture.

The younger man checked the screen through the recorder, then made a small adjustment.

“Ready.”

The interview became considerably less orderly once the crewman asked why people found Dutch recognizable.

“The plans,” Chris said. “Faith. Money. Tahiti. People back home kept taking those things and making the same jokes in different ways.”

“The people in the game?”

“People playing it. Whole audience of motherfuckers watching a man steer a family toward a wood chipper while asking whether everybody still believes in lumber.”

He stopped himself.

“Don't put that last part in the friendly notes.”

The pen paused.

“What are the friendly notes?”

“Whatever keeps your boss from saying some horrible shit to the actual man.”

The younger crewman wrote that down too.

Chris explained a meme. The older crewman tried writing down the definition, then crossed out half of it.

“So the same joke is repeated.”

“Changed. Sometimes it's just a picture. Sometimes you take a man's face and put it on something that makes his whole life look stupid.”

“Why?”

“Because people got spare time and no fucking supervision.”

“And Mr. van der Linde participates?”

“No. That's the part you need to underline.”

The younger man asked about the old man with back trouble.

“Uncle. Lumbago. That's another one people run into the ground. Doesn't mean every man from that country with a bad back is Uncle. You understand?”

“Yes.”

“Tell your boss twice.”

The recorder kept running.

“Dutch doesn't know he's got a fanbase,” Chris said. “You walk up grinning about Tahiti, he's gonna think you're either offering a boat or being a dick.”

The older man nodded. “Understood.”

They asked about the first game.

“Arthur finished that one,” Chris said. “Don't take me guessing as research.”

When they came back out, Billy released them onto the same bank where they'd entered. Their recorder and notebook came with them. Chris remained inside until Billy chose to exchange back.

Arthur gave them the first game's broad story from his own completed play. He distinguished John from adult Jack, the later setting from Dutch's own time, and the game's history from what had happened here. He didn't offer a complete recitation of everybody's death.

The older crewman asked what Jack liked.

“Books,” Arthur said.

“Any particular—”

“Ask him. He's got a mouth. You've been hiring it by the hour.”

The younger man lowered the recorder.

“Anything we should avoid?”

Arthur looked at both of them until the question stopped sounding routine.

“Don't use what happens to people as a party trick.”

He glanced at the notes already headed Endings and Personal History.

“And there's the sickness. I had tuberculosis. It's cured. You need to understand the story, write both parts. You want something funny to say to Dutch, pick something else.”

The older man wrote the distinction out in full. He read it back. Arthur nodded.

The research was accurate. What happened next would require a more expensive form of stupidity.

They left before evening, carrying filmed RDR2 material, Chris's account of community jokes, and Arthur's clearly attributed account of the first game. It was a bounded study, not two magically completed playthroughs.

On the ship the next morning, the crew laid the material before Dr. Evil.

He approved of the recorder. He approved of the labeled notes. He approved less of the section headed Things Not to Say to the People Concerned.

“This seems negative.”

“It is a precaution, sir.”

“I've asked for an understanding of their culture, not a list of ways to disappoint them.”

“The distinction is important.”

Dr. Evil studied the first page.

“A meme.”

“A joke repeated and changed by the audience. These examples come from Mr. Chris's recollection of that audience.”

“Excellent. Familiarity.”

“They are not familiar with them, sir.”

“Then I shall introduce them. Already we have found common ground.”

The older crewman looked down at his own warning section.

Somewhere in every organization there is a competent man watching a catastrophe receive stationery.

Dr. Evil selected three notes.

“Tomorrow's meeting. Have this room arranged as usual.”

“Yes, sir.”

“And have somebody remove this heading.”

“Which heading?”

“Suggested Casual Remarks.”

He considered it.

“It makes them sound prepared.”

By the time Dutch arrived for the next briefing, the papers had been placed out of sight.

That was the first warning.

The second was Dr. Evil standing beside his chair instead of sitting in it.

The third was the smile.

Dutch had seen confidence, appetite, concealed anger and men making a great deal of noise because they were frightened. This expression was a new little peninsula of human danger.

Dr. Evil held out a hand.

“Dutch. I have a plan.”

Dutch shook it.

“I should hope so.”

Dr. Evil waited.

Dutch waited too, politely enough to make it an act of labor.

“A plan,” Dr. Evil repeated.

“Yes.”

“For which we shall require faith.”

Dutch looked toward the table.

“And a map, perhaps.”

Dr. Evil smiled wider.

“Exactly. You're enjoying this.”

“Immensely.”

Every syllable had shoes on.

Clifford came through the door behind him, propelling his chair. His mask rested in his lap. The real lightsaber remained secured beside the wheel, the gift still very much given.

Brian followed in altered crew clothing. Someone had shortened the legs and sleeves, then shortened them again. The collar remained much too large. He looked like the sole survivor of a clothesline accident.

A narrow wooden step had been placed beside his chair. He climbed it without help, sat down, then discovered that his eyes were level with the table's edge.

He stood again.

Dr. Evil saw none of this. His attention had reached Clifford.

“Jack.”

“Doctor.”

“I understand you're a reader.”

“Yes.”

“Excellent. We have books.”

Clifford glanced at Dutch.

Dutch moved his attention to the ledger with the grim concentration of a man trying to become a piece of furniture.

“What kind?” Clifford asked.

Dr. Evil had not prepared for a second question about books.

“Bound.”

“Fiction?”

“Some of it. I haven't verified every claim.”

Brian gave a short, involuntary laugh.

Dr. Evil looked at him.

The laugh perished standing up.

Clifford said, “I'd appreciate a look.”

“Of course. I knew you would.”

The young man had sincerely accepted a gift and sincerely answered a question about a hobby. Somehow he had done both in ways that made his employer need a door.

They sat.

Dr. Evil folded his hands.

“Before we begin, I want you to know that this organization values its people.”

Brian waited.

“Its individual talents.”

Brian leaned forward.

“Its history.”

Brian opened his mouth.

Dr. Evil turned to Dutch.

“Tahiti.”

Dutch closed his own mouth.

Clifford looked down at his gloves.

A beat passed.

“I'm sorry?” Dutch said.

“Tahiti,” Dr. Evil repeated, with the confidence of a man tapping the correct password into a bomb.

“Yes.”

“Mangoes.”

Dutch's hand stopped on the ledger.

That word had Bob in it. A painting. Fruit carried for somebody who would never finish what he was looking at.

Dr. Evil had no idea. His notes had an island and a farming joke. They did not contain Dutch's dead twin.

“A fine place,” Dutch said.

“Exactly. I knew you'd get it.”

Clifford reached for his water.

His chair made a small sound against the floor.

Dr. Evil noticed the angle of his bare neck, then the unfinished marks visible above the collar and across his face.

He remembered the healthy adult Jack described in Arthur's recorded account, and the unmarked boy Chris had shown his men in the earlier game. Neither description explained a cowboy who currently looked assembled during a prison blackout.

Dr. Evil glanced at the crewman near the door.

The crewman stood ready for an actual instruction.

They hadn't dug deeply enough. Obviously. There must be some additional version. Some extended material. A director somewhere had become unnecessarily intimate with a staircase.

“Everything all right?” Clifford asked.

“Perfectly. A familiar face.”

Clifford's fingers touched the collar, hiding a little more of the rough work without a word.

Dutch looked up.

Dr. Evil returned to his papers.

“Now. The public.”

Brian prepared to speak.

“A recurring weakness in criminal enterprise is that people don't appreciate the enterprise.”

“Because it's criminal?” Brian asked.

“That is one of the difficulties, yes.”

“You're describing a reason.”

“Thank you. We can already see the value of your contribution.”

Dutch opened the cargo ledger.

“The port has storage space people cannot safely use. Broken roads make deliveries unreliable. Merchants lose goods, then pay twice as much to move what's left.”

Dr. Evil nodded.

This was the useful part. Men, machinery, a secure headquarters and somebody who could deal with local people. There was money to be made in remaining functional while everything around you had holes in it.

“We offer security,” Dutch continued. “Storage. Escorts along routes we've actually checked. We charge for what we can provide.”

“And later,” Dr. Evil said, “they discover how inconvenient it is to go elsewhere.”

Dutch met his eye.

“Later.”

Brian put both hands on the table.

“We need customers before we get proprietary about their inconvenience.”

Dr. Evil pointed at him.

“Yes. Very good.”

Brian stopped, surprised to have been right in a way somebody admitted.

Dr. Evil continued, “You will be delighted to learn that I have anticipated this.”

He rang for the crewman.

The man put a large covered board beside the table.

Brian frowned.

“Is this a presentation?”

“You may stand if you require a better view.”

“I am standing.”

“Then we have done everything we can.”

Dr. Evil got up.

Dutch did not let his expression change.

The board remained covered while its owner decided where to place himself. His first position blocked it. His second placed him behind the cover. The crewman moved the stand six inches. Dr. Evil moved it back three.

Then, apparently remembering that ordinary people enjoyed ordinary humor, he looked at Clifford.

“How is the lumbago?”

Clifford stared.

Dutch's eyes closed for half a second.

“My what?”

“The back. A little joke.”

Clifford looked down at his supported legs.

“Ah.”

“From your world.”

“I see.”

Dr. Evil nodded sympathetically.

Clifford made an expression that could, with sufficient money behind it, be mistaken for a smile.

“Very good.”

Oh, Jack. That man has just taken a community joke about a lazy old bastard and applied it to your spinal injury with the bedside manner of a potato peeler.

And you thanked him.

I'm not saying the lightsaber purchased your dignity. I'm saying its monthly payment has just cleared.

Dutch asked, “Shall we see the proposal?”

“In a moment.”

Dr. Evil checked a note below the board.

“We should not rush. Unlike Arthur, we have time before the tuberculosis—”

He stopped.

The room stopped with him.

There it was. The wrong line from the wrong section. He'd read beyond the friendly notes because he wanted to understand the references; then he'd carried a source-story death into a room containing people who loved the man.

Dutch's face became very still.

“Tuberculosis?”

Dr. Evil put the note down.

“In the game.”

“What happens in the game?”

Brian looked between them.

For once, he didn't interrupt.

Dr. Evil's eyes went to the crewman. The man didn't smile, nod or invent a different meaning for tuberculosis.

“The material described an illness,” Dr. Evil said.

“Arthur's illness.”

“Yes.”

Dutch sat back.

He remembered the mechanical hand. The eye. Arthur saying there were things here no picture had shown.

The older crewman spoke from the door.

“Mr. Morgan said the illness has been cured. We recorded that separately from the game's history.”

Dutch looked toward him, then nodded. The information helped. Hearing it this way still made him want to speak to Arthur himself.

Clifford spoke quietly.

“That record isn't what's happening in front of you.”

Dutch turned toward him.

Clifford didn't offer to explain Arthur's current body. He didn't know enough to make that promise.

Dr. Evil said, “Precisely. A historical reference.”

He had recognized his mistake. Unfortunately, recognition had arrived in the vehicle immediately behind the mistake, and everybody had already been hit by the first one.

Dutch looked back at him.

“Thank you for clarifying.”

Courteous. Controlled. An answer that allowed the employer to continue without granting him a laugh.

Dr. Evil picked up the edge of the cover.

“Our brand.”

He pulled.

The cloth came away.

On the board, in enormous neat lettering, stood Tampon Pandemic Productions.

Beneath it, someone had drawn a small circle containing the letters T and M.

Brian went absolutely motionless.

Dr. Evil stood beside the board.

“The name,” he said, “will be trademarked.”

Brian looked at Dutch.

Then at Clifford.

Then at the bald man unveiling Brian's own fucking organization as though he'd dragged it from a burning building.

“No.”

Dr. Evil blinked.

“I'm sorry?”

“That is my name.”

“Brian is your name.”

“The organization.”

“Yes. I know which organization we're discussing. I've had it written quite large.”

Brian hauled himself from his chair onto the table.

This time nobody had to wonder whether he intended to participate.

“I created Tampon Pandemic Productions.”

“And look how far it has come.”

“I named it.”

“I have chosen to retain that despite several opportunities to recover.”

“You don't get to take it.”

“Take it? Brian. I'm protecting it.”

“From who?”

Dr. Evil gestured toward the door.

“People.”

“Name one.”

“You would like me to identify a thief before he has stolen it?”

Brian stared at him.

Dr. Evil waited.

Dutch looked at the board.

An ocean of unpleasant comprehension passed between the two cowboys without either putting a boat into it.

Brian jabbed a finger at the little symbol.

“What is that?”

“A trademark symbol.”

“You just drew it.”

“I supervised.”

“That doesn't make you own the name.”

“I haven't said the process is complete.”

“Then why is it already on there?”

“Optimism. We were discussing faith earlier. You should try to keep up.”

Brian paced along the table's edge. His new legs were steadier now; anger gave him somewhere to take them.

“You arrived, what, a week ago? I built this before you ever met us. I came up with the concept, the identity, the entire presentation. I am the founder.”

“Nobody has taken that away.”

“You're putting your name on my name.”

Dr. Evil pointed to the board.

“My name isn't on it.”

“Your ownership.”

“Your concerns about my handwriting are becoming increasingly abstract.”

“I don't care who wrote it!”

“Then he has done an excellent job.”

The crewman stared at the wall.

Brian stopped pacing.

“You think because you've got a boat—”

“Submarine.”

“A boat that hides.”

Clifford looked down so abruptly that Dutch nearly did too.

Dr. Evil's smile thinned.

“A functioning headquarters.”

“It can't even stand up.”

“It's a submarine, Brian. Its posture is appropriate.”

“You know what I mean.”

“Increasingly less.”

Brian looked toward Dutch again.

“You know I named it.”

Dutch closed the ledger.

“You did.”

Dr. Evil turned his head.

Dutch met his gaze without apology.

“He did.”

Brian drew a breath.

There. One witness. One actual thing they couldn't shift beneath him.

“Thank you.”

Dutch continued, “And if we mean to sell protection, we ought to begin by understanding what belongs to the people at this table.”

Dr. Evil considered the sentence.

Brian did too.

Neither particularly enjoyed where Dutch had placed himself inside it.

“The name remains Brian's contribution,” Dutch said. “Our operations are a different question. The ship, the men, the equipment. Those are yours, Doctor. Nobody benefits by pretending one thing is the other.”

Dr. Evil rested a hand against the board.

“That is precisely the distinction I was about to make.”

“I thought you might.”

Brian looked at him with naked disgust.

“You were not.”

“Brian.”

“You just stood up and pulled a fucking curtain off it.”

“A cover.”

“It had suspense!”

“Would you have preferred I drop it on you without warning?”

Brian's mouth opened.

For a beautiful second there was simply too much wrong with the sentence for him to choose an entrance.

Dr. Evil used that second.

“Very well. We shall determine the appropriate arrangement before proceeding. You will be consulted.”

“Before.”

“Yes.”

“And that comes off the board.”

Dr. Evil looked at the little symbol.

Then at Brian.

Then he took the cloth and draped it across the lower corner, hiding the T and M.

“There.”

Brian stared.

“You covered it.”

“An elegant provisional solution.”

Nothing had been filed. No local authority had granted anybody anything. The room was still aboard Dr. Evil's vessel, his men still answered him, and Brian's victory consisted of making the attempted theft wear a little blanket.

But the objection had changed the plan. That mattered too.

Clifford touched the hilt beside his chair.

“Thank you again for this.”

Dr. Evil turned toward him with almost indecent relief.

“You're most welcome, Jack.”

“First new weapon I've been given that came with anybody explaining how not to hurt myself.”

“Naturally.”

“My father—”

Dr. Evil's hand moved an inch toward the receiver.

Clifford continued, “—would have asked what you wanted for it.”

The hand stopped.

“Nothing,” Dr. Evil said.

Clifford nodded.

“Good.”

Then he looked at the covered corner of the board.

Brian sat down on the table.

Dutch reopened the ledger.

And at last, with all the comforting friction of a man getting his penis out of a zipper one tooth at a time, the meeting returned to the fucking business.

The poultry seller's worker had reached the port two days earlier. He had spent one day asking around and another waiting for an answer from the men aboard the gray ship. Dutch brought his actual request into the briefing: secure storage and a guarded delivery route for food sold inland.

Not a government conspiracy. Not a secret military banquet. One merchant, some genuinely valuable stock, and a dog who had made returning to the old arrangements intolerable.

Dr. Evil approved a small trial. Two men would escort the next load. An empty stone storeroom beside the seller's loading yard could be used if the seller agreed to the price. Clifford would inspect its access and oversee the first delivery.

Brian asked, “And me?”

“Observe. Offer useful recommendations.”

“Do you hear yourself?”

“Very clearly. We repaired the speaker.”

Dutch asked for the worker to be brought aboard so they could agree on what was actually being provided.

Dr. Evil looked at him.

“Tell him Tampon Pandemic Productions will secure his poultry.”

Brian stared down at the covered corner of the board.

The name sounded considerably worse when somebody else was finally using it successfully.

After the others left, Dutch remained long enough to write a message for the worker to carry back. He wrote it himself.

Arthur. I would like to know whether you are well. Not asking what happens in the story. Asking you. Dutch.

He folded it and put it away until the worker was ready to leave.

Then he went to look at the route with Clifford.

Two mornings later, Chris stood outside the poultry shop watching men in gray unload a cart.

Daynuh was talking to the seller. Mahnuh sat beside his leg. Arthur had received Dutch's note, read it twice, and was now borrowing a piece of paper from the counter.

Kaze had come because Chris said someone was getting paid to guard lunch.

That was enough of a destination for him.

Clifford waited beside the storeroom door, masked again, one hand on his wheel. The road had coated his wheels in pale dust, and the two crewmen with him were glad to put down their loads.

He saw Chris.

His hand stopped.

Chris saw him too.

Then saw the hilt secured to the chair.

“Where'd you get that?”

Clifford said nothing.

Chris leaned slightly for a better look.

“That's new.”

Clifford's gloved hand settled over it.

“Yes.”

From the banjo Billy said, “Christopher. Perhaps admire it from where you are.”

Chris stopped leaning.

Kaze smiled at the chair, the armed crewmen, the food being unloaded.

“Good to see the business improving.”

Clifford's helmet turned toward him.

“It has.”

The men kept unloading, setting closed tins beside the still-locked storeroom.

For a moment, Kaze looked almost disappointed.

Then he looked interested.

Brian emerged from behind the cart in his altered gray clothes, carrying a small notebook against his chest.

Chris's face changed.

He looked at the little man's feet.

Then at his waist.

Then toward Arthur.

Arthur gave him one short shake of the head.

Chris understood enough to lose the joke he'd been about to make.

Brian looked past him toward Mahnuh.

“That the dog?”

Daynuh turned.

“What about him?”

“We've been retained to prevent a recurrence.”

Mahnuh looked at the notebook.

Chris looked at Brian's new trousers.

“They put you on the low shelf?”

Brian ignored him with an effort that involved his entire face.

“The vulnerable point,” he told the worker, “is during transfer. Once the doors are secured, the arrangement is adequate. While they're open, we need one man watching access and another handling the stock.”

Clifford nodded to the nearest crewman.

The man took that position.

At the storeroom, the seller struggled with the old chain across the doors. The key turned. The rusted link through the staple wouldn't move.

Clifford asked him what stood behind the doors.

“Empty room.”

“Stand clear.”

He positioned his chair beside the wall, drew the new hilt, and kept its business end pointed away from everybody. The blade lit. One short controlled movement parted the plain iron link. Hot ends dropped against the stone.

He switched the weapon off before the seller approached.

Chris had stopped talking.

The seller pulled the doors open. A crewman replaced the old chain with the sound one they'd brought to secure the room.

Clifford fastened the hilt back beside his wheel.

“Now you can unload.”

It was good advice. It worked.

Mahnuh's nose lifted. He could smell the food, see the moving tins and understand perfectly well where they were going. He couldn't walk through a shut door, and nobody had left a basket lying beside his feet.

Daynuh touched his shoulder.

“Stay.”

The dog settled.

The delivery finished without a single lost bird.

The seller counted the tins, checked the inner latch and nodded to Clifford.

“That's better.”

Clifford accepted the acknowledgment with a small inclination of his helmet.

Brian stood beside him.

The seller looked at the larger man again.

“Tell your employer.”

Clifford said, “I will.”

The seller paid the agreed five silver for the trial delivery and storage. Clifford secured it separately for the company; it wasn't his personal share, and no one had settled the operation's eventual division of profits.

Brian closed his notebook.

Kaze saw it.

“They hear you?”

Brian looked at him.

“What?”

“When you told them where to stand.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Kaze's smile didn't improve.

“Wouldn't want to do the useful part and watch somebody else take it home.”

He walked away before Brian decided whether to answer.

Chris watched him go.

Billy murmured, “That was unnecessary.”

“He knows.”

Arthur finished his reply. He gave it to Clifford, not Brian.

“For Dutch.”

Clifford took it.

“You read it?” Arthur asked.

“No.”

“Good. Wouldn't improve your morning.”

The young man tucked it away.

Inside, Arthur had written: I'm well. That part was fixed before you got here. If your doctor wants to know something about me, he can stop asking the fucking audience.

Clifford didn't know that. Dutch would have to receive it first.

Daynuh took Mahnuh down the lane while Chris spoke to the seller about the way he'd seasoned the duck. This time the conversation involved no concealed food and no claim of ownership. The two cooks disagreed about whether the juniper needed to be crushed.

They were still disagreeing when Brian came to the loading gate.

The workers had gone inside to count the empty containers. Clifford had moved around the front with the driver to discuss the next departure. The dog was outside the yard, visible down the lane beside Daynuh.

On the cart sat a separate covered dish.

The seller had prepared it as a complimentary meal for Dr. Evil: one roasted bird, a little pan gravy, his father's juniper under the skin. A successful first delivery deserved a gesture to the person paying the men who protected it.

Brian had heard the explanation.

He had watched the dish being set apart.

He looked through the gate at Mahnuh.

Then at the covered meal.

He put his notebook under one arm.

He was looking at the first useful thing he'd done in the organization he had founded, and at the special dinner being sent to somebody else.

He climbed onto the low cart step.

Lifted the cover.

And whistled.

Down the lane, Mahnuh's head turned.

Chris heard it from the shop doorway.

The seller was still explaining his seasoning.

Brian picked up a loose shred of roast from the edge of the dish and dropped it beside the open gate.

Chris stopped listening.

Through his headlamp, Billy saw exactly what he saw.

“Well,” the fish said softly.

Brian climbed down behind the cart.

Mahnuh rose.

Daynuh turned with him.

Chris looked from the food to the hiding place.

Then he stepped into the gate and shut it before the dog arrived.

Mahnuh stopped on the other side, nose working.

Chris crouched.

Picked up the scrap.

Looked beneath the cart.

“You trying to steal your own fucking security problem?”

Brian froze.

Billy's pleasure rolled out of the banjo.

“Christopher. I believe we have found the man feeding the dog.”

Daynuh reached the gate.

Looked at the scrap in Chris's hand.

Then at Chris.

Chris stood.

“I can actually explain this one.”

From behind the cart came Brian's small, furious voice.

“That was a controlled assessment.”

Clifford appeared at the far end of the yard.

The seller came to the doorway.

Kaze stopped halfway down the lane and turned around.

Billy said, “Do let him finish. I've been hoping to hear how that sounds from outside.”

Clifford rolled toward the cart.

“Come out.”

Brian came out.

The seller looked at the uncovered dish, the scrap in Chris's fingers and the dog waiting behind the gate.

“That was for your employer.”

“I was checking whether—”

“You called him,” Chris said.

“I didn't call him by name.”

“Neither does a fucking dinner bell.”

Daynuh took the scrap from Chris's hand. Mahnuh watched it leave with the concentration of an animal whose main argument had just changed lawyers.

Clifford looked at Brian.

“You'll explain it to him.”

“It wasn't stolen.”

“Because he shut the gate.”

Clifford indicated Chris. That acknowledgment cost him something. He made it anyway.

Brian looked up at the blank black mask.

“He wouldn't even have known.”

For a moment, the yard became quiet enough to hear Mahnuh breathing.

Clifford said, “Put the cover back.”

Brian did.

The delivery had worked. The food was safe. Now the founder of Tampon Pandemic Productions had to travel home beside a roast he'd tried to embezzle through a pit bull.

Chris put his hands on top of the gate.

Daynuh studied him.

“You stopped him.”

“Don't sound so fucking surprised.”

Billy said, “A useful precedent.”

Chris looked down at the banjo.

Then back at Daynuh.

“Can I have the gravy?”

Behind him, Kaze started laughing.
