Season 3, Episode 45: “Founding Father”

“I fucking hate him.”

Clifford kept looking down the road.

Beside him, Brian sat against an empty poultry container, his little boots planted wide to stop the cart's movement throwing him sideways.

“He wasn't even there,” Brian continued. “Was he there when I named the organization?”

“No.”

“Exactly. Then he turns up in a submarine and everybody starts acting like he invented leadership.”

Clifford adjusted the covered roast between the containers.

Brian watched him.

“You're taking better care of his chicken than you are of me.”

“Chicken didn't open itself.”

Brian turned away.

The wheels carried them toward the coast through the dark. Behind them lay the poultry shop, the closed gate, and several witnesses to Brian's attempt to feed Dr. Evil's complimentary dinner to Mahnuh.

He'd had the whole return journey to improve his explanation.

So far he'd improved it into six explanations that couldn't survive being said in the same room.

By morning, he'd selected sabotage assessment.

By the time he saw Dr. Evil, he'd decided to wait and hear what Clifford said first.

Dutch met the cart at the berth. He received the five silver from the successful delivery, keeping them separate from the older company purse. Then Clifford handed him Arthur's folded reply.

Dutch read it.

For a moment, the coast and its problems had to wait outside his face.

He folded the paper carefully.

“He's well?” Clifford asked.

“He says he is.”

“Good.”

Brian looked between them.

“Can we go inside? I've been sleeping against a cage.”

Dutch put Arthur's letter away.

“How did the delivery go?”

“Stock arrived,” Clifford said. “Client paid. Asked about doing it again.”

Dutch nodded.

“And the chicken?”

Clifford looked down at Brian.

Brian smiled without pleasure.

“There's a technical component.”

“Of course there is,” Dutch said.

Dr. Evil was waiting in the submarine's briefing room when they brought the covered dish aboard.

He let the roast be set before him. Lifted the cover. Breathed in.

Then he looked toward the doorway.

“Excellent. Proof of a satisfied client.”

Brian stepped forward.

Dr. Evil glanced down.

“And Brian.”

Dutch pulled out a chair. Clifford brought his own into position. Brian climbed onto a low storage box beside the table, getting his eyes above its edge.

Dr. Evil watched the final little scramble.

“We have chairs.”

“I can't see over the table from the chairs.”

“Neither can I see the floor when you speak from it. Yet I have adapted.”

Brian dragged his notebook onto the tabletop.

The doctor cut a piece of chicken.

“Report.”

Clifford gave it to him. The actual transfer. The rusted chain. The clear space before he used the lightsaber. The gate. The payment.

Dr. Evil nodded appreciatively.

“Very good, Clifford.”

Brian leaned forward.

“The receiving precautions were my—”

“I'm aware you attended.”

“I designed the precautions.”

“Then you have also done very well.”

Brian stopped.

The doctor ate another piece.

“At a smaller portion of the task.”

There it was.

Brian's smile went away.

Clifford finished.

“Then he opened your dish and called the dog.”

Dr. Evil's knife stopped moving.

He looked at the roast.

Then at Brian.

“This dish.”

“A vulnerability assessment.”

“My dish.”

“The cover was unsecured. I demonstrated that an interested animal could compromise—”

“My chicken.”

Brian took a breath.

“You're focusing on the object.”

Dr. Evil set down his knife.

“Yes, Brian. Because you attempted to feed the object to a dog. I find the object central to the discussion.”

Dutch sat back, letting Brian's chosen explanation reach the place it had been heading all night.

“Did the dog eat any?” the doctor asked.

“No,” Clifford said. “Chris shut the gate.”

“Chris.”

“Yes.”

Dr. Evil turned to Dutch.

“Please make a note. The man who isn't employed here has protected my lunch from the man who is.”

Brian pushed his notebook forward.

“The same man who created your security arrangement.”

Dr. Evil looked at the notebook.

“Did you include a section about you?”

“No.”

“An oversight.”

Brian began talking faster.

“I identified an access weakness. It was a live scenario. If you send somebody into a club to test the sound, you don't scream because he touches the fucking mixer. You let him demonstrate where the feedback is.”

Dr. Evil waited.

Brian pointed at the roast.

“That's the mixer.”

The doctor looked at it.

“I don't want to hear your chicken album.”

Clifford lowered his head.

Brian caught the movement.

“You can laugh. It's fine.”

“Thank you,” Dr. Evil said.

He laughed once, deliberately, directly at Brian.

Then resumed cutting.

Brian's fingers tightened around his pencil until the wood creaked.

“Nobody listened when I said the transfer worked because of what I told them.”

Dutch spoke at last.

“It was useful advice. I'll record it.”

“Oh, you'll record it.” Brian looked toward the doctor. “He gets a meal. I get a fucking footnote.”

Dr. Evil inspected a piece of skin on his fork.

“Would you like some?”

Brian hesitated.

“Yes.”

The doctor ate it.

“I'm sorry. I meant the footnote.”

Dutch closed his eyes briefly.

He'd ridden with murderers who needed less supervision at breakfast.

Dr. Evil reached for a small plate and put a piece of chicken on it. He added gravy, considered the amount, and removed a little with the spoon.

Brian watched every movement.

The plate slid across the table.

“There. A portion proportionate to your involvement.”

“I didn't ask for a children's meal.”

“Neither did the dog. Apparently you make these decisions for everyone.”

Brian shoved the plate back.

Dr. Evil caught it before the gravy spilled.

His expression changed.

“Careful.”

It was quiet. Completely without the little performance.

Brian took his hands off the plate.

The doctor kept looking at him for another second.

Then smiled again.

“Now. You won't be attending the next delivery.”

“What?”

“You've done so much to test our precautions. I should hate to exhaust you.”

“You're punishing me for finding a weakness.”

“I'm separating the weakness from the poultry.”

Brian stood on the box.

“I founded this organization.”

Dr. Evil looked him up and down.

“And now you're standing on it.”

Brian looked at the box.

He stepped off it immediately.

Which put his eyes below the table.

Dr. Evil waited.

Brian climbed back on.

“You are such a fucking asshole.”

“Yes. And I have a submarine. Imagine if I'd also been pleasant. You wouldn't have a single criticism.”

Dutch leaned forward before Brian could throw his entire body into the gravy.

“He can review the next arrangement here. Put his recommendations in writing. His name attached.”

Dr. Evil considered it.

“Very well.”

Brian looked at Dutch.

The doctor pointed his fork at him.

“But no food handling.”

“Fine.”

“No animal testing.”

“I wasn't—”

“No experimental chicken music.”

“That's not a fucking thing.”

“Then this should be an easy restriction to observe.”

Brian took his pencil again.

Dr. Evil moved the plate back within his reach.

“You may eat while you work.”

Brian glared at the chicken.

Then ate it as though the bird had personally sold him out.

The crew came in after the meal had been cleared. The two men who'd accompanied Clifford brought their transfer notes. Dutch moved the money aside and laid out the paper.

Brian had written three recommendations in the time Dr. Evil had taken to enjoy telling him he couldn't be trusted near a duck.

Keep the receiving gate closed until the cart was secured. Keep covered dishes separate from empty returns. Establish the actual load before promising a repeat price.

At the top he'd written his name.

Underlined it.

Then put a second line beneath the first in case the first failed to convey the full scope of Brian.

Dr. Evil held up the sheet.

“Who prepared this?”

Brian stared at him.

The doctor turned the paper over, checking the back.

Dutch took it gently from his hand.

“Brian's recommendations. We'll use them when we negotiate another run.”

One of the crewmen nodded.

Brian settled slightly on his box.

Actual listeners. Actual useful information. For a moment he had a surface on which to stand that wasn't packing material.

He explained the gate issue clearly.

Then the covered dishes.

Then he began explaining why this was fundamentally the same problem as managing a crowded dance floor with an inadequately isolated sound booth.

Dutch's pen slowed.

“The load,” he prompted.

“I'm connecting the principles.”

Dr. Evil put one hand up.

Brian stopped.

The doctor looked at the crewmen.

“You see? It can be done.”

Brian's jaw shifted.

“I was going to say that live birds require different handling from feed.”

“Then we have all been spared the nightclub.”

One crewman coughed into his hand.

Brian pointed at the three lines.

“Those are good recommendations.”

“Yes,” Dr. Evil said. “We are using them.”

That took some of the force out of Brian's next breath.

The doctor leaned back.

“You see how little speaking was required to establish that?”

There it went again.

Dutch turned the page before Brian could retrieve the argument.

The next delivery remained a possibility. No new price had been agreed. The crew needed to know what the merchant actually wanted moved before offering another run.

One man asked whether the empty cart should return by the same road.

Dutch marked the known route.

“Unless you learn a reason to change it.”

Dr. Evil put a finger beside the mark.

“And nobody offers a lower price without consulting me.”

Brian looked up.

“You haven't set a price.”

“Then they should find lowering it particularly difficult.”

The meeting moved on.

And Brian, who had been preparing to explain why Dr. Evil was an incompetent parasite on somebody else's enterprise, watched the room obey him.

No ray gun. No shouted threat.

A finger on a map and the assumption that people would wait for his decision.

It irritated Brian more than the chicken.

He knew how to make a room continue hearing him. He could fill every silence until somebody got tired enough to surrender.

The bald bastard could make one, then leave everybody else responsible for it.

Brian hated that too.

When the crewmen left, he remained beside the table.

Dr. Evil noticed.

“Was there something else?”

Brian pulled his notebook closer.

“The name.”

The doctor looked at Dutch.

“Oh, good. We had nearly completed something.”

Dutch stayed where he was.

Brian had seen the edge of the trademark drawing beneath a stack of briefing papers. He reached toward it.

Dr. Evil placed his hand on the stack.

Brian stopped with his little arm extended.

“You said we'd discuss it.”

“We are.”

“You keep saying we're discussing it while you're putting things on top of it.”

The doctor lifted his hand.

Brian pulled out the drawing.

Tampon Pandemic Productions sat inside Dr. Evil's proposed design, looking far more expensive than the circumstances under which Brian had originated it.

He hated that the lettering was good.

He hated the room for containing enough light to see that.

“I came up with this.”

“Yes.”

“All of it.”

“The name.”

“The concept.”

Dr. Evil looked around the submarine.

“Which part of the concept was watertight?”

Brian slapped the drawing.

“You know exactly what I mean.”

“I'm trying to establish whether I owe you for the torpedo tubes.”

“This isn't about your fucking submarine.”

“Then why are we having it in my fucking submarine?”

Dutch watched Brian absorb that.

The doctor had used almost the same tone as before. A little less ceremony. A little more ownership.

Brian looked toward the door and the men who had gone through it.

Then back at the drawing.

“I want the founding credit. And I want to be consulted before you put my name idea on anything.”

Dr. Evil steepled his fingers.

Then one hand came away, the little finger resting beside his mouth while he considered how much longer he wanted Brian to stand there.

Brian watched the hand.

It was an absurd thing to do in a discussion about somebody else's founding contribution. Yet somehow the doctor made it look as though the discussion had been brought here to entertain that particular finger.

Brian looked back at the drawing before the doctor caught him looking.

“Anything.”

“Anything representing the organization.”

The doctor drew the paper nearer.

“A letter?”

“If it's official.”

“A container?”

“Yes.”

“Your box?”

Brian looked down.

Dr. Evil was already smiling.

“We could put your founding credit on the side. Wherever you go, there it is. You could carry it to meetings.”

“I'm not carrying a fucking plaque that I have to stand on.”

“Then we agree it should remain here.”

Dutch set his pen down.

“We can acknowledge the contribution without settling the whole question today.”

Dr. Evil turned toward him.

“I have acknowledged it.”

“You offered to write it on a box.”

“In a prominent location.”

Brian crossed his arms.

“Why can't you just say I did something good without making me regret hearing it?”

The doctor regarded him.

For a second the argument had no stationery in it.

Then Dr. Evil looked at Dutch.

“Is this still the trademark discussion?”

Brian reached for his notebook.

“Forget it.”

Dr. Evil put one finger on the drawing before Brian could take that too.

“You may bring proposed terms. I will consider them.”

“That's what you said before.”

“And you have arrived with feelings.”

“I arrived with the company.”

“On a cart. With my chicken. Which had a more difficult journey than anticipated.”

Brian stared up at him.

The doctor leaned slightly over the table.

“Write. Them. Down.”

Brian picked up his notebook so hard that the pencil rolled off.

It struck the deck.

He looked at it.

Dr. Evil looked at it.

Nobody moved.

Eventually Brian climbed down and retrieved it himself.

Behind him, the doctor asked Dutch whether they had a smaller pencil.

“This one's fine,” Brian snapped.

“I was asking Dutch.”

Brian went out.

I would love to tell you the door slammed. It was a heavy submarine door, and he couldn't reach enough of it to make the statement he wanted.

He dragged it partway closed.

It stopped.

Dr. Evil waited until Brian had gone a few steps down the passage.

“Open or closed, Brian.”

The footsteps stopped.

Came back.

The door finally closed.

Dutch looked at the doctor.

“You work rather hard at that.”

Dr. Evil picked up the drawing.

“He's very responsive.”

Brian took his notebook to the small work space he'd been given. He set it down, climbed onto the seat and began writing terms.

Founding recognition.

Consultation over use of the name.

Authority over creative direction.

He stared at the third line.

Then added, in larger writing, independent authority.

That looked better.

The seam beneath his shirt moved once against the cloth.

His hand stopped.

He held still until the little pull passed, then pressed the fabric flat and returned to the page.

He didn't write about Tracy.

He wrote about credit.

He was still on the first page when two crewmen brought the empty returns down the passage outside.

Brian heard a container scrape the doorway.

“Not there,” he called.

The scraping stopped.

He climbed down and went out.

The men had stacked the empty containers beside an open store compartment. One of the folding frames leaned over the lower shelf, making the whole arrangement look closer to finished than it was.

Brian pointed toward it.

“You need to secure that first.”

“We're moving it,” one man said.

“I'm telling you how.”

The man looked at his partner.

Brian heard the silence and recognized it as the wrong kind.

“I've just reviewed the entire transfer procedure.”

“These are empty.”

“An empty thing can still fall on somebody. That's not an advanced concept. I don't know why we're all pretending weight becomes imaginary after the chicken gets out.”

The nearer man took hold of the upper frame.

Brian stepped closer to demonstrate where it should go.

The man's boot came backward toward him.

Brian darted sideways.

“Watch where you're fucking standing.”

The crewman turned with the frame still in his hands.

Its lower edge knocked the leaning one loose.

Brian saw it coming and moved. His new legs caught the deck awkwardly, one knee folding beneath him as he got clear.

The frame struck metal beside his foot.

Both men stopped.

So did the conversation at the far end of the passage.

Dr. Evil stood in the briefing-room doorway.

“Put it down.”

The man holding the upper frame began to lower it.

“Both of you.”

The other man took the far side. Together they set it flat against the bulkhead.

The doctor waited until their hands were free.

“One carries. One watches the route. If the route contains Brian, move Brian.”

Brian pushed himself upright.

“I'm standing right here.”

“We've located you. Thank you.”

The nearer crewman bent toward him.

Brian slapped the approaching hand away.

“Don't pick me up.”

The doctor raised a finger.

The man straightened.

“Very well. Brian will move Brian.”

“I was trying to tell them the same fucking thing.”

“Then apparently the route contains two problems.”

Brian looked up at him.

“They nearly dropped that on me.”

Dr. Evil's gaze moved to the fallen frame.

Then to the crewmen.

Neither man tried explaining that it was empty.

“You will secure it properly,” the doctor said. “I don't want to come out here again and find somebody flattened beneath our returns. It makes the whole operation look reversible.”

The men took the frame together.

Brian stepped out of their path under his own power. The leg held. He didn't thank anybody.

Dr. Evil watched him flex the knee once.

“Hurt?”

“No.”

“Good. Then we'll retain the box at its present height.”

Brian's head came up.

The doctor went back into the briefing room.

The crewmen waited until Brian was clear before moving the next container.

He watched them take it through the doorway. One carrying. One watching.

Exactly what he'd wanted done.

He returned to his notebook and sat down harder than necessary.

For a moment he could still hear the way Dr. Evil had said put it down.

No preamble about experience. No demonstration of superior knowledge. He hadn't even needed to tell them why he was entitled to be angry.

Brian picked up the pencil.

Then put it down again.

He didn't want to learn anything from that prick.

By the time Clifford came past, the first page contained enough underlining to suggest an emergency beneath every sentence.

“How's the work?” Clifford asked.

“He's deliberately misunderstanding me.”

“Probably.”

Brian looked up.

“You notice it too.”

“Hard to miss.”

“And nobody says anything.”

Clifford considered that.

“You do.”

Brian waited for the rest.

There wasn't any.

He looked back at the notebook.

“He likes you.”

Clifford's hand rested near the chair's wheel. The gifted lightsaber stayed secured to its frame.

“Gave me something useful.”

“Exactly.”

“Doesn't mean he knows me.”

Brian rubbed a thumb across the pencil's end.

From farther down the passage came Dr. Evil's voice, asking a crewman why a document described him as a passenger.

The crewman explained that it was a berth record.

Dr. Evil asked whether the berth had noticed whose submarine it was.

Brian listened.

Then made a small sound through his nose.

Clifford caught it.

Brian looked up sharply.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That was stupid.”

“All right.”

Brian turned a page.

“It was a stupid thing to say to somebody doing a berth record.”

Clifford nodded.

“You listened close.”

“I could hear him.”

“So could I.”

Clifford began to move on.

Brian stopped him.

“How does he do that?”

The chair stopped.

“What?”

Brian waved toward the passage.

“People tell me to shut up. He says something fucking ridiculous and they change the document.”

Clifford looked toward the briefing room.

“Owns the boat.”

“It's not just the boat.”

The admission annoyed Brian as soon as he heard it.

He put his pencil down.

“I mean, obviously the boat's a large part of it.”

Clifford looked back at him.

“Careful. You'll start looking up to him.”

Brian's head came up.

Clifford watched it happen.

“Already got the angle.”

“Fuck off.”

The chair continued down the passage.

Brian stayed over the notebook.

For a while he wrote nothing.

Then he crossed out the paragraph in which he'd explained the entire history of choosing Tampon Pandemic Productions.

Dr. Evil already knew who had named it.

That wasn't where the argument was.

Brian pulled the paper close and began again.

When he returned to the briefing room, he carried one sheet.

Dutch remained at the table, sorting the transfer notes. Dr. Evil had the trademark drawing turned toward himself.

Brian climbed onto his box without discussing it.

Set down the sheet.

“Founding credit. Consultation on the name. Actual authority over creative work.”

The doctor glanced at the paper.

“Much shorter.”

Brian kept his mouth closed.

Dr. Evil waited for the extra explanation.

It didn't come.

He looked at Brian.

Brian looked back.

Dutch took the page.

“These we can discuss.”

The doctor extended a hand for it. Dutch passed it over.

Dr. Evil read the three requests.

“Define creative work.”

Brian's little finger lifted toward the corner of his mouth.

He caught it halfway.

Closed the hand around his pencil instead.

“Presentation. The name. How people hear about us. Things I'm already contributing to.”

“Chicken acoustics.”

“Keep making that joke. It was nearly funny the first three times.”

Dutch looked down at the transfer notes.

Dr. Evil's eyes narrowed.

Brian held his gaze.

There he was again. Same mouth. Same offended little bastard who'd spent a night trying to rename sabotage until it sounded employable.

The doctor laid the paper beside the drawing.

“I will consider the first two. The third requires considerably more definition.”

“Then consider them.”

Brian stepped off the box.

Dr. Evil watched him collect his notebook.

“Brian.”

He stopped.

The doctor waited until he looked up.

“Your recommendations on the transfer were useful.”

Brian's face changed before he could prevent it.

Dr. Evil saw.

Let him have half a second.

“Try to submit the next set without a confession attached.”

Brian's face changed back.

“Go fuck yourself.”

He went out.

This time he left the door open.

Dr. Evil looked toward it.

Then at Dutch.

Dutch kept sorting papers.

“I'm not closing it for you.”

The doctor sat very still.

Out in the passage, Brian stopped beside a polished metal panel. He could see himself in it if he stood close enough.

He adjusted his collar.

Lifted his chin.

Considered the result.

Then pulled the collar back down and went to finish his work.

<!-- BEGIN LOGICAL OWNER: continuity/episodes/E46/S3_E46_The_Upper_Road_R2_FINAL_20261022.txt | ROLE: delivered_evidence -->
Season 3, Episode 46: “The Upper Road”

Before Brian's cart reached the coast, before Dr. Evil began subtracting gravy from Brian's breakfast, K.K. went looking for the place the water came from.

He stood above the camp's pear tree with his walking stick in both hands. Twenty feet of living timber, narrow enough to make his height feel like something the world had forgotten to finish.

“How far?” Daynuh asked.

“Until something interests me more.”

“That ain't a distance.”

“No. It's how I choose one.”

Chris was getting ready to go into town. The banjo rested at his belt; Billy watched through the headlamp from inside BELLY.

K.K. lowered his face toward him.

“I'd like to tell you what I find.”

“Town first,” Chris said. “Then I'll be here.”

Arthur pointed upstream.

“Road bends east after the old crossing. People work up there.”

Kaze watched the tree straighten.

“If somebody tells you what you are, ask why they need you to be it.”

K.K. tilted his head.

“You told me I was interesting.”

“Yeah.”

“Why did you need that?”

Kaze opened his mouth.

K.K. waited.

“Go find your fucking water.”

The leaves moved. K.K. stepped across the stream and went.

Several ridges upstream, an active lime works had arranged itself around the heat inside a long brick furnace. Limestone waited on the terrace. Fuel lay beneath a shed. An iron shutter hung over the deep feeding passage.

At the damaged crossing, a worker was trying to move a barrel across two inadequate boards.

He saw K.K.'s arms.

K.K. saw him seeing them.

“You're about to ask me to become furniture.”

“Only for a minute.”

“That's how it begins.”

They reached an agreement. K.K. wanted to look at what the men were doing with the hill. The man wanted his barrels across the gap.

K.K. rooted one hand into usable soil behind him and extended the other across the crossing. Living fibers stiffened under the first barrel. His fingers spread against the far stone.

“Not on the thumb,” he told the worker.

The barrel moved.

“There.”

When the last load crossed, K.K. withdrew the growth and stood. The worker showed him the furnace from the safe side. Heat trembled above the brick.

“Don't put anything in there you want back.”

K.K. examined his fingers.

“I was going to keep these.”

Then a cart slipped off the upper approach.

Its driver jumped, caught his leg, and began going over with it. The mule fought the harness. Barrels struck the tailboard.

The whole cart stopped over empty air.

Across the gap stood a man with a red-and-black face, short horns and yellow eyes. One hand extended. The other held a long, unlit hilt.

He turned his wrist.

The harness tore free. The mule stumbled onto surviving ground. The cart moved sideways through the air and settled on the terrace with its driver still caught against the seat.

The stranger lowered his hand.

“You have a map.”

The driver dragged his leg free.

“Take it.”

The chart had been strapped beneath the seat. The stranger unrolled it, studying the marked breaks in the local roads.

“Who caused this?”

“People say a man. Downriver. Kaze.”

K.K. became still.

The yellow eyes lifted.

“You know him.”

“You saved a man so you could ask his paper a question.”

“And you made yourself a bridge.”

“Briefly.”

The stranger crossed the narrow footing.

“My name is Maul.”

“K.K.”

Maul watched the last small roots withdraw into his heels.

“You could be considerably more useful.”

“There it is.”

They moved onto the stone apron above the furnace. The workers returned to their tasks, carefully finding things to do below the conversation.

Maul wanted a route back to the crisis he'd been torn from on Mandalore. Sidious's design was still unfinished in the last world he remembered. Here, he had neither his people nor his ships. He had a map, an injured driver's rumor, and something that knew the man named in it.

“Bring me to Kaze,” he said. “Help me learn what broke this land. You could have room to become what you are.”

K.K. rested his stick against one shoulder.

“What am I now?”

“Strength spent beneath other men's carts.”

“They asked.”

“They will always ask.”

That interested him. So did the way Maul looked at his hands while pretending not to measure them.

“I could introduce you,” K.K. said. “You'd have to ask him yourself.”

“Naturally.”

“He might say no.”

“Then I would persuade him.”

K.K.'s narrow face lowered.

“Would you like to practice?”

Maul looked up.

“No,” K.K. said gently. “There. That's the part you'll need.”

He enjoyed the silence that followed. He knew what he was doing with it.

Maul's fingers tightened around the hilt.

“I am offering you a purpose.”

“I had one.”

“Looking at water.”

“Yes.”

The walking stick flew from K.K.'s hand.

Maul caught it.

K.K. looked at his empty fingers.

“Give it back.”

“Tell me where he is.”

Roots entered the soil beyond the apron.

The worker came up the steps with an iron wedge. K.K. turned toward him.

“Go down.”

The man obeyed.

Long wooden fingers unfolded around the stolen stick. A second hand grew from K.K.'s forearm and closed around Maul's wrist.

Maul's saber ignited at both ends.

Red light filled the brick apron.

K.K. opened a real gap through the gripping arm. The first blade passed through it. The other took off two fingers.

The grip closed again.

“You should have kept asking.”

K.K. shoved him backward.

Maul turned with the force, struck the wall feet-first and sprang away, cutting through the wrist that held him. He landed beside the fuel shed.

K.K. recovered his stick.

Sap sealed the cut. New fibers pressed outward.

Maul drove his free palm forward. The cart slammed sideways into the rooted legs and broke around them.

K.K. caught a length of the frame and drove it at him.

Maul cut it in half.

The piece behind it struck his shoulder and sent him into the shed.

K.K. put his walking stick carefully beside the wall.

Then grew three more arms.

The first fist broke brick where Maul's face had been. The second caught his weapon wrist. Maul twisted the opposite blade through the grabbing wood and drove the other end toward the narrow chest.

K.K.'s torso parted around it.

Hardening ribs closed on the hilt.

Maul released it before they caught his hands. Under his outstretched palm the weapon jerked sideways, carving free of the growing cage.

He caught it and rolled.

The fist that followed cracked the furnace apron above the feeding passage.

Heat breathed through the widened opening.

Maul looked at it.

K.K. saw him look.

The tree withdrew from the furnace, reaching for the wall. Overhead growth spread, hardened and came down across Maul's route.

It crushed the shed. A branch struck his metal leg before he landed.

Maul came up badly, cutting through the roots reaching toward usable earth. A shove of the Force drove K.K. against the retaining wall.

His shoulder split. Hardened splinters answered, opening Maul's upper arm and side. He staggered behind the cart bed, using its broken frame against the pieces his saber couldn't intercept.

K.K. climbed.

An iron poker tore through his reaching arm and struck brick behind it.

He shed the pinned wood and dropped, compressing his long torso around the blade coming for him. One hand closed around Maul's damaged leg.

Metal screamed.

Maul cut the gripping wrist. Another fist carried him into the shutter's counterweight chain.

The iron shutter fell halfway, caught on wreckage, and held there.

Maul rose bleeding.

The broken cart bed struck K.K.'s folded middle and drove him toward the furnace.

Four hands braced against the stone.

One reached Maul's throat.

His feet scraped forward as the fingers tightened.

The red blade severed the reaching forearm.

Maul tore the disconnected grip away, cut the remaining braces and drove the cart forward with the Force.

K.K.'s compressed body struck burning fuel inside the chamber.

He opened himself. Flattened. Reached around the frame.

Maul held it across the mouth with one hand extended and cut the reaching growth with the saber in the other.

Fresh wood formed. Blackened. A narrow arm caught the iron edge and began dragging the body toward the opening.

Maul's damaged leg bent as the frame shifted against him.

He shouted and pushed it back.

The furnace roared around K.K.'s folded ribs.

“You wanted something beneath your feet.”

Maul kept holding.

Another hand reached stone outside.

The red blade came down.

It fell away.

Maul stayed at the opening while heat reached the protected inner folds. The living tissue stopped repairing itself. The last essential heartwood charred through.

He lowered the frame only after the body inside collapsed.

The ordinary walking stick stood unburned beside the wall.

Maul took the map. The stick stayed where K.K. had put it.

At the first switchback, his damaged leg locked. He caught the retaining wall, then lowered himself into an abandoned road shelter.

Below him, the furnace kept burning.

He bound his arm with torn cloth and pulled a bloody splinter from above his collar. The chart showed three routes into the valley. Two were marked beside collapsed road sections. The third passed the works.

The tree's people might return there. He could watch the approach while the leg carried less weight.

Afternoon light moved across the map on his knees.

Eventually he stood, found he could move if he kept the knee nearly straight, and began the slow traverse above the works.

The worker from the crossing had taken the longer road downriver.

By the time he reached the poultry shop, the light was failing.

The seller had begun closing up. The cart from Tampon Pandemic Productions was gone. Kaze and the others had taken the road back toward their camp only a little earlier.

The worker had to ask before anybody understood him.

“The tree. The tall one. His people.”

The seller came out from behind the counter.

“What happened?”

The man put a hand against the doorframe.

“Where did they go?”

The seller pointed.

The worker went after them.

He caught them at the turn where the road descended toward the stream.

Arthur heard his stumbling steps first and turned.

The man stopped when he saw the red eye under the hat.

Then looked past him at Kaze.

“You know the tree?”

Chris came closer.

“K.K.?”

The worker nodded.

“He helped us. At the upper works. There was a man.”

Chris stopped moving.

“What man?”

The worker described the red-and-black face. The horns. The two red blades on one handle. The invisible force that had held a cart over empty air.

Arthur's gaze moved toward the hills.

Kaze listened without speaking.

“Did you see him leave?” Chris asked.

“I ran when they started. I came for—”

“Did you see K.K. leave?”

The man shook his head.

Chris looked upstream.

Inside BELLY, Billy leaned toward the headlamp feed.

Kaze asked, “Which road?”

The worker pointed past the ridge.

“Old crossing. Then the kiln. It's far by the road.”

Kaze turned to Arthur.

“Bring him.”

Arthur nodded.

Kaze put one foot onto the stone beside the road and launched.

The stone split beneath him.

He crossed the first ridge in a low, hard arc. The next contact broke a shelf of rock and sent him over the upper valley toward the glow the worker had described.

He crossed the valley fast enough for the second impact to arrive before the first dust had settled.

When he landed on the terrace, the abandoned tools jumped.

He looked at the smashed cart.

The scored stone.

The blackened branches.

Then at the walking stick beside the wall.

The noise inside him went very quiet.

The furnace was still hot. He approached the damaged mouth and looked through it.

There was enough of the narrow shape left to understand what had been trapped there. Not enough left alive to answer him.

Kaze stood without moving.

For once, the place had nothing he wanted to destroy that would make the thing he wanted happen.

He picked up the stick.

On the terrace, drops of Maul's blood marked the direction he'd taken. A damaged mechanical foot had dragged through the dust between them.

Kaze crouched.

Blood and scorched cloth held a scent distinct from the furnace smoke. Kaze followed it past a scrape where a metal foot had caught the road.

He followed the marks to the upper road.

Then he saw a figure moving along the pale switchback beyond the works.

Dark clothes. One uneven step. A long hilt in one hand.

Kaze put the walking stick down beside the road, where it wouldn't be under the next impact.

He jumped.

Maul felt danger before the hillside in front of him broke.

He stopped and drew the saber as Kaze landed between him and the next bend.

Both red ends lit.

Dust moved around Kaze's bare shoulders. His gold upper grills showed for an instant as his mouth opened.

“You meet a tree?”

Maul looked at the visible name across his stomach, then at his face.

“Kaze.”

“I asked you something.”

Maul adjusted his grip. Blood had made one hand slippery.

“It chose to attack me.”

Kaze's head tilted.

“You always start the story where you look better?”

Maul moved.

The saber swept toward Kaze's neck while a thrust of the Force struck his body from the other side. It was a real attempt to control his position and cut through the space he'd be forced into.

Kaze saw the attack begin. His danger sense had already fixed his attention on it.

He drove against the displacement, broke the stone under his feet, and moved inside the blade's arc.

His right hand closed around Maul's weapon wrist.

The red end passed behind his shoulder without reaching his neck.

Maul kicked for his knee.

Kaze took the strike without losing the grip.

Then he bent the wrist backward until the bones broke through the skin.

The saber dropped.

Maul reached for it with the Force.

Kaze drove him into the rock face before the hilt could return.

The impact broke a deep bowl in the hillside. Maul's back hit first; his ribs collapsed under the hand that followed. Blood came out of his mouth onto Kaze's forearm.

He was still trying to lift the saber when Kaze caught his face.

“No,” Kaze said.

He pulled Maul away from the wall and slammed him down through the stone at their feet.

The road burst outward.

His skull broke beneath Kaze's palm. The upper body folded into the new crater, flesh and shattered bone driven against the mechanical frame below it. Red blood splashed Kaze's chest and face. The reaching hand stopped reaching.

The saber struck the ground beside them, still lit.

Kaze stood over what he'd made.

The red blade hummed against loose stone. Nothing in the crater moved.

Kaze looked down at his bloody hand.

Then back toward the works.

He hadn't gotten an answer he could use.

He walked away from the crater, leaving the weapon where it lay. He collected the stick where he'd left it and went back down to the furnace.

By the time Arthur reached the upper terrace with the others, the worker was struggling to keep up with him. Daynuh had come with Mahnuh. Chris stayed exterior, the banjo quiet at his belt.

Kaze was sitting beside the furnace with the walking stick across his knees.

Chris looked at the red blood on him.

“Where?”

Kaze pointed toward the upper road.

“Done.”

Arthur looked in that direction, then at the kiln.

He didn't ask for the man's name yet.

The worker stopped at the shattered cart.

“He was here.”

Chris walked past him.

He saw the wood inside the furnace.

Stopped.

Billy's voice came through the banjo, low enough that only the people near Chris heard it.

“Christopher.”

Chris didn't answer.

He moved closer, looking for something that still moved. Something green. A living fold protected from the heat. He knew K.K. could grow back from injuries; he'd seen wood close where another person would have kept a scar.

There wasn't anything left doing it.

The worker began explaining the crossing.

How K.K. had helped.

The conversation above the shed.

The demand for the walking stick.

“He told me to go,” the man said. “I thought if I found you—”

Chris turned.

“You did.”

The worker looked at him.

Chris swallowed.

“You found us.”

That was all he could give him.

Arthur waited until the worker had caught his breath.

“Start where you were standing.”

The man pointed toward the steps.

“He asked the driver about the broken ground. Then your friend said something to him.”

“What?”

“About saving a man to talk to his paper.”

Chris shut his eyes for a moment.

“Yeah. That sounds like him.”

“They moved up here. I went back for the wedge. When I came up, the stranger had his stick.”

Kaze looked at the timber across his knees.

“Took it?”

“I didn't see that part. Your friend said to give it back. The stranger wanted to know where you were.”

Arthur glanced toward Kaze, then returned to the worker.

“He give a name?”

“Maul. Before they went up the steps.”

“And you left when?”

“Your friend told me to. I saw the red thing come on. Then the first hit. After that I ran.”

He looked past Arthur toward the furnace.

“I should've stayed.”

“Where?” Chris asked.

The man pointed helplessly at the terrace.

Chris looked at the broken brick, the iron driven through the wall, the deep cuts across the stone.

“Which fucking bit?”

The worker's hand dropped.

Billy's voice came through the banjo.

“Did he have the stick when you last saw him?”

“I didn't see. It was there when I came back.”

Billy asked Chris to turn toward the wall. Through the headlamp he examined the little clear space beside it, protected from the cart's first broken timbers.

Then he asked to see the rest of the terrace.

Chris gave him the view slowly. The fish took in the damage without pretending he could watch backward through it.

Arthur wrote Maul's name on the back of a loose scrap. Beside it he put the worker's account, stopping at the point where the man had stopped seeing.

Daynuh put a hand on Mahnuh's shoulder. The dog had reached the scattered branches and was smelling along them, following the familiar scent into something he couldn't complete.

“Here,” Daynuh said.

Mahnuh came back to him.

Arthur stood beside Kaze.

“You see all of it?”

Kaze shook his head.

“Saw enough.”

Arthur looked toward the upper road again.

“We should get that weapon off the road.”

Kaze's fingers tightened around the ordinary stick.

“Then get it.”

Arthur went up the switchback. At the broken section, he found the body, the scorched stone beside the still-active blade, and the long hilt lying clear of Maul's hand.

He approached from the side, keeping out of both red ends. He'd just watched Clifford use a similar kind of weapon. That didn't make every control identical. He studied the hilt before touching the recessed switch with his gloved hand.

The blades went out.

He wrapped the hilt in a spare piece of cloth from his satchel and brought it back, keeping the control beneath a fold where a careless grip wouldn't press it.

The survey map lay torn beside the body. Arthur recovered that too.

Down at the works, Chris had found the workers' long iron tongs. He waited until they could safely reach what remained in the mouth of the furnace, then lifted the larger pieces into an empty stone trough away from the heat.

Nobody pretended the pieces would start talking if they were arranged correctly.

Billy asked to see the stick.

Chris turned toward it so the headlamp gave him the view.

Kaze held it up.

For a while the fish said nothing.

Then, “He put that aside.”

The worker looked at it.

“Had it when he came here.”

Kaze looked at the unburned timber in his hands.

He had taken care of the thing he was carrying.

That detail hurt in a place the blood on Kaze's chest couldn't reach.

The workers returned to the upper works one at a time after the noise stopped.

Arthur told them which stretch of road was broken now. He didn't tell them they had witnessed justice or try to sell Kaze as the man who made the country safer.

The foreman looked toward the furnace, then at the red blood drying on Kaze's skin.

“That one did all this?”

“Some,” Arthur said.

The man understood enough to stop asking that question.

He showed them an intact path back downriver. It went farther around the hill than the damaged road, but nobody needed to risk the new crater to reach the stream.

Arthur asked him to keep travelers off the upper bend until somebody had marked the damage.

“There's a body there too.”

The foreman's eyes moved toward Kaze.

“I gathered.”

“Weapon's with me. Don't let somebody go digging through the wreckage in the dark.”

The man called one of the returning workers over. Together they dragged an unbroken beam across the upper approach, well short of the cracked section. Arthur waited until it was in place before coming down the steps.

Before they left, the worker from the crossing approached Kaze.

“He didn't charge us.”

Kaze looked at him.

“For the bridge.”

“He wanted to look.”

The worker nodded.

“I said he could.”

Kaze stood.

For a second the man thought he'd done something wrong.

Then Kaze handed him the walking stick.

The worker took it automatically.

Kaze looked at the hand holding it.

He took it back.

“No.”

The worker let go immediately.

Kaze stared at the stick as though it had asked him a question in somebody else's voice.

Then he went down the steps.

The others followed.

Chris carried the cooled remains they could recover, wrapped in a work cloth the foreman had given him. He held the bundle carefully without pretending it was a patient.

Billy stayed quiet through the banjo.

That evening, they placed the remains in the ground near the pear tree K.K. had bought.

Chris lowered the bundle himself. He waited beside the open earth until Arthur asked him for room to finish.

Daynuh settled Mahnuh away from the open earth while Arthur worked. Chris stepped back. Kaze put the ordinary stick across the fresh ground.

The place where their guest had stood was empty.

Chris stood looking at the pear tree.

“He was gonna tell me what he found.”

Arthur leaned on the tool he'd borrowed from the works.

“I know.”

Chris rubbed his mouth.

“I planted a fucking vegetable.”

From the banjo came Billy's voice.

“And met somebody.”

Chris nodded once.

Nothing clever followed it.

Later, Kaze sat beside the stream washing Maul's blood from his hands. The water took what it could. Red remained beneath his nails and in the creases around his knuckles. His pants were still stained.

Arthur put the wrapped double-ended hilt on a dry stone beside him.

“Keeping it?”

Kaze looked at the shape beneath the cloth.

“You found it.”

“Didn't ask who found it.”

The water moved around Kaze's fingers.

“Not tonight.”

Arthur picked it up again.

Across the camp, Chris had put a little of the evening's food aside without looking at the empty space where K.K. usually stood.

Then he'd noticed what he'd done.

He left it there.

Daynuh sat with Mahnuh's head against his leg. Billy watched through the headlamp when Chris turned toward the tree, and did not supply a history lesson.

Kaze dried his hands on the grass and went back to the fire.

He stopped beside Arthur.

“That map.”

Arthur looked up.

“Got it.”

“Tomorrow.”

Arthur nodded.

Kaze looked toward the upper hills, where the damaged roads ran deeper into Noxus.

Then he sat down with the people who were still there.

Season 3, Episode 47: “A Busta Rhymes Situation”

“The tide is going out,” Dutch said.

Brian looked toward the water.

“Busta Rhymes could make a tide chart sound fucking dangerous.”

Dr. Evil turned slowly.

“Would he improve the tide?”

“I'm talking about delivery.”

“So was Dutch. Until you introduced a recording artist to the ocean.”

They stood on the quay beside the submarine the morning after Brian had submitted his shortened demands for recognition. The five silver from the poultry run had survived the discussion. The founding dispute had survived it too.

Dr. Evil had come outside to inspect the berth and discover why a vessel this impressive did not make everyone nearby look sufficiently impressed.

Brian had come because nobody had told him not to.

One of the crewmen called up a question about moving a rope.

Dutch answered him.

Brian watched the man lean into the work.

“That's what I'm saying. Presence. Some people can just stand somewhere and the whole fucking environment starts anticipating them. Busta walks into a room, you don't need a sign saying the room's different. You feel the air change.”

Dr. Evil looked at the crewman.

“Was that the rope, or did you feel the air change?”

The man wisely continued working.

“You don't get it,” Brian said.

“I'm receiving it in considerable detail.”

Brian stepped onto a low mooring block so he could see past the stacked rope.

“I'm describing command.”

Dr. Evil regarded him from above.

“Then perhaps describe mine.”

Brian looked at him.

There was a tempting opening. A normal person might have stepped through it, complimented the man providing the accommodation, and enjoyed a quiet morning.

Brian said, “It's a different kind.”

Dutch looked out to sea.

“How different?” the doctor asked.

“You're more controlled.”

That helped.

“Calculated.”

That helped more.

“Busta has that too, but then there's the explosive factor. Like a building that knows when to become a fucking drum.”

Dr. Evil's mouth closed.

“I see. I am the building before the interesting thing happens.”

“That's not what I said.”

“No. You used more words.”

He turned to a crewman near the gangway.

“Have the horn sounded. Once.”

The man went aboard. A short interval passed while he reached the control.

Then the submarine's horn rolled across the harbor.

Ropes trembled against metal. Men farther along the quay looked up. Dr. Evil stood still, allowing the sound to supply the weight beneath his next sentence.

“That,” he said, “is presence.”

Brian's face lit.

“Busta would absolutely murder that sample.”

The doctor looked toward the gangway.

“We're finished with the horn.”

It hadn't been scheduled to sound again.

He still wanted someone to know why.

Upriver, the previous morning, Arthur had unfolded Maul's torn survey map beside the stream.

K.K.'s walking stick lay across the fresh earth near the pear tree. Chris passed it carrying his rolled gear and looked toward the water instead.

Arthur put a finger on the works. Then on the road connecting them to the lower valley.

“This gets us past the broken section. I know the way to the port from there.”

Kaze stood over the map.

“And that's where the doctor is.”

“Last I heard.”

Chris looked at the wrapped hilt beside Arthur's hand.

“Clifford gets a laser sword. Next thing a different guy turns up with two.”

“One handle,” Billy said through the banjo.

“Thank you. We can all sleep now.”

Arthur kept his finger on the road.

“Having one doesn't mean that doctor knows everybody carrying one.”

Kaze looked up.

“Then he'll have an easy answer.”

He wasn't claiming he'd solved anything. He wanted to look at the man who gave Clifford a weapon like that, hear what he knew, and decide how much he enjoyed the answer.

Maul had come looking for him. K.K. had been the person standing in the way.

That particular fact had survived the night.

Daynuh crouched beside Mahnuh and checked one paw. The dog pulled it back, then permitted the indignity when Daynuh took it again.

“Long road?” Daynuh asked.

“We'll stop when we need to,” Arthur said.

“Good. Daynuh ain't racing a submarine.”

“It's tied up.”

“Then Daynuh's winning.”

Chris bent over the map.

Billy asked him to turn slightly so the headlamp could give him the whole chart.

“That's a local survey,” the fish said. “Don't let its neat little lines persuade you the rest of the country has agreed to them.”

Arthur folded it along the existing creases.

“I won't.”

He secured the wrapped saber where the switch stayed protected. The weapon had no new title, no oath attached to it. It was a dangerous thing he'd picked up beside a dead man, and he meant to keep it from becoming somebody else's accident.

They left the pear tree standing.

By late the following morning they had reached the coast, following surviving road around the damaged ground. They came into the harbor on foot, dusty and hungry, while Dr. Evil was still considering whether a second horn blast would look needy.

One of his crew recognized Arthur from the visit to the camp.

The man spoke to Dutch before anybody began treating the arrivals as customers.

Dutch turned.

“Arthur.”

Arthur lifted a hand.

“Dutch.”

Dr. Evil studied the group approaching along the quay. The enormous dog. The man carrying a banjo. The tattooed, bare-chested man who looked at the submarine without offering it the smallest facial reward.

Dutch glanced toward him.

“Kaze.”

“Yes,” the doctor said. “I had begun to suspect.”

The name across Kaze's stomach saved everyone a round of introductions.

Brian hopped down from the block.

Chris saw him.

“Shit. Somebody left the founder outside.”

Brian looked at the banjo, then at Chris.

“I can go outside.”

“We've been finding that out.”

Dr. Evil stepped forward before the conversation could settle permanently around Brian's ankles.

“Welcome. I understand you've already met several of my associates.”

Kaze looked at Clifford, who had come out through the gangway doorway and was moving toward the open space on the quay in his chair.

The gifted hilt remained fastened to its frame.

“Hard to miss some of them.”

Clifford stopped beside Dutch.

His mask stayed on.

He looked at Chris for a long second. Then turned toward Arthur.

“How's the camp?”

Arthur's expression changed.

“We lost somebody.”

Dutch moved closer.

“Who?”

“K.K. The tree.”

The two crewmen who had visited the camp went quiet. They knew who that meant. Dr. Evil had only their descriptions.

Brian opened his mouth.

Nothing came out before Kaze spoke.

“Guy with horns. Red face. Two ends on one of those.”

He nodded toward Clifford's weapon.

Arthur drew the wrapped hilt from his gear, keeping the control covered.

“Called himself Maul.”

Dr. Evil looked at it without reaching.

“And you believe I know him.”

“I'm asking,” Kaze said.

“I don't.”

Kaze watched his face.

The doctor let the answer stand.

Arthur put the wrapped weapon on a clear section of an empty crate between them.

“He was asking about the broken ground. Wanted Kaze.”

Dutch looked from Arthur to the dark stains still worked into the seams of Kaze's pants.

“Where is he now?”

“Upper road,” Kaze said.

“Is he coming here?”

“Not together.”

A gull screamed over the berth.

Dr. Evil looked at Kaze again.

That answer had given him rather more information than the first one.

Brian stepped beside the crate.

“The important distinction is that matching presentation doesn't establish common manufacture. It's like when people hear an aggressive vocal and immediately say Busta Rhymes. No. There's breath placement. There's the architecture of the whole fucking delivery. You can't just hear a man shout and call it Busta.”

Chris turned toward him.

“We brought a murder weapon, Brian.”

“I'm explaining attribution.”

“You found a way to make a dead tree about your fucking playlist.”

“He made a relevant distinction,” Dr. Evil said.

Brian looked up.

The doctor continued, “Shortly before losing custody of it.”

Kaze's mouth moved at one corner.

Arthur drew back the cloth enough to expose the hilt, leaving his thumb beside the protected control.

Dr. Evil examined its length and construction. Then looked at the weapon attached to Clifford's chair.

“That one came with me. This one did not.”

“You make yours?” Kaze asked.

“I employ people.”

“Wasn't what I asked.”

“No. I did not personally manufacture it.”

“You got a way back to where it came from?”

Dr. Evil paused.

The question mattered enough that Dutch stopped watching Brian.

“Not at present,” the doctor said.

Kaze looked past him at the submarine.

“That's a lot of boat to be lost in.”

“It has been a considerable inconvenience.”

He said it with the irritation of a man whose hotel had misplaced the continent.

Chris rubbed his mouth.

From the banjo, Billy said, “A vessel can be excellent at the wrong sort of departure.”

The doctor looked at it.

Chris tapped the banjo.

“That's Billy.”

“I see.”

“Not from there, you don't,” Billy said.

Brian was already nodding.

“That's projection. Busta doesn't need to stand right in front of you to dominate the entire space.”

Dr. Evil turned toward him.

“Does this man handle all your examples?”

“If the example fits.”

“We were discussing transportation.”

“Movement. Momentum. It's connected.”

Chris stared down at him.

“You'd find Busta Rhymes in a fucking stool sample.”

Brian pointed at him.

“If somebody had eaten a CD, yeah, there'd be a reason to investigate.”

For a moment nobody answered.

I need you to appreciate that he thought he'd defended himself. He'd climbed into that sentence, pulled the lid shut, and was waiting for us to compliment the hinges.

Kaze laughed.

Dr. Evil waited for him to stop.

He didn't stop quickly enough for the doctor's liking.

“Brian is developing our public presentation,” Dr. Evil said.

“Apparently through the colon,” Billy replied.

Brian looked at Chris.

“Do you have to keep doing that?”

Chris lifted both hands.

“That one wasn't me.”

Dutch drew the attention back to the crate.

“If you don't know the man, perhaps one of your people can tell whether the weapons have anything in common.”

Dr. Evil considered it.

“A comparison. Certainly. That is a much more reasonable request than arriving with a corpse's property and asking whether I misplaced the rest of him.”

Kaze looked at Arthur.

Arthur's hand stayed beside the hilt.

“They can look here.”

“Our tools are aboard,” the doctor said.

“Then bring what you need.”

Dr. Evil looked at the crate, the open quay, and the group that had declined to become a tour.

“This is not my usual consultation arrangement.”

“Mine either,” Arthur said.

Dutch stepped in with the smoothness of a man laying a rug over a hole.

“No one needs to move anything sensitive. Have someone familiar with Clifford's weapon make an initial comparison. Then we decide whether there's anything worth pursuing.”

Dr. Evil called to a crewman. Asked him to bring the crewman who'd explained the gift's controls to Clifford.

The man went aboard.

The pause became Brian's almost immediately.

He moved toward the open end of the crate and straightened his little jacket.

Dr. Evil noticed.

“What are you doing?”

“Helping with presentation.”

“I have already presented myself.”

“You said welcome. That's a door mat. It doesn't communicate scale.”

Kaze's eyes moved to him.

Brian mistook attention for an invitation.

“When you're introducing somebody at this level, you've got to understand the room before the room understands what's happening. Give them a reason to anticipate. You don't walk out and say here's a guy.”

Dr. Evil looked toward the group.

“You see the difficulty.”

Brian held up a hand.

“No. Let me finish. You're actually proving my point by resisting the buildup.”

“I shall try to resist more efficiently.”

Brian turned toward Kaze.

“What you're looking at here is a man with infrastructure. People. Reach. Most people say they have an organization, they have a fucking room and somebody owes them twenty dollars. This is an operation.”

Dutch glanced at him.

That part hadn't been bad.

“You don't judge it by whether the man himself is making every sound,” Brian continued. “Busta doesn't personally build the fucking speakers. That's what I'm trying to get across. You put him at the center and everything around him becomes part of the performance.”

Dr. Evil's expression became very carefully blank.

“Am I at the center yet?”

“I'm establishing the analogy.”

“I seem to be behind Mr. Rhymes.”

“You're missing the point.”

Clifford spoke from behind his mask.

“He got introduced first.”

Brian pointed at him.

“No, he didn't. I used him as an example.”

“He got the speakers,” Chris said.

“It's a metaphor.”

Kaze folded his arms.

“Does the metaphor have a submarine?”

Brian hesitated.

Dr. Evil looked at him.

For once, he and the shirtless visitor wanted the same answer.

“Not that I'm aware of,” Brian said.

The doctor spread his hands.

“Finally. A distinction in my favor.”

“You can't reduce the entire comparison to who owns a submarine.”

“I can from this one.”

Brian's mouth stayed open.

Kaze looked at Dr. Evil.

Then laughed through his nose.

The doctor saw it and relaxed by a fraction.

Brian saw that too.

He'd spent a minute trying to provide something impressive. Dr. Evil had picked through it, found the part he wanted, and taken it without asking Brian whether the rhythm was right.

It was infuriating.

It was also, against every useful intention Brian had brought to the morning, something he wanted to get better at.

He stepped back from the crate.

“You know what gets overlooked? Control. Everybody hears speed and thinks that's the whole thing. It isn't. Busta could make silence sound like it's about to punch your landlord.”

Dr. Evil's eyes moved toward him.

“Has he considered using some?”

“Who?”

“You, on his behalf.”

Brian crossed his arms.

“You don't have to like hip-hop.”

“I would like to finish meeting the people on the dock.”

“I was adding context.”

“You have added an entire other man.”

Daynuh put a hand against Mahnuh's chest before the dog could investigate the opening beside the gangway.

“Mahnuh stays here.”

Brian watched the dog settle.

“See, that's loyalty. Busta has that energy. You know if he's in your corner—”

“Does he know?” Kaze asked.

Brian stopped.

“Know what?”

“That you're in his corner. With a fucking shovel. Digging tunnels between every conversation on Earth.”

Chris bent over, laughing into his hand.

Brian looked toward Dutch for something useful.

Dutch was looking at the water.

“I'm a fan,” Brian said.

“Nigga, a fan moves air. You've built that man a church in your throat.”

Dr. Evil's head turned toward Kaze.

He considered the phrasing.

Then looked down at Brian.

“We shall not be funding the church.”

“Nobody asked you to.”

“Good. A productive agreement.”

The crewman returned with the man who knew Clifford's gift. He carried a small tool roll and asked Arthur to keep the weapon switched off.

Arthur folded back the cloth himself.

The man examined what he could see. Asked Clifford for permission to compare the exterior of the other hilt. Clifford brought his chair closer and held the gift where both men could reach it.

The crewman worked without opening either weapon.

Brian leaned toward Chris.

“Busta would've appreciated the precision.”

Chris looked at him.

“You don't know what he's doing.”

“I appreciate precision in general.”

“Then say general.”

The crewman straightened.

“They aren't the same design. I can't tell you who made that one from looking at the outside.”

Dr. Evil nodded.

“There. An answer from a man qualified to be uncertain.”

Kaze studied the crewman.

“Could it take you home?”

The man looked at the hilt.

“I have no reason to think so.”

“Didn't ask what you hoped.”

“Neither did I,” Dr. Evil said.

Kaze looked back at him.

For the first time that morning, the doctor wasn't performing for Brian.

“We arrived here,” he said. “We have a functioning vessel. We are learning where it can go. Those are the facts. I won't invent another because your visitor carried a similar weapon.”

Kaze held his gaze.

Then nodded once.

Arthur rewrapped the saber.

No miraculous address fell out. No little light blinked the answer into a room. They had carried a question to somebody with a reason to know, and his answer had remained no.

That still changed where they would look next.

Dutch touched the edge of the survey map visible in Arthur's open gear.

“He had that?”

“Took it from a driver,” Arthur said. “Upper works. Marked roads.”

“Then the driver may know which direction he came from.”

Kaze looked down at the folded chart.

It was an ordinary suggestion. Good enough that he couldn't enjoy dismissing it.

“Yeah,” he said.

Dutch withdrew his hand.

“I can listen here. If anyone else arrives asking for the man who broke the ground, I'd prefer to know before he starts moving it again.”

“Don't promise him where we are,” Arthur said.

Dutch looked at him.

Then nodded.

“I'll bring the question to you.”

Brian took a breath.

Dr. Evil raised one finger without looking.

Brian closed his mouth.

The doctor's hand remained up.

Kaze saw the exchange.

So did Chris.

Brian saw both of them seeing it and moved his jaw as though the silence had been entirely his own idea.

The crewman packed his tools. Clifford secured his hilt again. Arthur put the other away, retaining it and the map.

Dr. Evil considered the gathering.

“Well. Now that nobody is accusing me of issuing the horned man, perhaps we can introduce ourselves properly.”

“You first,” Kaze said.

The doctor straightened.

“Dr. Evil.”

Kaze waited.

“That's it?”

“It has generally been sufficient.”

“Sufficient for what?” Chris asked. “Getting out of parent-teacher conferences?”

The banjo gave a low, satisfied chuckle.

Brian looked up at his employer.

He knew that expression now. Knew the careful pause before the correction. He was waiting for it with a small, unpleasant excitement.

Dr. Evil looked at Chris.

“I understand you protected my meal.”

“Shut a gate.”

“Yes. Brian supplied a more ambitious description. I thought we'd try yours.”

Chris's smile widened.

Brian's went away.

There. Everybody had received something.

Dutch offered to show Arthur where they could sit out of the traffic and talk. Arthur accepted. Daynuh took Mahnuh toward a patch of shade along the quay. Chris went with him, keeping Billy's view turned toward the group until the stacked rope blocked it.

Arthur and Dutch stopped beside a stack of unused mooring timbers farther along the berth. Dutch sat on one. Arthur stayed on his feet until the wrapped hilt was settled securely beside his gear.

“I was glad to get your letter,” Dutch said.

“Figured.”

“You could have made it less difficult to appreciate.”

Arthur looked at him.

Dutch smiled.

For a moment it almost fit a place neither of them was standing in.

Then Dutch looked back toward the others.

“How's Chris taking it?”

“He buried what we could bring back.”

Dutch nodded slowly.

“And Kaze?”

Arthur followed his gaze.

“You've seen the answer he got.”

“I meant afterward.”

Arthur rested a hand on the timber.

“He came here.”

Dutch looked at him again.

That was an answer too.

Somebody began hammering at a berth farther down the waterfront. The sound traveled over the water and came back thin beneath the hull.

“I haven't heard anything that would help with Daniel,” Dutch said. “A great many stories. None that put the man you want where someone actually saw him.”

“Don't send me a story because it sounds good.”

“I won't.”

Arthur studied his face.

Dutch held the look without adding a speech.

“And if somebody asks where we're staying,” Arthur said, “that includes your doctor.”

“You think I'd sell him your location?”

“I think you like being useful to the man with the boat.”

Dutch's jaw tightened.

“I'm useful to a number of people.”

“I'm asking you to choose how.”

The hammering continued.

Dutch looked down at his hands, then toward the gangway.

“I'll ask before I pass it along.”

Arthur nodded.

They hadn't repaired the world. They had reached one small agreement that would now be somebody's choice to keep.

From beyond the rope stack came Brian's voice explaining that breath control was also a form of leadership.

Dutch shut his eyes.

Arthur looked toward the sound.

“He always do that now?”

“He found a subject nobody here could correct.”

“Sounds like somebody should've let him finish a conversation once.”

Dutch opened his eyes.

“Arthur, we are trying to leave the harbor standing.”

Kaze stayed a moment, looking at the submarine.

Dr. Evil stayed beside him.

“Impressive,” the doctor said.

Kaze glanced at him.

“You asking me or telling me?”

The doctor considered the distinction.

Kaze nodded toward Clifford farther down the quay.

“You give everybody one of those?”

“It was a gift.”

“Yeah. I saw the part where he kept it.”

Dr. Evil's eyes moved toward the secured hilt.

“A particular expression of appreciation.”

“Appreciate me.”

The doctor looked back at him.

Kaze smiled.

“I'm standing right here. Put some feeling into it.”

“You arrived with a weapon of your own.”

“Arthur's carrying that.”

“Then I suggest you discuss your distribution arrangements with Arthur.”

Kaze laughed softly.

He hadn't reached for anything. He'd wanted to see how quickly the generosity found a fence.

Dr. Evil straightened his cuffs.

“Clifford's gift remains Clifford's. This is not an open weapons counter.”

“Got it.”

Brian, who should have left with the others, chose that instant to help.

“It's like Busta. You don't have to explain why it's impressive.”

Dr. Evil closed his eyes.

Kaze started laughing again.

Later, when the arrivals had moved down the quay, Dr. Evil returned to the gangway with Brian at his heels.

“You will keep your enthusiasm,” he said.

Brian looked up, suspicious.

“But occasionally direct it toward the people actually providing your accommodation.”

“I can admire more than one person.”

The doctor stopped.

Brian stopped too.

For half a second neither of them improved the sentence.

Then Brian added, “Professionally.”

Dr. Evil looked down at him.

“Your next professional contribution will be a concise account of the meeting.”

Brian took out his notebook.

“Fine.”

“No lyrics.”

“I wasn't going to—”

“No guest appearances.”

Brian glared.

The doctor went aboard.

Brian stayed on the quay and wrote the heading.

Busta Rhymes Situation.

He looked at it.

Crossed it out.

Underneath he wrote: Initial Contact.

Then, smaller, where the rest of the page wouldn't have to know, he added: excellent presence.
