Season 3, Episode 48: “A Little Off the Top”

Brian had written excellent presence beneath Initial Contact.

Now he was trying to decide whether the words looked worse crossed out.

Dr. Evil stopped beside the crate.

“Finished?”

Brian covered the lower half of the page.

“Mostly.”

“An encouraging measurement.”

“It's an account of the meeting. Not a fucking weather report. There's interpretation involved.”

The doctor looked toward the harbor.

“The weather has shown considerable restraint about introducing Busta Rhymes.”

Brian moved his hand.

Dr. Evil took the sheet. Read the heading, the short account of the weapons, the proposed inquiry about the driver.

Then the little line at the bottom.

He paused.

Brian looked out at the water with the strained innocence of a man whose diary had developed witnesses.

“Whose presence?” the doctor asked.

“The overall meeting.”

“The meeting had excellent presence.”

“As an event.”

“I see.”

He folded the paper with the last line facing inward.

Brian watched it disappear.

“I was speaking professionally.”

“Then we have both had a very professional afternoon.”

Dr. Evil went aboard.

Brian remained beside the crate, furious that he'd neither received a compliment nor been given a clean reason to object.

Farther along the quay, Chris was looking at a notice nailed beside a warehouse door.

“Arthur.”

Arthur turned.

Chris pointed.

The paper had come from the district inland. A description of the ruined Golden Heron. A request for information about an armed group. Two names, acquired by different men on different roads and now occupying the same unpleasant square of paper.

Kaze.

Christopher Graham.

The description gave clothes, weapons and the places witnesses had seen them. Nothing to help a tallyman decide whether the men reading it were about to become his problem.

Chris read his name again.

“They got the spelling.”

Arthur came beside him.

“You signed it.”

“I know. Still. Standards.”

Billy's voice came from the banjo.

“A rare occasion on which your paperwork has traveled farther than your tip.”

Chris turned his head slightly, giving Billy the whole notice through the headlamp.

“They didn't serve the meal.”

“They are certainly serving something now.”

Kaze stopped behind them.

He read the account of the tollhouse. The broken barrier. The name he'd given the runner. His apparent claim about the land rupture was described as a claim, rather than a fact some district captain could prove by writing harder.

Kaze tapped that part.

“Apparent.”

Arthur looked at him.

“Leave it.”

“I told the motherfucker.”

“He wrote what he could establish.”

Kaze looked toward the warehouse door.

An adult tallyman stood just inside, watching them notice the notice.

His gaze traveled from the name on the paper to the name across Kaze's stomach.

The little book in his hands stopped moving.

Kaze smiled at him.

“See? Yours works.”

The tallyman said nothing.

Chris looked over his shoulder.

“You want a signature too?”

“Christopher,” Billy said.

“What?”

“You have demonstrated the difficulty with those.”

Daynuh came up with Mahnuh. The dog sniffed the lower edge of the warehouse door, where old fish water had soaked into the timber. Daynuh drew him back with a hand against his chest.

“That about us?”

“Some of us,” Arthur said.

Daynuh read the paper.

“Daynuh ain't even on it.”

“You can survive the disappointment,” Chris said.

“Was planning to.”

Kaze stepped closer to the tallyman.

The man backed up once, then stopped when the table touched his legs.

“Who put that up?”

“Post runner.”

“Where'd he go?”

“Harbor watch.”

Kaze looked down the quay.

Arthur moved into his sightline.

“We just came here to ask a question.”

“Asked it.”

“And now you want to make the answer somebody else's afternoon.”

Kaze's eyes returned to his face.

“Maybe I wanna hear what the watch has to say.”

“You heard it. It's nailed to a door.”

For a moment, the harbor continued around them without joining in.

Kaze looked past Arthur again.

The tallyman held his little book against his chest. He hadn't reached for a weapon. He hadn't shouted for help. He was trying to remain a man who had been counting rope before his work acquired a catastrophe.

Kaze looked back at the paper.

“You got a pencil?”

Arthur shut his eyes.

The tallyman offered one.

Kaze took it and drew one line beneath his own name.

Then another beneath apparent.

He gave the pencil back.

“Tell him I said it clearly.”

He walked away before the man could decide whether that counted as a message or a threat.

Chris watched him go.

“He's correcting his fucking wanted notice.”

“Request for information,” Arthur said.

“He's giving it notes.”

Billy plucked one low note through the banjo.

“The artist remains available for comment.”

At the Immortal Bastion, the report had arrived by a surviving military route with dust inside its folds.

The courier stood in a room that had lost one window and acquired three arguments about the cost of replacing it. He had changed mounts where he could, walked where he couldn't, and carried the district captain's packet around more than one place where a road had become an opinion.

Swain let him finish describing the route before asking about the contents.

“Who spoke to the man?”

“The runner, General. The tollkeeper heard him at the post.”

Swain read the name.

Kaze.

Darius stood at the other side of the table, his enormous axe resting within reach against the wall.

“He claims the rupture.”

“He does,” Swain said.

“Could be boasting.”

“It would be an ambitious choice of audience.”

The red fingers of Swain's left hand held the paper against a draft. His silver hair moved slightly as air came through the broken window.

The restaurant account lay beside it. Christopher Graham's signature had been copied from the surviving book. The constable's description distinguished dead staff and diners from the marksman beyond the canal. Two names acquired separately. Whatever had joined the men on the road, the paper gave Swain no account of it.

Swain put a finger beside the signature.

“The original?”

“Held at the district station.”

“Keep it there. Guard it. I want the man who found it available to answer questions.”

Darius read the account of the tollhouse occupation.

“The captain kept his men at the crossings.”

“Sensibly.”

“Some will call it retreat.”

Swain looked up.

“They may volunteer their own crossing to prove the distinction.”

The courier kept his face still.

Darius moved to the route map. Several roads carried new marks over old ink. A line drawn through a broken district did not become usable because a commander disliked the interruption.

“They've left the post,” he said.

“By the time this was written.”

“And by now they could be somewhere else entirely.”

Swain nodded.

“Then we shall avoid an impressive assault on an empty building.”

He called for an officer from the passage. Gave him the two names and the descriptions actually supported by the accounts.

“Question witnesses separately. Ask where they saw them, when, and doing what. No promises of pardon to improve a memory. No patrol sent into a contest it cannot report back from.”

The officer listened.

“Arrest on sight?”

“Observe first. If you can contain them without losing the district, contain them. If you cannot, tell me what would be required.”

Darius looked toward the courier.

“The first man who turns this into a chance to win a personal reputation will answer for the men he spends.”

The officer nodded and went to make the order travel.

It would take time. Horses, boots, surviving bridges. The empire had learned two names. It had not acquired the ability to stand beside them by saying them aloud.

Orra appeared in the doorway carrying a dirty length of survey cord.

“Your lower passage has a new problem.”

Swain folded the report.

“New since the rupture?”

“New since yesterday.”

That brought Darius away from the map.

They followed her below the repaired stair. Workers had shored the approach with timber. Lamps showed the old arch, the braced door and the iron fastening she'd ordered everyone to leave alone.

A soldier stood beside the entrance. He kept his hands where Orra could see them.

She showed Swain the end of the cord.

“I tied it across there.”

“It broke?”

“It was cut.”

The fibers ended cleanly. Not crushed beneath falling stone. Not pulled until the knot gave.

Darius turned toward the soldier.

“Who entered?”

“No one while I was here.”

“You weren't always here.”

The man swallowed.

“Relief was late. I went up for a lamp. Mine was failing.”

Orra lifted the old lamp from a stone shelf. Its reservoir was dry.

“That part's true.”

Darius held out his hand for the lamp.

Orra passed it to him.

“Who was your relief?”

The man gave a name.

“You'll tell the watch commander. He'll send for him. Both of you will give the times separately.”

“Yes, General.”

Darius put the empty lamp down.

“And the next man posted here gets a full one before he takes the stair.”

Orra looked at the soldier.

“Two,” she said. “Unless you want this conversation twice.”

Darius nodded once.

Swain looked past the broken cord.

“What moved?”

“The little plate below the fastening. A finger's width. There's fresh scraping beneath it.”

She crouched without touching the iron.

The door still stood where they'd braced it. The visible damage had not obligingly opened the entire secret. But somebody had used the gap in the watch, and had been more careful about leaving than entering.

Darius called two men from the stair.

One stayed with the soldier. The other took a lamp and stood where he could watch Orra's hands and the passage beyond her.

Swain lowered himself enough to examine the scraped stone.

Beyond the lamp's reach, the narrow gap disappeared into blackness. He kept his hands outside it.

“Can you remove the plate without shifting the support?”

Orra considered it.

“If your men stop trying to improve the answer with their fingers.”

“They will.”

She wedged the surrounding masonry, checked the load, and asked Darius to hold the outer bracket while she eased the loose plate away.

He took the weight with both hands. The metal moved only when she told him it could.

Behind the plate, a narrow recess ran into the newer ironwork.

Orra brought the lamp close.

An oily thumbprint marked the inside edge. Below it lay a short sliver of newly cut cord.

Someone had pushed the evidence out of sight, but had not pushed it far enough.

Swain watched her recover it with the tip of a small iron tool.

“The passage is being used,” Darius said.

“Part of it,” Swain answered.

He looked up toward the braced door.

“Leave the plate as it was.”

Orra turned.

“You want them to come back.”

“I want them to believe the same mistake remains available.”

Darius looked toward the soldier waiting at the stair.

“It won't.”

On the coast, Brian had found a mirror that could be tilted toward the edge of a crewman's desk.

He'd borrowed scissors. Asked for a razor. Been asked why.

“Presentation.”

The crewman had looked at his hair.

Then at the scissors.

“Do you want help?”

“I know what a haircut is.”

The man had left the razor in its case and gone back to work.

Brian now had the first lock between his fingers.

He stared at it.

He could still put the scissors down. There was no contract. Nobody had demanded a transformation. Dr. Evil had not asked for a smaller copy of himself.

That last fact irritated Brian enough to move his hand.

The scissors closed.

Hair fell onto the cloth he'd spread across his knees.

He looked in the mirror.

One side of his head had become an argument against stopping.

He cut the other.

Then the top.

He changed the mirror's angle, lifted his chin and found three different lengths competing to represent him.

“It's transitional,” he told the empty room.

The crewman returned for a spool of line.

Stopped at the desk.

Brian looked up.

The man looked back.

“Do you want help now?”

“I was getting to the finish.”

“I can see where you stopped.”

Brian put down the scissors.

The crewman fetched a second cloth and asked before moving the mirror. He used the scissors to shorten what Brian couldn't see properly, then worked with the razor while Brian held still.

It took longer than Brian wanted. The man's tools were ordinary human tools. The head beneath them was considerably smaller than the one he usually shaved.

“Don't make it uneven,” Brian said.

The crewman looked at the cloth full of Brian's first attempt.

“Doing my best.”

When it was finished, Brian leaned toward the mirror.

His face was still his face.

That was a relief he resented needing.

Above it, the bare scalp changed the whole outline. He turned left. Then right. Pulled his collar up, considered it, and left it where it had been before.

One change was enough to have to explain.

“Good,” he said.

The crewman began gathering his tools.

“Thank you,” Brian added, as though supplying a correction to the room.

“You're welcome.”

“Busta Rhymes would understand the commitment.”

The crewman looked at the scissors he was cleaning.

“Is that another barber?”

Brian stared at him.

“No.”

“Right.”

“That's such a small room to put him in.”

The man looked around the actual small room.

“I only work here.”

Brian considered explaining the full significance. The crewman had already begun folding the cloth, carefully trapping the cut hair inside it.

“Never mind.”

It felt less like restraint than having an important cultural conversation interrupted by somebody disposing of most of his former head.

Brian climbed down from the seat.

The seam beneath his shirt pulled once as he stretched. He put a hand over it until it settled, then straightened his jacket.

Nothing under the cloth had asked to admire Dr. Evil. Nothing there had promised to stop being hungry because Brian had changed his head.

He left the borrowed tools where the man wanted them and went to find his employer.

Dr. Evil sat at the briefing table with Dutch and Clifford. They were discussing which stores could be moved without interfering with the crew's work.

Brian stopped in the doorway.

Dutch saw him first.

His sentence lost its ending.

Clifford turned.

Then Dr. Evil looked up.

The room went quiet.

Brian put his notebook against his chest.

“What?”

Dr. Evil continued looking.

“Have we had an accident?”

“It's a haircut.”

The doctor looked toward Dutch.

“Was any of it recovered?”

Brian climbed onto his box beside the table.

“I decided to change my presentation.”

“To mine.”

“You don't own bald.”

Dr. Evil touched his own scalp with the mild interest of a landlord hearing somebody question the lease.

“No. But I have occupied it for some time.”

Clifford looked down at his hands.

Brian saw.

“You can say something.”

“Looks colder,” Clifford said.

Dutch shifted a paper over the corner of the ledger.

“A change can be a useful declaration of purpose.”

Brian pointed at him.

“Exactly.”

“Unfortunately,” Dr. Evil said, “we shall still have to hear the purpose.”

Brian's hand dropped.

The doctor went back to the stores list.

That was worse than the staring.

Brian opened his notebook.

“The public-facing impression matters. If people immediately understand you're serious, you don't spend the first ten minutes explaining the position.”

Dr. Evil glanced at the page.

“How many minutes have you budgeted for this?”

“Busta Rhymes understands reinvention.”

The doctor set the paper down.

“Did he take the rest of your hair?”

“I'm talking about committing to a direction.”

“You have certainly committed. We could hardly ask you to put it back before supper.”

Dutch's mouth tightened at one corner.

Brian turned toward him.

“You were just agreeing with me.”

“I agreed that a change could mean something.”

“It does.”

Dr. Evil folded his hands.

“Then I look forward to discovering what.”

Brian's little finger rose toward his mouth.

He saw the doctor's eyes follow it.

The finger stopped.

He lowered the hand onto the notebook instead.

For one long second, neither spoke.

Then Dr. Evil turned to Dutch.

“Continue.”

Dutch got through the next item before a crewman appeared carrying the recorder used for their earlier research.

Brian watched him cross the doorway.

“Actually. We could use that.”

Dr. Evil shut his eyes briefly.

“Could we.”

“A reference recording. Company presentation. We keep it here. See what works before anybody has to see it in person.”

“We've just had several people see it in person.”

“And now we can improve.”

The doctor opened his eyes.

“Whose presentation?”

“The company.”

“With me.”

Brian paused.

“Yes.”

“Well. There may be something to it.”

The crewman looked at Dutch. Dutch looked at the small patch of table still available between the papers.

“Nothing leaves this room,” Dutch said.

“It hasn't even entered the fucking recorder,” Brian said.

The crewman set the device down and checked its remaining space. Then he asked where they wanted him to stand.

Dr. Evil settled back in his chair.

Brian stood on his box.

The crewman lowered the recorder until both heads were in view.

Dr. Evil examined the angle.

“Why are you interviewing my chin?”

The man raised it.

Brian vanished below the frame.

“I'm still here,” Brian said.

“We had all hoped otherwise,” Dr. Evil said.

Brian pointed at the table.

“I could stand there.”

“Food goes there.”

“Not now.”

“I prefer to preserve the possibility.”

Dutch moved Brian's box farther from the chair. The crewman stepped back. Both men now fit without placing Brian among the stores lists or giving Dr. Evil the looming perspective of a disappointed dentist.

“There,” Dutch said.

Brian inspected the distance.

“We look separate.”

Dr. Evil smiled.

“Technology is extraordinary.”

The crewman started recording.

Dr. Evil put one hand on the chair arm.

“Tampon Pandemic Productions represents an opportunity—”

“Founded by Brian.”

The doctor stopped.

The crewman stopped recording.

Dr. Evil turned his head very slowly.

“Were you planning to interrupt with the entire birth certificate?”

“I founded it.”

“Then you have had your moment. Some of us are attempting to provide it with a future.”

Brian folded his arms.

Dutch set down his pencil.

“Let him finish the opening. Then introduce yourself.”

“As founder.”

“Yes, Brian.”

Clifford shifted his chair out of the background without being asked.

They started again.

The doctor delivered his opening. Brian waited through it, watching him hold the little room's attention without raising his voice. The pause at the end was so complete Brian nearly missed it.

Then he straightened.

“I'm Brian. Founder. I handle the creative direction and music.”

His mouth remained open for one perilous extra second.

Somewhere behind his teeth, Busta Rhymes was approaching an intersection at speed.

Brian closed his mouth.

The crewman stopped the recording.

“That's usable,” Dutch said.

Brian looked at him.

“Yes. It is.”

They gathered around the recorder's small viewing screen. The crewman played back what they'd just made.

On it, Dr. Evil sat motionless and bald. Brian stood beside him, also bald, looking up at the doctor before remembering to look toward the lens.

Nobody spoke.

Brian pointed.

“Take out that bit.”

“Which bit?” the crewman asked.

“Before I speak.”

Dr. Evil leaned closer.

“Oh, I think we should keep the respect.”

“I'm checking the cue.”

“A wonderfully attentive check.”

Clifford looked over Dutch's shoulder.

“Good picture.”

Brian turned.

“For what?”

“Evidence.”

The doctor laughed once. Brian looked back at the tiny image of himself looking up.

“It's a height issue.”

“Several,” Dr. Evil said.

The crewman stopped playback and put the recorder away. Brian watched the screen go dark. He wanted to see it again, preferably when fewer people were standing behind him, and couldn't think of a way to ask that wouldn't give the doctor the rest of his afternoon.

Brian sat down on the box.

He hated the man.

He had also spent the afternoon making it more difficult to explain how much.

Above the harbor, the Sins took the road out before the watch had decided whether the tallyman's message needed an escort.

They had gathered their own gear, filled their water from an accessible public trough, and left the notice nailed where it was. Arthur retained the map and the wrapped saber. Chris remained exterior. Billy watched the harbor diminish through the headlamp when Chris looked back.

“Upper works?” Chris asked.

Arthur nodded.

“Find the driver while there's still a driver to find.”

“And then?” Chris asked.

Kaze turned.

“Then we hear what he says.”

“I'm asking whether we're walking to a place or just away from another one.”

“You can stay.”

“I know. That's why I'm asking before I walk.”

Arthur spread the map against a low wall. The quay lay behind them. Ahead, the road divided around a drainage cut before joining the surviving inland route.

Kaze looked at the two lines.

“I wanna know what Maul asked him. Exactly. Where he came from before he went looking for me.”

“Might not tell us how to get home,” Arthur said.

“Might not.”

“Might tell us nothing.”

“Then I'll know that motherfucker knows nothing.”

Chris adjusted the banjo strap.

Billy spoke near his ear.

“A limited undertaking. How refreshing.”

“You coming, then?” Chris asked.

“I retain the pleasure of declining the next road.”

Kaze looked at the headlamp.

“You always sound like you're about to eat the person you agree with?”

“Not always.”

“Comforting,” Chris said.

Daynuh watched Mahnuh investigate the edge of the drainage cut. He called the dog back before looking at the map.

“Which side ain't gonna put us in that?”

Arthur pointed to the broader branch.

“This one. We keep above it.”

“All right, then.”

Arthur folded the map. One question for a driver did not make every road beyond him an agreement. Chris waited until the map was put away, then chose the broader branch himself.

Kaze walked ahead of them, looking toward the damaged country.

Daynuh waited until Mahnuh had finished sniffing a wheel rut, then called him on.

Behind them, a watch officer stood in the warehouse doorway while the tallyman described the tattooed visitor and the two lines he'd added.

“He threatened you?”

“He gave the pencil back.”

The officer waited.

“I don't know what that means,” the tallyman said.

Neither did the officer yet.

He looked at the underlined name.

Then sent a man to see which road they had taken.

On the submarine, the stores discussion had moved on without Brian's permission.

He made himself take notes.

Dr. Evil asked for a figure. Brian gave the one written on the page, clearly, without attaching a musical comparison.

The doctor looked at him.

“Thank you.”

Brian's shoulders changed by a small amount.

Dr. Evil waited until he had felt it.

“We should have removed the hair earlier.”

Brian closed the notebook.

“It's not where I keep the information.”

The doctor looked at the closed cover.

“Apparently neither is that.”

Brian opened it again.

Season 3, Episode 49: “Public Facing”

“Don't step on that.”

Kaze looked down at the plank across the roadside drain.

Then at Daynuh.

“It'll hold me.”

“I know. It'll also snap, tip that stone into the ditch and leave a hole for the next wagon. You get to be right and everybody else gets a fucked axle. Wonderful arrangement.”

Kaze put one foot on the stone beside it instead.

“You always got something to say about a board.”

“Boards generally listen.”

Chris stopped behind them, the banjo hanging at his belt. Billy was inside, watching through the headlamp.

“Could take it,” Chris said.

Daynuh bent, examined the split end and turned the plank over.

“Could. Good piece above the crack.”

Kaze looked at him.

“You just said leave it.”

“Said don't step on it. Different conversation.”

Chris nodded gravely.

“Important distinction.”

“You ain't taking the fucking bridge.”

“Now it's a bridge,” Chris said. “He thought it was a board till we showed interest.”

Arthur stopped at the low wall with the map still folded. The harbor lay below them, close enough to see men moving between warehouses. The inland road climbed away beyond the drain. They had barely begun the return toward the upper works.

Daynuh settled the plank back on its supports, sound side uppermost.

“There. Still a bad idea. Now it's a bad idea somebody can cross.”

Chris inspected the pale, protected underside.

“Could make a shelf.”

Daynuh looked toward Kaze without turning his head.

“Two shelves.”

Kaze smiled slowly.

“You enjoy this shit.”

“Yeah. Took you long enough.”

“You gonna give him shit when he's got half a house in there?” Kaze asked.

Daynuh looked at Chris.

“Depends. Good half?”

“Useful things,” Chris said.

“That's what people say before they show you seven broken wheels and a door that goes nowhere. But if he's got good hinges, I'm interested.”

“See?” Chris said.

Daynuh pointed at him.

“Didn't finish. If you bring me a whole fucking church because you like the hinges, we're having another conversation.”

Billy spoke through the banjo.

“Architecture deserves to be appreciated in context.”

Daynuh slowly turned back toward Kaze.

“There's your real problem. One of them collects. The other one can eat the neighborhood.”

“And you encourage both.”

“I like hinges.”

Mahnuh stepped across on the stones. Daynuh scratched his shoulder when he reached the other side.

The man following them from the harbor stopped below the culvert.

Arthur had seen him coming. So had Kaze. Neither had mistaken his repeated interest in the same patch of road for expert concealment.

“You lost?” Arthur asked.

The man wore the harbor watch's short coat. His eyes moved to Kaze's stomach and stayed there long enough to establish that his assignment had become unpleasantly easy.

“My officer wants to speak with you.”

Kaze stepped toward him.

“Which you?”

The watchman swallowed.

“Kaze.”

“Here I am.”

“At the station.”

“Here I am,” Kaze repeated.

The watchman looked past him at Daynuh, then at Arthur's hands, then at Chris.

“I'll tell him.”

He turned back downhill at a walk that became a jog once he had something between himself and the tattooed name.

Daynuh watched him go.

“We waiting?”

“He wants to ask me something.”

“Everybody wants to ask you something. Usually it's why the fuck their house is over there now.”

Kaze leaned against the wall.

“Could be interesting.”

“Could be a man doing a job.”

“That too.”

Daynuh considered the space beside him, then sat on a sound stretch of stone.

“All right. But if this turns into you arguing with a uniform till sunset, I'm eating before you finish.”

Down at the quay, Brian was attempting to accompany a crewman's stores inquiry without looking like something the man had brought to compare against a bolt.

The warehouse keeper leaned over his counter.

“That one yours?”

“I represent the company,” Brian said.

“I asked him.”

The crewman inspected the folded canvas he'd come to price.

“He's with us.”

“Founder,” Brian added.

The keeper looked at his bare scalp.

“Was it a hard winter?”

Brian put his notebook on the lowest accessible corner of the counter.

“It's deliberate.”

“Must be. Nothing grazed it that evenly.”

The crewman turned his face into the canvas.

Brian heard the breath escape.

“We are evaluating suppliers. A professional impression would help.”

“Then let him evaluate,” the keeper said. “He knows which end of the canvas is canvas.”

Outside, the watchman passed the open door on his way to fetch his officer. Brian recognized the name he gave the man waiting by the warehouse.

Kaze.

Brian went still.

Then looked up the road.

From the quay he could see the enormous seated shape beside the culvert, the standing men and the small dog.

He picked up his notebook.

“I'll be back.”

The crewman lowered the canvas.

“We're only getting a price.”

“I'm developing an opportunity.”

“Don't develop one in my name.”

Brian went uphill under his own power, already arranging the encounter into something he could report as initiative.

Inside BELLY, Charles Manson had come to his own communication station because the exterior feed showed uniforms approaching a conversation.

He liked conversations where somebody believed the wrong person was in charge.

Master Shake stood beside him, yellow hands planted against his white cup.

“We should be outside for this.”

Meatwad rolled closer.

“I wanna go outside anyway.”

“Exactly,” Shake said. “Public representation. I have been saying this.”

“I wanna see if the sky still looks like that.”

“That is not what I have been saying.”

Charles leaned toward the station's outward channel.

“Billy. You got people out there saying who people are. I'd like to stand there when they say it.”

His voice came through the banjo at Chris's belt.

Chris looked down.

“You can already talk.”

“Talking ain't standing. You're standing. You tell me they're the same.”

Shake crowded him.

“I require an appearance.”

Daynuh looked toward Chris.

“That another one?”

Chris stared at the banjo.

“That's the milkshake.”

“Still got the milkshake.”

“Yeah.”

“And the meat.”

“Right here,” Meatwad said through Charles's station.

Daynuh rubbed his chin.

“You got a whole fucking lunch arguing in there.”

Billy's voice followed, pleasantly deliberate.

“I have heard the requests.”

Chris tilted his head.

“You want them out?”

“I would enjoy seeing what they do with the privilege.”

“That's a terrible reason.”

“You keep bringing home things for less.”

Chris looked at the plank.

Daynuh looked at him looking.

“Don't put that on the board,” Chris said.

They changed places. Billy became the sole exterior body beside the wall; Chris arrived full-sized inside his home, where Frylock was waiting near the lounge.

“You're letting Shake speak to officials?” Frylock asked.

“Billy is.”

“That distinction won't help.”

“I know. I enjoy having it.”

Outside, Billy moved to a level patch off the road and opened his enormous mouth. His release choice brought Charles through first. Boots found the stone. Charles straightened, looked around and breathed deeply.

Meatwad came next, rolling clear of the teeth onto the dry verge.

Shake followed with both hands raised.

“Do not wipe me on anything. I am not the wiping thing.”

Billy shut his mouth.

Three residents stood outside. No prisoner had followed them. Inside, Chris watched the same road through the live monitor, with Frylock beside him.

There we go. The Seven Sins' public image now included a milkshake arriving through a giant fish's mouth while disputing his classification as a wet wipe. I have worn a red suit through some medically indefensible afternoons, and even I know when the branding department should crawl into the sea.

Meatwad looked up.

“Yeah. That's the sky.”

He sounded pleased.

Brian reached the culvert just as Shake turned toward Kaze.

“Before anyone speaks, I will handle the public.”

Kaze stared at him.

“Who the fuck elected you?”

“Master Shake requires no election.”

“Master of what?”

“That is the complete name.”

Daynuh leaned forward.

“If the second half's a warning, I appreciate it.”

Brian stopped beside the wall.

Chris's laugh came out of the banjo.

Then stopped.

“Oh, Brian. Buddy. What happened?”

Kaze looked down.

His smile arrived in pieces.

“No fucking way.”

Brian held the notebook against his side.

“I changed my appearance.”

“To the doctor,” Kaze said.

“Independently.”

Daynuh studied him with the interest he'd given the split plank.

Brian saw the comparison happening and hated it before the man spoke.

“Well?”

“I'm looking for where the rest screws on.”

“I'm a person.”

“Didn't say you weren't. You came up here looking like a knob somebody took off a serious man.”

Charles bent slightly, smiling.

“You want us looking at your head or listening to you?”

“Both would be customary.”

“Then say something. Head's finished.”

Brian opened the notebook.

“I thought there might be value in a coordinated public position.”

Arthur looked downhill.

The watch officer was coming up with the original watchman. No line of soldiers followed them.

“Here comes the public,” Arthur said.

Brian straightened.

Shake stepped in front of him.

“Good. You may announce me.”

“I don't work for you.”

“I assumed you were a promotional item.”

“I'm the founder of Tampon Pandemic Productions.”

Shake turned toward the approaching officer.

“He's not with us.”

Kaze looked at the milkshake.

“Neither are you.”

The officer stopped at the edge of the level ground.

He had come prepared to speak to armed men. He took in Billy's immense teeth, Daynuh's size, Kaze's tattoos and Arthur's quiet attention.

Then Charles.

Then the talking cup attempting to stand at the front.

His preparation died without leaving a forwarding address.

“Kaze?”

Kaze lifted one hand.

“You got my message.”

“The tallyman gave it.”

“Clearly?”

“With the pencil marks.”

The officer held his gaze.

“He says you returned the pencil.”

“Want it back?”

“I want to know whether your message was a threat to my station.”

The absurdity around them didn't make the question less serious. The man kept enough room between himself and Kaze to draw a weapon, though nothing in his expression suggested he mistook that for a solution.

Kaze's smile thinned.

“If I wanted your station gone, why would I borrow a fucking pencil?”

“People warn.”

“Do I look like people?”

Meatwad rolled into the gap beside him.

“A little.”

Kaze looked down.

Meatwad looked up.

“Mostly the legs.”

For one extraordinary second, nobody helped.

Daynuh pressed his lips together. Arthur looked at the road. From the banjo came one small, betrayed sound from Chris.

Kaze pointed at Meatwad.

“I'm trying to do something.”

“Oh. Okay.”

Meatwad moved two feet to the left and watched him do it.

The officer waited until Kaze looked back.

“You claimed responsibility for the rupture.”

“Yeah.”

“And the tollhouse.”

“Yeah.”

“Christopher Graham?”

Chris answered through the banjo.

“Depends who's asking.”

The officer's eyes moved to Billy.

Billy smiled without explaining his interior.

“I'm the man asking,” the officer said.

“Then yeah.”

The officer took a breath.

Charles stepped closer to the wall.

“You asking because you don't know, or asking because you want them saying it in front of you?”

“Who are you?”

“Charles.”

“Are you part of this group?”

“I live with people. You live with people. That make you responsible for their socks?”

“Charles,” Billy said.

He looked back at the fish.

“You wanted fresh air.”

Charles opened his hands and took another conspicuous breath.

Shake immediately occupied the silence.

“I can clarify the hierarchy.”

“No,” Kaze said.

Shake occupied the next silence more quietly.

The officer looked back at Kaze.

“I can't answer a district report by pretending I didn't find you.”

“Then don't.”

“Where are you going?”

Arthur's eyes lifted.

Kaze stayed against the wall.

“Somewhere else.”

“Which road?”

“The one I fucking pick.”

The officer nodded once. Not agreement. Acknowledgment that he'd received the answer he was going to get.

“Who sent the report?” Kaze asked.

“District command.”

“Who do they answer to?”

“Noxian command.”

“A name.”

The officer considered him.

“Grand General Swain.”

Kaze repeated the name softly.

Then smiled again.

“Tell him he can ask me himself.”

“I'll report what you said.”

“There you go.”

Brian stepped forward.

“A distinction may be useful here.”

Everyone looked down.

He had wanted everyone looking at him. The physical experience contained several drawbacks.

“Our company has no operational responsibility for these incidents.”

Arthur looked at him.

“You walked up here to say that?”

“Clarity matters.”

“It did,” the officer said. “Till you came.”

Brian's jaw set.

“I'm identifying an independent commercial interest.”

“Then identify it somewhere else. I'm speaking to him.”

Shake pointed at Brian.

“I've been trying to establish that for minutes.”

“You just offered to clarify their hierarchy.”

“As a courtesy. I am extremely generous with information.”

From inside, Frylock's voice reached Chris rather than the road.

“Shake's going to get himself arrested.”

Chris leaned toward the outward channel.

“Shake. Ask him if the cell has seating.”

Shake turned toward Billy.

“I know what you're doing.”

“Then you're ahead of everybody out here.”

Brian put himself between the cup and the officer's sightline.

“I can help organize a conversation that doesn't become this.”

The officer looked at him for a long moment.

“Were you in the restaurant?”

“No.”

“The tollhouse?”

“No.”

“Did you see the rupture happen?”

“No.”

“Then all you've added is another person I'll have to describe.”

Brian looked at the watchman's little writing book.

The man had opened it.

“I haven't done anything.”

“I'm aware,” the officer said.

Daynuh's laugh finally escaped.

It wasn't delicate.

Brian turned on him.

“At least I'm attempting to contribute.”

Daynuh leaned forward, elbows on his knees.

“You want a contribution? Quit lifting your chin like you're waiting for somebody to hang a price tag under it. He asked about a crime. You came in advertising yourself. Now he's got to remember which bald head was talking and why the cup says it's your supervisor.”

“I never said supervisor,” Shake said.

“You fucking radiate supervisor. All mouth, no legs, arrive after the work and demand a better place to stand.”

Chris made an appreciative noise through the banjo.

Shake looked around for a different audience.

Brian looked at Daynuh again.

“Busta Rhymes could command this entire conversation without—”

“Then fetch him,” Daynuh said. “Quit sending the travel-size fucking introduction.”

Brian shut his mouth.

Meatwad came closer.

“I like your head.”

Brian looked down at him.

“Thank you.”

“Makes you look like you got plans.”

Brian's shoulders lifted.

“I do.”

“I don't think they're working, but I can tell you got 'em.”

The watchman covered his mouth with the back of his writing hand.

The officer didn't.

That was somehow worse.

He closed the conversation himself.

“I've heard you. I'll send the account. I won't promise what follows it.”

Kaze stepped away from the wall.

“Didn't ask you to.”

The officer held his ground while Kaze passed him. Only after the tattooed back had turned did he look again at the three residents standing beside Billy.

“And you?”

Shake raised one yellow hand.

Charles said, “Taking a walk.”

Meatwad looked at Shake until the hand came down.

“Same,” Shake said.

The officer went back toward the harbor with his watchman. His account would have witnesses, admissions and several descriptions he would have preferred to acquire on a different day.

It would not include the Sins' destination. Arthur had kept the map folded.

Shake watched the officer disappear below the bend.

Then turned to Brian.

“Now. What can your company offer?”

Brian lowered his notebook.

“You just told him I wasn't with you.”

“Publicly. I maintain a private sector.”

Charles laughed through his nose.

“He means he wants something.”

“I can negotiate for myself.”

“Then do that. Don't bring a sector into it.”

Brian considered Shake. A talking milkshake had drawn immediate attention without having to explain why he deserved it. That observation annoyed him. It also interested him professionally.

“Do you perform?”

Shake spread his hands.

“You've seen the range.”

“I've seen you interrupt the police.”

“Nobody interrupted me back. That's stage presence.”

Charles turned toward Billy.

“You hear this? We go outside once, he starts selling the air.”

“You've been breathing an awful lot of it,” Shake said.

Billy settled his great weight comfortably beside the wall.

“Continue. I am fascinated by the economy.”

Meatwad had found a smooth stone in the dry verge. He pushed it toward Brian.

“This one could perform.”

Brian stared at it.

“It's a rock.”

“He don't interrupt.”

“Then he's ahead,” Charles said.

Meatwad positioned the stone upright. It fell over. He turned it onto a flatter edge and tried again.

“There. That's his face.”

Brian looked at Shake.

“I mean a repeatable act. Something with an introduction, a structure, a finish.”

“I enter. They respond. I receive compensation.”

“That's not an act.”

“That's because you're describing it without my name.”

Chris leaned toward his outward channel inside BELLY.

“Ask what the rock charges.”

“He ain't decided,” Meatwad said. “He's new.”

Brian rubbed his forehead.

“I'm trying to work.”

Charles crouched on the other side of the stone.

“Then work. You asked what he does. He said take money. You know more now than when you asked.”

Brian looked at him.

“You have an opinion on everything.”

“You keep giving it a place to sit.”

Shake leaned across Charles.

“My appearance fee must include transport.”

Billy's smile showed a little more tooth.

“Discuss that item carefully.”

“Naturally. I retain control of my travel arrangements.”

“You asked me to let you out.”

“And successfully negotiated it.”

Brian almost smiled.

Shake saw.

“Don't do that. You look like someone polished a grudge.”

Brian's expression shut.

“Your entire negotiating position is that people look at you.”

“Yes.”

“That isn't sufficient.”

“You removed your hair to improve it.”

Charles laughed properly this time. Brian turned his notebook sideways against his chest, hiding the blank page from nobody in particular.

Meatwad pushed his stone into the center again.

“You can both look at him.”

“I'm not competing with a fucking stone.”

“Good,” Meatwad said. “He don't need that pressure.”

Brian looked at the small round creature guarding his new possession.

“What's his name?”

“Death Mountain.”

Charles examined the pebble.

“That's a lot of name.”

“He can grow into it.”

“No,” Brian said. “He can't.”

Meatwad turned toward him slowly.

“You don't know his life.”

Billy laughed. Brian had to wait for him to finish.

Brian's grip tightened on his notebook.

“Busta Rhymes would understand building an identity before an audience understands the ambition.”

Charles looked between him and the stone.

“Which one you talking about?”

Brian glanced down.

Death Mountain lay at his feet, bald, silent and apparently ahead on audience engagement.

“Neither.”

Shake lifted one hand.

“If we are discussing representation, I own the mountain.”

Meatwad immediately moved the stone behind himself.

“No you don't.”

“I discovered the commercial possibility.”

“I found him in the dirt.”

“That was pre-commercial.”

Brian shut his notebook.

“You don't own something because you announced it loudly while somebody else was holding it.”

Meatwad looked pleased.

“Yeah.”

Charles pointed at Brian.

“There. That sounded like you knew what you wanted.”

“I do know.”

“Then why'd we need the other man's name and his haircut to get there?”

Brian stared at him.

“Those are two different men.”

“You in there anywhere?”

Brian stepped closer.

“I built my own company. I make the music. I don't need a cup taking credit for someone else's work just because he can make a room worse by entering it.”

Shake lifted his chin.

“So you have seen the range.”

Brian considered answering.

Then deliberately turned his back on him.

Behind it, Meatwad rolled the stone toward Billy, pushing patiently when it caught against a crack. Charles watched Brian's back with a small, satisfied smile. He'd obtained an argument, fresh air and a new person who regretted speaking to him. A productive outing.

Brian looked back toward the harbor.

“This was an opportunity.”

Charles stood beside him.

“You keep saying what it was. You were right here. Why didn't you make it that?”

“Because everyone interrupted.”

“Everybody's everybody. You waiting for everybody to sit down before you stand up?”

Brian stared at him.

Charles smiled, then looked toward Billy.

“I'm done walking.”

“You stood there,” Chris said through the banjo.

“I was free to walk. That's different.”

Meatwad rolled beside the fish.

“Wind keeps sticking things on me.”

A little grit had gathered along one side of him. He regarded it with annoyance rather than tragedy.

Shake looked downhill toward the harbor, then uphill at Kaze waiting farther along the road.

“I will return to the interior office.”

“The couch?” Chris asked.

“You call it what you need to.”

Billy allowed them back through his mouth, one after another, into the same living domain. Meatwad went willingly, with Billy taking Death Mountain in alongside him. Charles paused only to get a last look at the harbor. Shake insisted on entering last, then complained about the delay he had created.

Frylock watched him arrive beside the lounge.

“How was the public?”

“Unqualified.”

Chris laughed and stayed inside. Billy remained exterior, following the others onto the inland branch. The road to the upper works still had to be traveled; a watch interview hadn't moved the driver an inch closer.

Daynuh caught up with Kaze.

“Swain.”

“Yeah.”

“You got another name to aggravate now.”

Kaze looked at him.

“You were laughing.”

“At the small one. You ain't taking credit for that haircut.”

Kaze looked back down the road.

Brian stood alone at the culvert, notebook open.

For once, he hadn't written anything.

By the time he returned to the submarine, Dr. Evil had heard from the crewman that Brian had abandoned a canvas inquiry to pursue an opportunity.

The doctor waited beside the briefing table.

“Developed?”

Brian put down his notebook.

“There was a discussion with the watch.”

Dutch looked up.

“About us?”

“I clarified that we weren't involved.”

“Were they asking?”

Brian paused.

Clifford lowered the paper in his hands.

“They are now.”

Dr. Evil held out one hand for the notebook.

Brian kept it.

“I can give the account myself.”

The doctor considered that. Then sat down.

“Very well.”

Brian opened to a clean page. Began with the officer, the two names and the actual questions. Got through the invitation to Swain without trying to turn it into a transport analogy.

Dutch listened carefully.

“And you gave our name?”

“Yes.”

“For no reason they required.”

“To establish independence.”

Dr. Evil touched one finger to his lip.

Brian's own hand twitched.

He pinned it against the notebook.

“They understand I wasn't in command.”

The doctor smiled.

“Finally. A witness we can trust.”
